https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.64898.title: Linking clinical border morphology to cell-scale growth mechanisms in melanoma: a segmentation-to-simulation alignment study
https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.64898.abstract: An irregular border is among the most informative visual cues for melanoma, yet the prevailing quantitative treatment of that irregularity, the box-counting fractal dimension, has rarely been connected to the cell-scale mechanism that produces it. We measured seven boundary descriptors on 1,581 lesions from the 2018 International Skin Imaging Collaboration archive segmented by an automatic thresholding route, retaining the expert ground-truth route as a sensitivity arm, and compared their medians across benign, in situ, and invasive grades. We then built a hybrid cellular automaton and swept four canonical cell-level mechanisms, scoring every simulated boundary with the same measurement code used on the patient images, before testing two mechanisms that lift the empty-neighbour division rule and aligning them to the observed malignant signature with a variance-based sensitivity analysis. The malignant signature is lobulation, not roughness: compactness rises from 1.351 to 1.810, solidity falls from 0.910 to 0.853, and convexity falls from 0.936 to 0.839 from benign to invasive lesions, with areas under the curve near 0.74, while the fractal dimension varies by only 0.024 across the three grades. All four canonical mechanisms, including loss of contact inhibition, converge on near-circular clusters at a distance of 1.147 to 1.166 from the malignant target. A long-range spatial heterogeneity in the growth rate, by contrast, reproduces the observed signature to a distance of 0.187, with the correlation length of the field, not its amplitude, the dominant parameter by total-effect index. A smooth, long-range growth-rate field is therefore sufficient to generate the lobular borders that characterise invasive melanoma, whereas the empty-neighbour assumption common to cellular automata is not. Because the winning field is imposed rather than emergent, the study resolves the alignment between border morphology and cell-scale mechanism while leaving open how such heterogeneity could arise from cell-autonomous dynamics.

https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.64898.title: Quantifying subcellular organization from localization to co-occurrence with InSpace
https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.64898.abstract: Cell identity and function depend not only on molecular abundance, but also on how molecules are organized within cells. Although spatial transcriptomics now resolves individual RNA molecules within cells, routine computational workflows reduce these measurements to cell-by-gene count matrices, retaining abundance while discarding information about intracellular localization and molecular co-occurrence. This loss of spatial information creates a need for scalable methods that preserve subcellular detail and enable comparisons across diverse cellular morphologies. Therefore, we present InSpace, a scalable framework for quantifying these complementary dimensions of subcellular organization. InSpace-R maps transcripts onto a continuous radial coordinate anchored to nuclear and cell boundaries, while InSpace-C measures distance-dependent co-occurrence or depletion of molecular pairs. Simulations and orthogonal biochemical references support accurate measurements, with scalability demonstrated on datasets containing 275 million transcripts. RNA-RNA and RNA-DNA analyses recover organelle-linked neighbourhoods and associations between nascent transcripts and their genomic origins. Analysis of B and plasma cells across 58 tumour datasets spanning 12 cancer types reveals that reduced MHC-II transcript abundance accompanies more peripheral localization and stronger mutual co-occurrence, separating these transcripts from a program enriched for ER-targeted proteins. InSpace makes intracellular organization accessible alongside abundance, enabling discovery of spatial programs that distinguish cellular states and generate hypotheses about their functional specialization.

https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.64898.title: Megakaryocytic proteomic signatures define myeloproliferative neoplasms
https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.64898.abstract: The classical Philadelphia-negative myeloproliferative neoplasms (MPNs) are clonal stem cell disorders of the bone marrow with significant niche dysregulation driven in part by abnormal megakaryocytes. The three classical MPNs: polycythemia vera (PV), essential thrombocythemia (ET) and primary myelofibrosis (PMF), display established megakaryocytic morphological differences which aid in their diagnostic classification. The paucity of megakaryocytes in the bone marrow aspirate has previously limited a proteomic analysis of megakaryocytes in clinical samples. We aimed to undertake an unbiased proteomic analysis of in situ megakaryocytes from the bone marrow of patients with PV, ET, and PMF. Using a novel, deep visual proteomics strategy, we dissected and analyzed megakaryocytes from 60 MPN patients and 20 controls (patients with limited stage non-Hodgkin lymphoma who had uninvolved bone marrow). We reveal that megakaryocyte proteomics from MPN patients are distinct to those from control patients, and further, that the megakaryocytes from the three MPNs have unique, disease-specific signatures. The disease-specific megakaryocyte proteome highlights novel pathways of disease.

https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.64898.title: APR-246 and DNA polymerase theta inhibitor Novobiocinsynergize to eliminate TP53 mutant AML cells
https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.64898.abstract: Patients with TP53-mutant myelodysplasic syndromes (MDS) and acute myeloid leukemia (AML) are usually elderly and frail with highly resistant malignant clones and a median survival of less than one year. The molecule APR-246 targets mutant p53 but also perturbs redox homeostasis. APR-246 showed favorable safety in a phase 3 trial in TP53 mutant MDS/AML but did not meet efficacy endpoints in combination with azacitidine (AZA), highlighting the need for more effective combination strategies. Conversion of APR-246 to the active compound MQ releases formaldehyde which generates DNA-protein crosslinks. AML cells depend on DNA polymerase theta (Pol[O]) to repair such lesions and Pol[O] protects cells from ferroptosis. Using a panel of isogenic MOLM13 AML cell lines each carrying a common TP53 variant, we show that the Pol[O] inhibitor Novobiocin (NVB) synergizes with APR-246 to induce AML cell death. We demonstrate strong synergy with this combination in all TP53 mutant cell lines and to a lesser extent in the TP53 wildtype and null cells, indicating both p53-dependent and p53-independent mechanisms behind the synergy. APR-246 provides selectivity for TP53-mutated cells while NVB enhances p53-independent apoptosis and p53-dependent ferroptosis. Levels of ferroptosis induction correlate with the observed synergy in TP53-mutant and WT cells. Combination of APR-246 and NVB induces potent in vitro growth inhibition of primary TP53-mutated AML/CMML patient samples, with significant activity achieved at low micromolar or nanomolar concentrations of APR-246. Our findings hold promise for combination of APR-246 and NVB as a new therapeutic strategy tailored for TP53-mutated AML patients with high efficacy and low toxicity.

https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.64898.title: TROP2 and immune gene expression by African ancestry in triple-negative breast cancer
https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.64898.abstract: Purpose: TROP2 is a treatment target in triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC). TACSTD2 encodes TROP2, while PDCD1 encodes the immune protein PD-1. We investigated whether these genes differ by race or African genetic ancestry and whether the reported link between higher TACSTD2 and lower immune-gene expression partly reflects the mixture of cells in tumor samples. Methods: We analyzed TNBC tumors from TCGA (n = 107) and GSE268851 (n = 253; ancestry data for 229), together with spatial, normal-breast, and protein datasets. Regression models adjusted for age, tumor stage, and a score based on epithelial gene expression. We compared TACSTD2 with other epithelial markers using paired bootstrap analysis. Results: TACSTD2 was detected in nearly all tumors, with no significant differences by race or ancestry. Higher African ancestry was linked to higher PDCD1 expression in TCGA (P = 0.00039), but not in GSE268851. In GSE268851, higher TACSTD2 remained associated with lower CD8A, GZMB, and cytotoxic score after epithelial adjustment (all q < 0.003). These associations were stronger than those for EPCAM; the CD8A association was also stronger than that for KRT8. TACSTD2 was 1.55-fold higher in TNBC than in normal breast and correlated with TROP2 protein (Spearman rho = 0.74). Conclusion: TACSTD2 was widely expressed in the TNBC groups studied, while the ancestry-PDCD1 association differed between cohorts. Epithelial gene expression did not fully explain some negative TACSTD2-immune associations, and some were stronger than those for other epithelial markers such as EPCAM.

https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.64898.title: Age-based shifts in multicellular community organization and abundance in HPV-Negative Head and Neck Cancer
https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.64898.abstract: Aging represents a fundamental driver of cancer risk and progression, yet the mechanisms by which aging reshapes the tumor microenvironment remain incompletely understood. To interrogate how aging alters cellular and microenvironmental organization in cancer, we developed an integrated single-cell atlas of HPV-negative head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC) encompassing 73 patients aged 18-91 years. Using a multi-layered computational framework combining NMF-based module discovery and partial correlation network analysis, we reveal that age-associated differences in tumor composition are driven primarily by selective shifts in cell type abundance and organization rather than widespread age-dependent transcriptional rewiring. We identify an age-enriched cellular community centered on basal-like squamous epithelial states linked to epithelial-mesenchymal transition, matrix-associated myofibroblast-like CAFs, and FOLR2+ macrophages, which secrete immunosuppressive and ECM-remodeling factors. Cross-dataset in-silico validation via TCGA transcriptomes, spatial transcriptomics, and mouse tumor models confirms the correlation of these cell types across patients, specific ligand-receptor usage, and increased proportions of epithelial and stromal cells in aged mouse models. Among epithelial cell-intrinsic age-associated transcriptional changes, midkine (MDK) emerges as a rare but robust tumor-derived signal linked to stromal remodeling, immunosuppression, and invasive epithelial programs. These findings reveal conserved mechanisms of age-dependent cellular reorganization in the tumor microenvironment and identify MDK and associated stromal-remodeling pathways as potential intervention points for age-stratified cancer therapy.

https://aacrjournals.org/cancerdiscovery.title: The Landscape of Prostate Tumor Methylation
https://aacrjournals.org/cancerdiscovery.abstract: Abstract Prostate cancer is characterized by profound clinical and molecular heterogeneity. Although its genomic heterogeneity is well characterized, its epigenomic heterogeneity remains less understood. We therefore created a compendium of 3,001 multiancestry prostate methylomes spanning normal tissue through localized disease of all grades to polymetastatic disease. A subset of 884 samples had multiomic DNA and/or RNA characterization. We identify four epigenomic subtypes that risk-stratify patients and reflect distinct evolutionary trajectories. We demonstrate extensive regulatory interplay between DNA copy number and methylation, with transcriptional consequences that vary across genes and disease stages. We define epigenetic dysregulation signatures for 15 important clinicomolecular features, creating predictive models for each. For example, we identify specific epigenetic features that predict patient outcome and are synergistic with clinical prognostic features. These results define a complex interplay between tumor genetics and epigenetics that converges to modify gene expression programs and clinical presentation, in part through modulation of epigenetic aging. Significance: We define the largest prostate cancer methylome resource to date, revealing four epigenomic subtypes that stratify cancers by their genetics, evolution, and clinical phenotypes. These data demonstrate that genome–epigenome interactions are stage-dependent, positioning DNA methylation as a central, clinically informative driver of prostate cancer heterogeneity.

https://aacrjournals.org/cancerdiscovery.title: Targeting KRAS Codon 13 Mutations Using Direct Combination Approaches in Non–Small Cell Lung Cancer
https://aacrjournals.org/cancerdiscovery.abstract: Abstract Direct inhibitors of KRAS G12C are now used as standard-of-care therapy in KRAS G12C -mutant non–small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), but less is understood about the molecular mechanisms and consequent treatment vulnerabilities of KRAS codon 13 mutations in this setting. In this study, we characterized the tumorigenic properties of NSCLC harboring KRAS G13X in a large multinational cohort of patients with NSCLC and in preclinical models of KRAS G13X NSCLC. Induction of KRAS G13C or KRAS G13D expression confers reduced oncopotency compared with allele-specific controls affecting KRAS codon 12, particularly KRAS G13C . We identified functionally relevant comutations in KRAS G13X NSCLC, including KEAP1 , STK11 , BRAF , and NF1 . The novel RAS(ON) G13C-selective inhibitor, RMC-8839, reduces viability in a panel of KRAS G13C NSCLC cell models. To determine combination partners that enhance RAS(ON) mutant-selective inhibition, a drug repurposing screen revealed that KRAS G13C models are selectively vulnerable to chemotherapy. Combination of docetaxel with RMC-8839 demonstrated robust antiproliferative activity in KRAS G13C -driven NSCLC models in vitro and in vivo . Significance: We characterize the second most common KRAS mutational hotspot in NSCLC after codon 12, KRAS G13X , from tumor initiation to advanced disease. KRAS G13C is a novel, directly targetable subset of NSCLC, with vulnerability to the combination of chemotherapeutics and the mutant-selective RAS(ON) inhibitor RMC-8839, a finding immediately relevant to patient care. See related commentary by Araujo and Skoulidi, p. 2206 See related article by Seamon et al., p. 2256

https://aacrjournals.org/cancerdiscovery.title: Gut Pathobionts Translocate into the Liver and Reshape Intrahepatic Microbiome to Facilitate Hepatocellular Carcinoma
https://aacrjournals.org/cancerdiscovery.abstract: Abstract The role of intrahepatic microbiome in hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) remains elusive. In this study, we profiled matched gut and intrahepatic microbiomes from patients with HCC and healthy subjects. Compared with healthy subjects, we observed increased gut–liver microbiome similarity and a gut pathobiont–centered network in HCC, implying microbial transfer via the gut–liver axis. Consistently, HCC stool transplantation to germ-free mice impaired gut barrier function and increased bacterial load in the liver. Multisite analysis of intrahepatic microbiome and host transcriptome revealed that gut pathobionts in tumor regions positively correlate with host cytokine expression and oncogenic pathways. Administration of HCC-enriched Bacteroides fragilis disrupted gut barrier in mice and led to live bacteria translocation to the liver. B. fragilis exacerbated liver damage and promoted HCC development in mice. Mechanistically, B. fragilis surface protein enolase interacts with and activates vimentin on hepatocytes, triggering oncogenic cascades. Our findings provide insight into how gut pathobionts translocate to the liver to promote hepatocarcinogenesis. Significance: Parallel characterization of stool and intrahepatic microbiomes from patients with HCC and healthy subjects revealed gut–liver microbial transfer. The gut pathobiont B. fragilis disrupts gut barrier and translocates as live bacteria to the liver. Its surface protein enolase binds hepatocyte vimentin to activate proinflammatory and oncogenic signaling, thereby promoting liver tumorigenesis. See related commentary by Chojnacka and Grivennikov, p. 2214

https://aacrjournals.org/cancerdiscovery.title: EML4−ALK Mediates Resistance to KRAS G12C Inhibition and Induces an Oncogenic Dependency by Rewiring Signaling through the Wild-Type RAS Pathway
https://aacrjournals.org/cancerdiscovery.abstract: Abstract KRAS mutations are common oncogenic drivers in human cancers, with the KRAS G12C variant being a key target in lung adenocarcinoma. Despite the FDA approval of KRAS G12C -selective inhibitors, their clinical efficacy has been limited, as evidenced by trials showing modest response rates and resistance development through the selection of acquired genomic alterations. Our study explores the mechanisms underlying acquired EML4–ALK fusion in KRAS G12C -driven tumors developing resistance to KRAS G12C inhibitors and potential therapeutic strategies to overcome it. Our findings reveal that combined ALK/KRAS G12C inhibition is an effective therapeutic approach in this context. Moreover, we observed that KRAS G12C /EML4–ALK tumor cells kept under constant pressure with KRAS G12C inhibitors exhibit sensitivity to single-agent ALK inhibitors, suggesting a potential for rationally designed sequential treatments. Mechanistically, EML4–ALK bypasses KRAS G12C inhibition by activating wild-type RAS, highlighting an additional therapeutic opportunity for multiselective RAS inhibitors under clinical investigation. Significance: Acquired EML4–ALK fusions confer resistance to KRAS inhibition in KRAS G12C -driven lung adenocarcinoma. By rewiring the oncogenic signaling under inhibitor pressure, EML4–ALK creates a new oncogenic dependency that can be exploited for more effective therapeutic strategies. See related commentary by Araujo and Skoulidi, p. 2206

https://aacrjournals.org/cancerdiscovery.title: CDK8 Inhibition Induces Mediator Trapping and Impairment of the EWSR1::FLI1 Transcriptional Program in Ewing Sarcoma
https://aacrjournals.org/cancerdiscovery.abstract: Abstract Ewing sarcoma is characterized by a chromosomal translocation resulting in the fusion protein EWSR1::FLI1. We utilize endogenous EWSR1::FLI1 target gene reporters in patient-derived cell lines to perform a high-throughput phenotypic screen to identify small molecules that impair the EWSR1::FLI1 transcriptional program. We discovered that inhibitors of cyclin-dependent kinase 8 (CDK8), including a novel pyridyl imidazole, altered transcription of EWSR1::FLI1 target genes and CDK8 co-localized with EWSR1::FLI1 preferentially on single GGAA DNA-binding motifs. Using pooled CRISPR screening, biochemical studies, and chromatin profiling, we discovered that CDK8 inhibitors suppressed proliferation of Ewing sarcoma cells through a gain-of-function mechanism by inducing molecular trapping of the CDK8 kinase module and Mediator complex on chromatin. This mechanism has implications for the development of small molecules to target transcription and suggests that impairment of transcriptional regulatory complex dynamics might serve as a vulnerability in cancers in which the dominant oncogenes act as dosage-sensitive transcription factors. Significance: A high-throughput screen using endogenous EF target gene reporter alleles identified CDK8 as a modifier of EF transcriptional regulation. Using pooled CRISPR screening, biochemical studies, and chromatin profiling, we discovered that CDK8 inhibitors impaired transcriptional regulation through molecular trapping of CDK8 and the Mediator complex on chromatin. See related commentary by Stevens and Hatley, p. 2210

https://aacrjournals.org/cancerdiscovery.title: Serpins Establish Fibrin-Rich Suppressive Niches in Pancreatic Cancer
https://aacrjournals.org/cancerdiscovery.abstract: Major Finding: Serpins drive fibrin-dependent immune suppression and resistance to PD-1 blockade. Concept: Tumor-derived serpins locally reshape the extracellular matrix and promote macrophage polarization to suppress immune surveillance. Impact: Targeting the serpin–fibrin axis may enhance immunotherapy by reducing suppressive macrophages and promoting CD8 + T-cell infiltration.

https://aacrjournals.org/cancerdiscovery.title: Selective Inhibition of KRAS G13C Reveals an Increased Dependence on Wild-type RAS Isoforms in Codon 13 RAS-Mutant Cancers
https://aacrjournals.org/cancerdiscovery.abstract: Abstract Covalent KRAS G12C inhibitors have changed the treatment landscape for patients with non–small cell lung cancer and colorectal cancer, but numerous RAS-mutant cancers lack approved targeted therapies. In this study, we describe RMC-8839, an oral RAS(ON) G13C-selective, covalent, tricomplex inhibitor that induced tumor regressions in selected KRAS G13C -mutant xenograft models. However, one third of KRAS G13C -mutant human cancer cell lines in vitro showed incomplete RAS pathway suppression despite near-complete KRAS G13C engagement, suggesting a role for wild-type RAS(ON). We find that codon 13–mutant RAS differs from other KRAS mutations, exhibiting decreased stability, increased nucleotide exchange, and substantial intrinsic and guanosine triphosphatase-activating protein–stimulated GTP hydrolysis, which decreases oncogenicity. Furthermore, co-occurring RAS pathway mutations leading to increased wild-type RAS activation are enriched in codon 13–mutant tumors. Consistent with a role for wild-type RAS(ON) signaling, the combination of RMC-8839 with a RAS(ON) multiselective inhibitor resulted in deeper inhibition of KRAS G13C -mutant xenograft tumor growth than either inhibitor alone. Significance: An enhanced understanding of the underlying biology of RAS mutations is critical to inform therapeutic strategies. Our preclinical data highlight that codon 13 mutant tumors are more reliant on wild-type RAS signaling than codon 12 tumors and demonstrate that this can be addressed by combining RAS(ON) G13C-selective and multiselective inhibitors. See related commentary by Araujo and Skoulidi, p. 2206 See related article by McDaid et al., p. 2274

https://aacrjournals.org/cancerdiscovery.title: Macropinocytosis Enables Recyclable Lysosome-Targeting Chimeras
https://aacrjournals.org/cancerdiscovery.abstract: Major Finding: A receptor-independent lysosome-targeting chimera (LYTAC) shuttles its target to the lysosome for degradation and recycles to the cell surface. https://aacrjournals.org/cancerdiscovery.title: Phase III Trials Test First-Line Options in Advanced NSCLC
https://aacrjournals.org/cancerdiscovery.abstract: Abstract: Presented at the 2026 World Conference on Lung Cancer, two phase III trials—PAPILLON and REZILIENT3—established amivantamab and zipalertinib combination therapies as effective first-line strategies for advanced NSCLC with EGFR exon 20 insertions, with significantly improved progression-free survival, although high crossover rates prevented them demonstrating an overall survival benefit. https://aacrjournals.org/cancerdiscovery.title: Microplastics and Cancer: Still Searching for Causation
https://aacrjournals.org/cancerdiscovery.abstract: Abstract: Micro- and nanoplastics have been found in tumors throughout the human body, from the gut and lung to the brain and prostate, and laboratory work ties them to inflammation, DNA damage, and other cancer-related changes. But nearly all that evidence is either associative or drawn from animals and cells. Researchers say a causal verdict will require studies that measure exposure before disease appears, a bar the field has not yet cleared.

https://aacrjournals.org/cancerdiscovery.title: Spatial Lineage Tracing Reveals Tumor–Microenvironment Coevolution
https://aacrjournals.org/cancerdiscovery.abstract: Main Finding: Lineage tracing links subclonal expansion to hypoxic niches that promote metastatic cell states. Concept: Tumor subclonal expansion reshapes local ecosystems, generating hypoxia and immunosuppressive microenvironments that promote metastatic programs. Impact: These findings suggest that hypoxia-driven remodeling of the tumor ecosystem might be a potential target for preventing metastasis.

https://aacrjournals.org/cancerdiscovery.title: A Pan-Cancer Single-Cell Analysis of Intratumoral Copy-Number Diversity and Evolution
https://aacrjournals.org/cancerdiscovery.abstract: Abstract Aneuploidy is a hallmark of human tumors. Although patient-level copy-number alteration (CNA) differences have been investigated extensively in large cohorts, their intratumoral heterogeneity remains understudied. In this study, we conducted a pan-cancer analysis of 94 human tumors at single-cell resolution, representing seven cancer types: bladder, breast, colon, glioblastoma, kidney, lung, and ovarian. Single-cell copy-number profiling was used to analyze 62,646 aneuploid cells, in addition to bulk exome sequencing of most patients and single-nucleus RNA sequencing of six samples. In many cancer types, increased subclonal diversity was associated with higher CNA burden, whole-genome doubling (WGD), TP53 mutations, and increased geographic diversity. Cancer cells from each patient shared a set of truncal CNAs, suggesting evolution from a single ancestral cell. Many tumors accumulated CNAs in bursts of evolution, suggesting that punctuated evolution is common in diverse cancer types. This study greatly improves our knowledge of intratumoral chromosome diversity across human cancers. Significance: This study presents one of the largest pan-cancer single-cell DNA sequencing analyses, profiling intratumoral copy-number heterogeneity across seven major cancer types. The data identified punctuated evolution, clonal origins, subclonal WGD, spatial heterogeneity, and associations between copy-number and transcriptional diversity, with implications for both cancer diagnosis and treatment.

https://aacrjournals.org/cancerdiscovery.title: Breaking Barriers: Gut Pathobionts Promote Hepatocellular Carcinoma
https://aacrjournals.org/cancerdiscovery.abstract: Summary: Although studies of microbiota in hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) and possible involvement of the gut–liver axis are of significant interest, the origin and functional role of the liver and intratumoral microbiota in HCC have remained unclear. Liu and colleagues show that gut pathobionts, in particular Bacteroides fragilis , translocate through the gut–liver axis, colonize and reshape the intrahepatic microbiome, and promote HCC through a distinct mechanism in which bacterial enolase binds hepatocyte vimentin, revealing potential therapeutic opportunities. See related article by Liu et al., p. 2392

https://aacrjournals.org/cancerdiscovery.title: Expanding the RAS-verse: Novel Inhibitors, Emergent Dependencies, Fresh Opportunities in RAS -Mutant NSCLC
https://aacrjournals.org/cancerdiscovery.abstract: Summary: In this issue, two studies establish KRAS G13C as a directly targetable oncoprotein in non–small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) while revealing distinct dependence of codon 13–mutant NSCLC on wild-type (WT) RAS and enhanced sensitivity to standard-of-care chemotherapy. A third study highlights rewired oncogenic signaling through WT RAS as a therapeutically tractable mechanism of resistance to KRAS G12C inhibitors in the context of acquired oncogenic kinase fusions. See related article by Scaparone et al., p. 2242 See related article by Seamon et al., p. 2256 See related article by McDaid et al., p. 2274

https://aacrjournals.org/cancerdiscovery.title: CDK8 Inhibition Releases the Muscle Differentiation Block in Fusion-Driven Alveolar Rhabdomyosarcoma
https://aacrjournals.org/cancerdiscovery.abstract: Abstract Alveolar rhabdomyosarcoma (aRMS) is a fusion-driven pediatric cancer with poor survival and limited therapeutic options. To uncover novel vulnerabilities, we used complex-Map functional genomic data, identifying CDK8 as a dependency in aRMS. Both CDK8 knockout and pharmacologic inhibition impaired tumor cell growth and induced myogenic differentiation in vitro and in vivo . Compared with genetic loss, CDK8 pharmacologic inhibition induced more dynamic transcriptional changes. With a genome-scale CRISPR–Cas9 drug modifier screen, we determined that the maximal antitumor activity of the CDK8 inhibitor requires the presence of the Mediator kinase module, including CDK8, and transcriptional cooperation with the SAGA complex. We further identified SIX4 as a key transcription factor mediating CDK8 inhibitor–induced transcriptional activation of myogenic differentiation genes and impaired tumor proliferation. These findings suggest a distinct gain-of-function mechanism of the CDK8 inhibitor and establish a strong rationale for CDK8 inhibition as a differentiation-inducing therapeutic strategy in aRMS. Significance: We provide a framework for uncovering therapeutic targets by network-based analysis of functional genomic screens. We identify CDK8 as a druggable target in aRMS and determine that CDK8 inhibition drives myogenic differentiation and impairs tumor progression via a collaborative mechanism involving the Mediator kinase module, SAGA complex, and SIX4. See related commentary by Stevens and Hatley, p. 2210

https://aacrjournals.org/cancerdiscovery.title: It’s a Trap! CDK8 Inhibition Reveals a Shared Vulnerability through Mediator Trapping in Fusion-Driven Pediatric Sarcomas
https://aacrjournals.org/cancerdiscovery.abstract: Summary: A large proportion of pediatric sarcomas are driven by neomorphic transcription factors that are challenging therapeutic targets. In this issue, two independent studies identify CDK8 as a shared therapeutic vulnerability in pediatric fusion oncoprotein–driven sarcomas and reveal that CDK8 inhibitors disrupt oncogenic transcriptional programs through an unexpected gain-of-function mechanism involving Mediator complex trapping on chromatin. See related article by Zhang et al., p. 2344 See related article by McGinnis et al., p. 2366

https://aacrjournals.org/cancerdiscovery.title: Anti–B7-H3 ADCs Take Center Stage against SCLC at WCLC
https://aacrjournals.org/cancerdiscovery.abstract: Abstract: Separate phase III trials of the anti–B7-H3 antibody–drug conjugates tambotatug pelitecan and risvutatug rezetecan significantly improved overall survival, progression-free survival, and objective response rates compared with topotecan in patients with relapsed small-cell lung cancer. In a third trial, the combination of the investigational PD-L1 x VEGF-A bispecific antibody pumitamig plus the anti–B7-H3 ADC elfetabart drozuntecan showed encouraging early efficacy in SCLC across lines of therapy and doses. The studies were presented at the 2026 World Congress on Lung Cancer in Seoul, Republic of Korea.

https://aacrjournals.org/cancerdiscovery.title: How a Rare Inherited Lung Cancer Mutation Took Root in Appalachia
https://aacrjournals.org/cancerdiscovery.abstract: Abstract A rare inherited EGFR mutation took root in Southern Appalachia after being carried to the United States by European settlers in the 1700s. Mapping the distribution of this germline EGFR T790M variant could help clinicians identify people at elevated risk of lung cancer and target them for genetic testing and closer surveillance.

https://aacrjournals.org/cancerdiscovery.title: Caloric Intake Impacts Somatic Mutation Burden Across Mouse Tissues
https://aacrjournals.org/cancerdiscovery.abstract: Major Finding: Caloric intake directly influences somatic mutation burdens in mouse kidney, liver, and brain. Concept: Caloric restriction reduces mutations more in regions of low transcriptional activity. Impact: The study establishes that aging-related mutation is modifiable in mice, and understanding the mechanisms via future studies may enable interventions to broadly influence cancer risk.

https://aacrjournals.org/cancerdiscovery.title: Tumor Microbial Burden Drives Immune Responses through Regulation of Interferon Signaling
https://aacrjournals.org/cancerdiscovery.abstract: Abstract Tumor microbes are increasingly recognized for modulating tumor behavior and therapy responses. Intratumoral microbial burden (ITMB) analysis across cancers revealed regulation of immune pathways and activated mast cells, mostly in colorectal and gastric cancers. High-ITMB colorectal cancer leads to interferon (IFN) regulation and is associated with improved outcomes in advanced disease. Single-cell sequencing revealed induction of IFN-related genes (IRG) within microbe-containing human colorectal cancer. Gastrointestinal-luminal mismatch repair–deficient (MMRd) tumors had higher ITMB than proficient tumors. In a rectal MMRd cohort with 100% remission after immune checkpoint blockade (ICB), tumor microbes and microbe-containing mast cells increased. In ICB-sensitive syngeneic murine MMRd tumor models, local tumor microbial depletion impaired ICB efficacy while downregulating IFN signaling. Forced upregulation of IRGs in ADAR1-deficient cancer cells restored immunotherapy responses during microbial ablation. These data highlight dynamic interplay among ITMB, host defense, and immunogenicity, which seems key to determine therapy responses. Significance: The ITMB is linked to transcriptional and immune functional changes that seem to determine tumor sensitivity to immunotherapy. These findings highlight the key role of tumor-resident microbes in shaping the tumor ecosystem, which could be targeted to modulate therapy responses.

https://aacrjournals.org/cancerdiscovery.title: Deconvolving SARS-CoV-2 mRNA Vaccine Impact on Immunotherapy-Related Survival
https://aacrjournals.org/cancerdiscovery.abstract: Abstract Real-world data suggest that SARS-CoV-2 mRNA vaccines, administered within 100 days of immune checkpoint inhibitor (ICI) treatment (“peri-ICI vaccination”), may improve ICI effectiveness through synergistic immune priming. In an independent real-world cohort and reanalysis of a published cohort, both from tertiary cancer centers in the United States, multiple analyses did not support a treatment-synergy hypothesis. Applying a prior analytic framework, although longer survival with peri-ICI vaccination was observed at the start of the pandemic, this association was not seen in periods when vaccination was broadly available. Longer survival with vaccination in the early pandemic was also not specific to ICI therapies. Progression-free survival during periods of high vaccine uptake was not longer than in prevaccination periods. Together, these findings indicate that the previously reported vaccination survival advantage is largely explained by selection bias, with patients who had more favorable prognoses more likely to receive the SARS-CoV-2 vaccination, particularly in the early pandemic. Significance: The impact of tumor antigen–agnostic vaccination on immunotherapy response is unclear. In a reanalysis of published data and in an independent cohort, after adjustment for multiple confounders, SARS-CoV-2 mRNA vaccination did not improve immunotherapy-related survival in patients with cancer.

https://aacrjournals.org/cancerdiscovery.title: Targeting RAS for Pancreatic Cancer Interception
https://aacrjournals.org/cancerdiscovery.abstract: Summary: Multiple strategies to target RAS are now available to treat pancreatic cancer. As pancreatic precancers also have KRAS mutations, these tools hold great promise for cancer interception.

https://aacrjournals.org/cancerdiscovery.title: New Studies Showcase Capabilities of Organoids
https://aacrjournals.org/cancerdiscovery.abstract: Abstract: Three recent papers show the potential benefits of several hundred new organoids, spheroids, and other cancer models. One study demonstrates that more than 600 of the models mirror their parent tumors. A second study uses organoids to uncover new cancer dependencies, or essential genes, in 147 organoids from 10 cancer types. The third study also identifies new cancer dependencies and shows that organoids from individual patients might lead to new treatment choices.

Impact: 9( S )-HODE may potentially be leveraged for therapeutic benefit in breast cancer management.

https://aacrjournals.org/cancerdiscovery.title: Highlighted Research Articles
Nucleoporins in Cancer: Functional Roles and Therapeutic Opportunities
https://aacrjournals.org/cancerdiscovery.abstract: Abstract The nuclear pore complex (NPC) and its building-block proteins, nucleoporins (NUP), play fundamental roles in maintaining cellular fitness by regulating nucleocytoplasmic transport, chromatin and transcriptional activity, and genome stability. These core biological processes are critical for cancer cells, and thus, tumor-driven co-option of NUP-regulated functions has emerged as an important mechanism contributing to the pathogenesis of multiple malignancies. This review discusses how NUP dysregulation mechanistically contributes to tumor initiation and progression and how these insights open opportunities for innovative anticancer therapies, including using clinical-grade molecular glues that induce selective NUP degradation and pharmacologically inhibiting NPC-regulated epigenomic/transcriptomic signaling and nucleocytoplasmic transport. Significance: Recent studies demonstrate that NUPs play fundamental roles in cancer pathogenesis by dysregulating key NPC functions and driving tumorigenesis and disease progression. NUPs and NPC-regulated mechanisms can be pharmacologically targeted, providing a strong rationale for developing much-needed innovative therapeutic strategies to combat cancer.

https://aacrjournals.org/cancerdiscovery.title: Binding-To-Release Enhances Efficacy of Small Molecule–Drug Conjugates
https://aacrjournals.org/cancerdiscovery.abstract: Major Finding: Binding-to-release (BTR) drug conjugates inhibit tumor growth in multiple tumor models by specifically and efficiently delivering a membrane-permeable cytotoxic payload. Concept: PhoPEx-based conjugates can be cleaved upon extracellular target binding, eliminating the need for endocytosis-mediated payload release. Impact: Domain-level gene engineering could unlock new therapeutic cell states, with implications for cell engineering for anticancer therapies.

https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.64898.title: Coupled Modeling of Tumor Volume and ctDNA Dynamics in HPV-Associated Anal Squamous Cell Carcinoma
https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.64898.abstract: Response to anti-PD-1 immunotherapy in advanced HPV-associated anal squamous cell carcinoma (ASCC) varies and is assessed by infrequent imaging that lags behind tumor biology. Circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) can be sampled frequently and reflects near-real-time tumor activity yet is rarely built into mechanistic models of treatment response. Using longitudinal tumor volume and HPV ctDNA from 26 patients treated with pembrolizumab, we found that baseline ctDNA scores tracked tumor burden but did not distinguish responders from non-responders, whereas ctDNA after one treatment cycle had a higher relative decrease in responders, six weeks before the next scan. We developed an ordinary differential equation model linking tumor volume to the ctDNA released by tumor cells. Sensitivity, identifiability, and model-selection analyses reduced it to two patient-specific parameters, proliferation and shedding rates, which reproduced individual volume and ctDNA trajectories, including a transient ctDNA spike at treatment onset. Proliferation was faster in non-responders. This framework supports model-based, ctDNA-guided monitoring of immunotherapy response.

https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.64898.title: KaryoTap-based scDNA seq assessment of aneuploidy induction by hydroquinone in hematopoietic stem cells
https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.64898.abstract: Monosomy 7 is a frequent cytogenetic alteration associated with poor outcomes in myelodysplastic syndrome and acute myeloid leukemia. The benzene metabolite hydroquinone (HQ) has been reported to induce chromosome 7 loss in cultured hematopoietic cells, suggesting a mechanism linking benzene exposure to these diseases. However, these findings were largely based on FISH analysis of selected chromosomes in relatively small numbers of cells. Here, we tested whether HQ increases aneuploidy in primary human CD34+ hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells (HSPCs) using KaryoTap, a single-cell DNA sequencing approach that measures copy number across all 22 autosomes, together with interphase FISH. We first identified 20 uM as the highest HQ concentration tested that preserved sufficient viable cells for single-cell analysis. We then examined cord blood and adult mobilized CD34+ cells, including the MPS1 inhibitor reversine as a positive control in the cord blood experiment. Reversine increased whole-chromosome gains and losses, including those of chromosome 7. HQ did not produce a reproducible increase in aneuploidy across three donors and two sources of CD34+ cells, including two concentrations and two timepoints in the adult donor. A modest increase in chromosome 7 loss in one cord blood donor was not reproduced in the other donors. In the other cord blood donor, the estimated upper bound on the HQ-associated increase was approximately 1.4 percentage points. HSPCs also showed a greater increase in chromosome losses than epithelial cells or melanocytes following the same reversine exposure. These findings do not support a substantial, reproducible increase in whole-chromosome aneuploidy after HQ exposure under the conditions tested. They are consistent with a model in which benzene exposure favors the expansion of pre-existing monosomy 7 clones, although this possibility requires direct testing.

https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.64898.title: AMD1-driven MTA production sustains chemoresistance by rewiring PMN-MDSC immunosuppression
https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.64898.abstract: Chemoresistance reflects both tumor cell-intrinsic adaptation and remodeling of the immune microenvironment. However, the mechanisms by which chemoresistant tumor cells orchestrate and sustain an immunosuppressive microenvironment remain poorly understood. Here, we demonstrate that chemoresistant tumors exhibit marked accumulation of polymorphonuclear myeloid-derived suppressor cells (PMN-MDSCs), which exert potent immunosuppressive effects on CD8+T cells and are critical for drug resistance. Metabolomic profiling reveals that resistant tumor cells release the metabolite 5'-methylthioadenosine (MTA). MTA enhances the immunosuppressive function of PMN-MDSCs by bolstering JAK-STAT3 signaling. Mechanistically, MTA binds to the protein tyrosine phosphatase PTPN2 to block its phosphatase activity, thereby potentiating activation of JAK-STAT3 signaling pathway. Moreover, we uncover that adenosylmethionine decarboxylase 1 (AMD1) is the key metabolic determinant of MTA accumulation in chemoresistant tumor cells. Genetic or pharmacological AMD1 inhibition significantly decreases MTA level, diminishes PMN-MDSC immunosuppressive function, and re-sensitizes the resistant tumors to chemotherapy and immunotherapy. Our findings identify MTA as an important metabolic link between chemoresistant tumor cells and PMN-MDSCs to sustain immunosuppression and therapeutic resistance. Targeting AMD1-dependent MTA production represents a valuable strategy for overcoming chemo-immunotherapy resistance.

https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.64898.title: SMARCA4 MUTATIONS PROMOTE CHEMOTHERAPY RESISTANCE IN T-ACUTE LYMPHOBLASTIC LEUKEMIA THROUGH ALTERED CHROMATIN REMODELING AT AP1-ASSOCIATED REGULATORY REGIONS
https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.64898.abstract: Chromatin remodelers play a critical role in orchestrating chemotherapy responses in cancer cells. Components of the SWI/SNF complex are frequently mutated across cancer types, with the ATPase subunit SMARCA4 among the most commonly altered. In T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia (T-ALL), however, SMARCA4 mutations are rare at diagnosis but enriched in relapse samples, suggesting a potential role in therapy resistance. Using isogenic T-ALL cell lines with or without SMARCA4 mutations, we show that mutant SMARCA4 confers resistance to a broad range of chemotherapeutic agents. By combining ATAC-seq and RNA-seq, we demonstrate that SMARCA4-mutant cells display an attenuated transcriptional response to chemotherapy accompanied by impaired remodeling of AP-1-associated regulatory regions linked to stress response. These cells downregulate stress-related genes while maintaining expression programs associated with cellular fitness. Pharmacological inhibition of AP-1 phenocopies this response, further supporting a functional link between SWI/SNF-mediated remodeling at AP-1-associated regulatory regions, AP-1 activity, and chemotherapy sensitivity. Together, our findings indicate that SWI/SNF-mediated remodeling of these regions contributes to an effective chemotherapy-induced stress response, and that its failure provides T-ALL cells with a survival

https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.64898.title: ANABOLIC FAILURE, NOT CATABOLIC ACTIVATION, UNDERLIES GLYCOGEN DEPLETION IN CERVICAL CARCINOGENESIS: A MULTI-COHORT TRANSCRIPTOMIC ANALYSIS
https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.64898.abstract: Abstract Background. Cervical epithelium loses its glycogen as disease grade rises, an observation old enough to underpin iodine-based visual screening, but which arm of glycogen metabolism accounts for the loss has not been established. The expectation from cancer metabolism is catabolic: that stored glycogen is mobilized and glycolysis activated. Methods. We analyzed 238 specimens from four publicly available cohorts across three sample types: 128 laser-capture-microdissected epithelial samples, 35 bulk-tissue samples, and 75 exfoliated cytology samples in two sets (44 and 31; GSE27678). We prespecified a 33-gene panel comprising four modules: glycogen synthesis, glycogen degradation, glycolysis, and squamous differentiation. For each specimen, we calculated module scores using single-sample gene set enrichment. Differential expression was assessed with limma, pathway enrichment with fgsea, and classification performance with bootstrap confidence intervals for ROC curves. We documented all analytical decisions and their rationale. Results. Synthesis and differentiation fell with grade in all four cohorts, while degradation and glycolysis stayed at their normal-tissue baseline. All seven differentiation genes were reduced in carcinoma, and all seven occupied the top 5.1% of the ranked transcriptome, with CRNN the most down-regulated of 21,755 genes. Synthesis failed selectively, through GYS2 and PPP1R3C only, with the ubiquitous synthase GYS1 unchanged. The glycolytic module separated from normal epithelium at no grade (p 0.45 to 0.62), classified CIN3 or worse at an area under the curve of 0.569 with an interval spanning chance, and showed no enrichment in carcinoma. Synthesis separated from normal first, at CIN2, and differentiation at CIN3. The composite index tracked grade in the discovery cohort (Spearman rho 0.652, p 7.9e-17) but offered no discriminatory advantage over its differentiation component alone (0.832 against 0.832). Conclusions. Glycogen depletion in cervical carcinogenesis reflects failure of a tissue-restricted synthetic axis, GYS2 and PPP1R3C, within a collapsing squamous differentiation program, not catabolic activation. Measuring all four candidate mechanisms on one scale in the same specimen is what allows the catabolic explanation to be excluded rather than merely left untested. The pattern holds across two array chemistries and three specimen preparations, including the exfoliated cytology that screening already collects, and the synthesis and differentiation modules together are the molecular counterpart of what iodine staining reports. These are transcript-level findings and define no clinical threshold.

https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.64898.title: Structure-Function Analysis of an Infantile Rhabdomyosarcoma Fusion-Oncogene Reveals Domain Requirements for Tumorigenesis
https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.64898.abstract: Rhabdomyosarcoma is a pediatric soft-tissue sarcoma that reflects impaired skeletal muscle differentiation. Spindle cell/sclerosing rhabdomyosarcoma is a histological subtype found in children and adults. In children under two, spindle cell rhabdomyosarcoma is genetically driven by fusion-oncogenes of transcription factors or co-activators important for skeletal muscle lineage commitment and development. The most common fusion-oncogene in this group is VGLL2::NCOA2, a fusion between vestigial-like family member 2 (VGLL2) and nuclear receptor coactivator 2 (NCOA2). Children with fusion-driven rhabdomyosarcoma are treated with general chemotherapy, surgery, and radiation, which are not specific to the molecular underpinnings, and increase risk of secondary malignancies and premature death. Previously, we showed that VGLL2::NCOA2 is transforming in mouse myoblasts and transgenic zebrafish tumor models. Here, we build on this work by detailing the structure-function relationship of the retained VGLL2::NCOA2 protein domains to define domain requirements and their molecular interactions for tumorigenesis. We created deletion mutants of the VGLL2 vestigial/Tondu (TDU) domain and the NCOA2 activating domains 1 and 2 (AD1 and AD2), and a double mutant lacking the TDU+AD1 domains and assessed their function in a mouse myoblast model. We find that the TDU and AD1 domains support nuclear fusion-oncogene localization, transformation in vitro, and tumorigenesis in a mouse allograft model. Furthermore, transcriptomic analysis demonstrates that the TDU or AD1 mutant VGLL2::NCOA2 drives an upregulation of myogenesis gene sets and supports terminal differentiation. Overall, our results indicate that VGLL2::NCOA2 requires the TDU and AD1 domains for optimal transformation, and that targeting these domains, or their interacting protein partners, represents a therapeutic opportunity.

https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.64898.title: Endogenous PROM1 activation redistributes liver cancer cells along a preexisting differentiation axis
https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.64898.abstract: CD133 is widely used as a marker of stem-like cells in hepatocellular carcinoma, yet its functional contribution remains incompletely defined. In PLC/PRF/5 cells, acute CRISPR activation of endogenous PROM1 suppresses hepatic programs, whereas PROM1 knockdown elicits an opposing hepatocyte-identity response, together defining a PROM1-responsive transcriptional axis. Single-cell profiling shows that this axis is preexisting and tracks endogenous PROM1 heterogeneity, separating a hepatocyte-like, PROM1-low compartment from a PROM1-enriched, less hepatocyte-like compartment. Sustained PROM1 activation reduces the hepatocyte-like compartment and shifts the population toward intermediate positions along this axis. Related transcriptional patterns are detectable in an independent HuH-7 dataset and a human HCC case. Endogenous ALFA tagging identifies candidate CD133-associated proteins. Together, these findings support CD133 as an active contributor to tumor-cell state redistribution, extending its role beyond a mere marker of stem-like populations.

https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.64898.title: Decoding stress-induced adaptation of cancer cells in spatial confinement by integrating live-cell imaging and mathematical modeling
https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.64898.abstract: The adaptive strategies employed by cancer cells to combat stress when grown in 2D cultures have been extensively studied, including applying evolutionary game theory. However, relatively little is known about these strategies when the cells are grown in confinement that resemble the tumor microenvironment more closely. Here, we used cisplatin-sensitive and -tolerant lung cancer cells that were grown as monotypic or heterotypic spheroids in a microfluidics system and monitored in real time. Competition and cooperation between these cells were modeled by estimating the parameters through the best fit of observed measurements using a modified version of the Cellular Potts model. The results indicated that the two sensitive and tolerant populations exhibited different cooperative and competitive strategies under changing environmental conditions. Importantly, we found that in addition to initial cell type composition, the population fitness was governed by the spatial organization, intercellular interactions, and dynamic remodeling of the local microenvironment by these cells. Further, tolerant cells exhibited similarities to a persister trait and appeared to cooperate with sensitive cells, enabling them to evade chemotherapy.

https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.64898.title: ORTHOTOPIC TUMOUR INDUCTION PROTOCOL SHAPES TUMOUR MICROENVIRONMENT
https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.64898.abstract: Robust preclinical cancer models are essential for studying tumour progression and evaluating therapeutic strategies. Orthotopic implantation of tumour cells into the mammary gland is widely used to model triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC), yet substantial variation exists in the number of cells used to initiate tumours, often without explicit consideration of how this parameter shapes tumour biology. Here, we systematically assess how tumour cell number at implantation influences the tumour microenvironment using the 4T1 orthotopic TNBC model. Mammary tumours initiated with different cell numbers exhibited comparable early growth kinetics and gross size, yet diverged markedly in cellular density, hypoxia, necrosis, proliferation, vascular integrity, and immune cell infiltration. High-density tumours displayed increased HIF-1 staining and necrosis, alongside differences in vascular-associated markers and increased macrophage recruitment. Conversely, low-density tumours remained highly proliferative, less necrotic and exhibited higher PDGFR{beta} staining. Importantly, tumour cells disseminated systemically within days of implantation across all conditions, although differences in colony recovery and ex vivo expansion were not statistically significant. Together, these findings demonstrate that tumour initiating protocols are powerful determinants of tumour state, with potential implications for dissemination frequency and tumour cell fate at distant sites. Rather than representing a source of experimental variability alone, this understanding provides an opportunity to intentionally tailor orthotopic models to investigate specific stages of disease progression and therapeutic response, thereby enhancing cross-study reproducibility and translational relevance.

https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.64898.title: Polycomb Marked Promoter Methylation Gains in Aging and Cancer are Independent of Replication
https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.64898.abstract: DNA methylation alterations are hallmark features of aging and cancer, occurring early during tumor initiation. Yet how these changes evolve during early tumorigenesis, and whether oncogenic signaling actively drives them, remains poorly understood due to limitations in resolving this at the longitudinal and clonal level. Here we developed a genome-wide DNA methylation profiling method for low DNA amounts and applied it to single stem cell-derived clones from a BRAFV600E -inducible mouse colon organoid model, tracking nucleotide-level methylation heterogeneity over time. BRAFV600E induction produced stepwise methylation divergence consistent with progressive clonal takeover, in contrast to gradual epigenetic drift in uninduced controls. Strikingly, while the specific CpG sites altered differed between BRAFV600E and control lineages, they converged on the same genomic elements. Particularly, Polycomb-marked promoter CpG-island methylation gains were not induced or accelerated by BRAFV600E, challenging models in which oncogenic signaling or cell proliferation actively instructs de novo methylation of Polycomb-targeted promoters. Instead, these gains tracked with "biological aging" independent of replication, which was validated across independent aging, cancer, and cell-line datasets. BRAFV600E -induced clones additionally showed progressive loss of intestinal lineage-specification transcription factor programs, consistent with selection for cells adapted to oncogenic stress. Together, these findings show that epigenetic trajectories during early tumor development, are rooted in baseline, age-dependent drivers of epigenetic alterations, and that oncogenic signaling acts primarily by selecting and expanding clones bearing pre-existing, age-associated epigenetic drift rather than instructing new methylation. Our findings have implications for how promoter methylation is interpreted as a cancer biomarker and for identifying upstream aging-associated processes as targets for early intervention.

https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.64898.title: Single-cell characterization of 3D CLL spheroid model that recapitulates lymph node microenvironment-driven phenotypes and in vivo drug responses to ibrutinib
https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.64898.abstract: Lymph node (LN) microenvironmental signals promote chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL) cell survival, proliferation, and treatment resistance. We previously developed a 3D culture model that recapitulates key features of this protective LN niche. Using single-cell RNA sequencing of ex vivo paired peripheral blood and LN samples, together with matched patient-derived CLL spheroids, we investigated how microenvironmental cues shape CLL phenotypes and their response to ibrutinib. A total of 3 functional CLL states (resting, activated, proliferating) were identified, with expanded populations of activated and proliferating subsets in 3D cultures. After 5 days of in vitro ibrutinib treatment, CLL cells shifted toward a resting phenotype, reflecting published responses in patients at 6 months. Activated CLL cells showed relative resistance to ibrutinib, associated with TLR9-MALT1-MYC pathway activation. The 3D model recapitulated tissue-specific T cell phenotypes observed in patients, and computational analyses predicted several T-to-CLL cell-mediated interactions supporting the LN niche. Collectively, these data reveal distinct ibrutinib responses among CLL subsets and establish the 3D model as a physiologically relevant platform.

https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.64898.title: Strategies of mechanical adaptations of circulating tumor cells and properties of their cellular microenvironment have predictive and prognostic biomarker value
https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.64898.abstract: Mechanically demanding conditions in the blood circulation damage and kill majority of tumor-shed circulating tumor cells (CTCs). Mechanical fitness: a set of mechanical properties detected with atomic force spectroscopy based force spectrometry supports survival of CTCs. We propose that live CTCs isolated from peripheral blood of prostate cancer patients represent distinct strategies of fitness promoting mechanical adaptations to the fluid shear stress. Some of the cells mimicked properties of erythrocytes (high stiffness) or leukocytes (high deformability). The clustering strategy characterized by exceptionally high adhesion is ingenious to CTCs and not found in blood cells. The abundance of CTCs with elevated adhesion has a predictive value for prostate cancer patients starting first round of androgen deprivation therapy. Moreover, a high adhesion score based on individual cells or average patient-specific adhesion is instrumental to stratify recurrent patients that underwent diagnostic imaging by PSMA-PET/CT and clarify inconclusive PSMA scan results. Including contribution of erythrocyte-like strategy broadened the predictive power of CTC mechanophenotyping. Improved biomarking opportunities to predict early castration resistances were noted when the composition of CTC microenvironment was included alongside the mechanical properties. We demonstrated previously that the CTC microenvironment is formed by large cells co-purifying by microfiltration of the blood of cancer patients. Analysis of the association of particular components of CTC microenvironment with the clustering strategy led to pointing at highly adhesive CTC-EMT. However, in the advanced patients adhesiveness of CTC-EMT was surpassed by tumor hybrid cells (THCs), a distinctive kind of invasive species formed by incomplete phagocytosis of CTCs by macrophages. THCs changed their mechanical phenotype and strategy preference with disease progression pointing at the dynamic nature of adaptations of tumor-shed cells to circulation conditions.

https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.64898.title: Revamped transposon-induced hepatocellular carcinoma model reveals deep similarities of cancer-driver landscapes across mice and humans
https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.64898.abstract: Genome-scale cancer-driver discovery is limited by statistical uncertainty in driver calling and by experimental constraints on mutations available for selection. We developed 3xfOnc3 - a three-frame Sleeping Beauty (SB) mutagenesis system designed to broaden functional perturbations and reduce integration biases of traditional SB screens - and tested it in vivo in mouse liver. Within 12 months, 60% of mice developed heterogeneous hepatocellular tumors. Tumor-selected integrations were interpreted against an empirical reference from SB-based therapeutic gene delivery to hepatocytes, enabling correction for gene targetability. Background-aware filtering prioritized 315 driver candidates, including 243 protein-coding genes. Tumors were multiclonal, and identical integration-marked lineages expanded differently across lesions, supporting context-dependent clonal expansion. SB hits within young L1 subfamily members were selectively enriched in tumors. Human orthologues of candidate drivers were enriched for Cancer Gene Census genes and protein-altering pan-cancer mutations. Together, 3xfOnc3 reveals a background-corrected driver landscape linking driver selection to clonal tumor evolution and cross-species cancer relevance.

https://www.nature.com/articles/s41571-0.title: Interpreting surgical consolidation in oligometastatic gastro-oesophageal cancer

https://www.nature.com/articles/s41419-0.title: The convergence of senescence and ferroptosis amplifies DNA damage and triggers apoptosis in patient-derived melanoma models
https://www.nature.com/articles/s41419-0.abstract: Therapy-induced senescence (TIS) is a common response to anticancer treatment that enforces durable cell-cycle arrest but can also promote tumor persistence and disease relapse if senescent cells are not efficiently eliminated. The “one–two punch” therapeutic paradigm aims to overcome this limitation by coupling senescence induction with senolytic targeting. In this study, using distinct, clinically relevant BRAF- and NRAS-mutant melanoma PDXs, we identify a novel combination strategy in which a vulnerable cell state is induced and then selectively targeted. Through a high-throughput one–two punch screen, we identified auranofin as a top candidate selectively targeting senescent melanoma cells. Auranofin synergized with multiple senescence-inducing agents, including volasertib, palbociclib, everolimus, and temozolomide, and retained activity across multiple PDX models. In particular, the PLK1 inhibitor volasertib induced robust senescence characterized by G2/M arrest and senescence-associated β-galactosidase expression, while auranofin triggered oxidative stress through thioredoxin reductase inhibition. Sequential volasertib–auranofin treatment resulted in marked accumulation of reactive oxygen species, intracellular iron, and metabolic stress, consistent with activation of ferroptotic pathways. Importantly, ferroptosis cooperated with senescence to amplify DNA damage and genomic instability, as evidenced by increased γH2AX foci, nuclear enlargement, and micronuclei formation, culminating in apoptotic cell death. In vivo, combination therapy significantly suppressed tumor growth and prolonged mice survival without overt toxicity, demonstrating robust therapeutic efficacy in both BRAF- and NRAS-mutant melanoma PDXs. Together, our findings define a mechanistic framework in which volasertib-driven senescence creates a ferroptosis-sensitive state that is therapeutically exploited by auranofin, leading to oxidative stress–mediated DNA damage and tumor cell elimination. This study identifies ferroptosis as a critical vulnerability of senescent cells and provides strong preclinical rationale for repurposing auranofin in combination with senescence-inducing therapies, supporting rapid translational advancement of this strategy for aggressive melanoma.

https://www.nature.com/articles/s42003-0.title: Mathematical and experimental models of interactions among subclones and immunity in melanoma
https://www.nature.com/articles/s42003-0.abstract: Melanoma tumors often contain heterogeneous subclones, typically with proliferative or invasive phenotypes. These subclones interact with each other and the immune system to shape tumor progression. Understanding interactions between subclones and the tumor microenvironment is a fundamental challenge for melanoma treatment. To analyze such interactions, we developed dedicated in vivo melanoma mouse and mathematical models. In the experimental models, admixtures of proliferative and invasive subclones of varying proportions were implanted into immunocompromised and immunocompetent mice. Tumor growth and subclone composition were tracked over time. In parallel, we built a computational model to capture the system dynamics. By estimating parameter values of our mathematical model using experimental measurements, we found that, while the proliferative subclone outgrew the invasive subclone, T cell activities selected for the invasive subclone. Initial subclonal proportion in this dynamic system determines the overall tumor sensitivity to immune response. The key interactions identified in this study provide insights into how intratumor heterogeneity and immune pressure influence melanoma progression, suggesting strategies for optimizing individualized therapy. Mouse and computational models of interactions between heterogeneous melanoma subclones and the immune system are developed that show that initial subclonal ratios and the strength of interactions determine overall sensitivity to immune response.

https://www.nature.com/articles/s41698-0.title: Integration of single-cell and spatial transcriptomics reveals stromal cell features in breast cancer
https://www.nature.com/articles/s41698-0.abstract: Stromal cells are key components of the breast cancer tumor microenvironment, yet their heterogeneity, spatial organization, and interactions with tumor and immune cells remain incompletely defined. We integrated single-cell RNA sequencing data from 233,518 non-immune stromal cells across 349 patients with spatial transcriptomic data from 51 patients. This analysis identified 36 fibroblast, endothelial, and mural cell subsets with distinct transcriptional programs, spatial distributions, and functional associations. ABCA8+ lipid-associated fibroblasts were observed at tumor margins, showed predicted interactions with malignant cells, and were associated with exhaustion-associated T-cell phenotypes. CCL19+ inflammatory fibroblasts showed spatial patterns associated with tertiary lymphoid structure formation, whereas tumor-associated pericytes showed predicted interactions with PGF+ tip endothelial cells that may be involved in extracellular matrix deposition and vascular remodeling. Together, these findings provide a high-resolution stromal atlas of breast cancer, resolving stromal subtypes, spatial context, and potential intercellular communication. This resource provides a framework for investigating stromal contributions to tumor progression and immune regulation, although further experimental validation is required.

https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-0.title: Preliminary results and clinical experiences of [177Lu]Lu-FAP-2286 for brain metastases in advanced lung cancer
https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-0.abstract: Brain metastases in advanced lung cancer present a therapeutic challenge with limited effective options. Fibroblast activation protein (FAP) is overexpressed in cancer-associated fibroblasts within brain metastatic lesions, making it a promising target for radionuclide therapy. This prospective study evaluated the intracranial efficacy and safety of peptide-targeted radionuclide therapy (PTRT) with [177Lu]Lu-FAP-2286 in 14 patients with FAP-expressing advanced lung cancer and radiologically confirmed brain metastases who had failed prior treatments. Patients received [177Lu]Lu-FAP-2286 (7.4 GBq/cycle, ≥ 2 cycles). Intracranial objective response rate was 57.1% and disease control rate was 92.9% by RECIST 1.1, with a metabolic response rate of 64.3% by PERCIST 1.0. Median overall survival was 11.0 months and median progression-free survival was 8.0 months. Patients achieving metabolic response had significantly longer survival. Neurological symptoms and brain-specific quality of life improved significantly, and no grade III/IV adverse events occurred. These findings suggest that systemic [177Lu]Lu-FAP-2286 PTRT is safe and effective for brain metastases in FAP-expressing advanced lung cancer, achieving intracranial tumor regression, symptom relief, and improved quality of life, thereby offering a promising therapeutic option for this refractory population.

https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.64898.title: HER3 mediates metabolic reprogramming in metastatic colorectal and pancreatic cancer
https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.64898.abstract: Liver metastases are a major cause of mortality in colorectal cancer (CRC) and pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC), yet the oncogenic signals that shape tumor metabolism in the hepatic niche remain poorly understood. Here, we show that HER3 activation drives a liver metastasis-specific glycolytic program in both cancer types. Genetic or pharmacological HER3 inhibition suppresses cancer glycolysis while increasing dependence on oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS), rendering liver metastases vulnerable to OXPHOS inhibition. Combining the HER3 inhibitor sapitinib with distinct OXPHOS inhibitors led to in vitro synergy and durable tumor-free survival in orthotopic CRC and PDAC liver metastases models, with further validation in patient-derived xenografts. Mechanistically, HER3 promotes glycolysis through activating PFK2 and reduces OXPHOS through activating DRP1-mediated mitochondrial remodeling, both pathways were activated in liver metastases compared to matched primary tumors. Together, our findings identify the HER3-AKT/RSK-PFK2 axis as a driver of glycolysis and metastatic growth and reveal an OXPHOS dependency induced by HER3 inhibition that may be exploited through combined HER3 and OXPHOS targeting in metastatic CRC and PDAC.

https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.64898.title: Seesaw configuration of the ODC-OAZ1-AZIN1 axis governs sensitivity to polyamine-targeting inhibitors of breast cancer cells
https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.64898.abstract: Polyamines are endogenous metabolites crucial for various cellular functions, and maintaining their cellular levels is critical for normal cell survival and fate. Polyamine homeostasis is managed by a complex metabolic network, wherein the ODC-OAZ1-AZIN1 protein-protein interaction axis plays a central role in regulating polyamine synthesis and membrane transport. While existing research has established that polyamine-targeted inhibitors (PTIs) significantly perturb this axis in various cancers, and that different breast cancer subtypes display distinct PTI sensitivities, the fundamental mechanism of drug sensitivity difference has remained poorly understood. Here, we combine large-scale bioinformatic analysis with comprehensive experimental verification to reveal a polarized seesaw configuration of the ODC-OAZ1-AZIN1 axis across diverse tumor types, including breast cancer. We show that this seesaw configuration is not only distinct across breast cancer subtypes but also associated with unique cellular states. Furthermore, we reveal that this configuration underpins the distinct sensitivity profiles of these subtypes to both single and combination treatments of PTIs. Crucially, we demonstrate that targeted re-configuration of this axis can shift the drug sensitivity of resistant cells. This study provides the first systematic mechanistic framework linking the configuration of the ODC-OAZ1-AZIN1 axis to PTI sensitivity, thereby providing a configuration-based framework for rational selection of PTI combination regimens and new personalized therapeutic strategies in breast cancer.

https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.64898.title: SDHB deficiency silences ABCB1 expression and confers therapeutic vulnerability across multiple cancer types
https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.64898.abstract: Succinate dehydrogenase B (SDHB)-deficient cancers, including pheochromocytoma and paraganglioma (PPGL), renal cell carcinoma (RCC), and gastrointestinal stromal tumor (GIST), exhibit aggressive clinical behavior with limited treatment options. To identify novel therapeutic vulnerabilities, we performed high-throughput drug screening using co-cultured human SDHB-deficient and SDHB-reconstituted UOK269 human renal cell carcinoma cells with dual fluorescence labeling. Several compounds displaying preferential cytotoxicity toward SDHB-deficient cells were known substrates of the ATP-binding cassette B1 (ABCB1) transporter, also known as Multidrug Resistance Protein 1 (MDR1). Accordingly, SDHB-deficient cells demonstrated markedly reduced ABCB1 expression, a phenotype confirmed across human SDHB-deficient PPGL, RCC, and GIST samples, but absent in IDH- or FH-deficient tumors. Mechanistic investigation revealed that KDM4A histone demethylase is downregulated in SDHB-deficient tumors, and KDM4A loss (or inhibition) is sufficient to reduce ABCB1 expression, globally increase H3K9me3 levels, and sensitize cells to cytotoxic ABCB1 substrates. TCGA analysis confirmed correlated KDM4A-ABCB1 expression in SDHB-deficient cancers, with ABCB1 levels predicting drug sensitivity across cancer cell lines. Clinical analysis demonstrated that SDHB-mutant PPGL patients treated with vincristine-containing chemotherapy exhibited significantly longer progression-free survival compared to non-SDHB patients. These findings establish a novel metabolic-epigenetic pathway linking SDHB deficiency to ABCB1 silencing and provide rational basis for repurposing vincristine, and related ABCB1 substrate vinca alkaloids, across SDHB-deficient cancer types; offering an alternative precision treatment approach for these challenging malignancies.

https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.64898.title: A mouse model of metastasis-induced breast cancer cachexia with non-cachectic controls bearing isogenic primary tumors
https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.64898.abstract: Background Patients with advanced cancer frequently develop cachexia, an involuntary weight-loss condition that correlates strongly with metastatic burden. Despite this clinical association, metastasis is rarely considered in preclinical research of cancer cachexia, which is in part due to the lack of rigorously established animal models to investigate metastasis-associated cancer cachexia. Methods To establish an animal model of metastasis-associated cancer cachexia, here we focused on syngeneic mouse models of breast cancer. Using the metastatic 4T1 murine breast cancer cell line and its isogenic non-metastatic 67NR cell line, we generated primary tumors via orthotopic injection into the mammary fat pad and surgically resected the primary tumor to allow sufficient time for spontaneous metastatic outgrowth, or generated experimental lung metastases by direct intravenous injection into the tail vein. Across these tumor-bearing groups, we systematically characterized the metastatic burden and cachectic phenotypes of the mice, including body weight, food intake, body composition, muscle mass, grip strength, locomotor activity, energy expenditure, and respiratory exchange ratio. To isolate the contribution of reduced food intake to the cachectic phenotypes, we pair-fed orthotopic 4T1 tumor-bearing mice (which were non-cachectic) to mice with 4T1 lung metastases (which were cachectic). We further measured muscle atrophy gene expression and profiled circulating cytokines and metabolic hormones for the mouse groups. Results Body weight loss occurred exclusively in mice bearing lung metastases from 4T1 tumors, with no weight loss observed in mice bearing either primary 4T1 tumors or 67NR lung tumors, thus presenting a model of cancer cachexia that is driven by 4T1 lung metastasis. Comprehensive cachexia characterization demonstrated that the 4T1 metastasis model recapitulates all key features of cachexia, manifesting as reduced food intake (or anorexia), depletion of adipose tissues, loss of lean mass including muscle mass loss, and reduced grip strength. Pair-feeding non-cachectic primary 4T1 tumor-bearing mice to 4T1 metastatic mice led to the same losses in body weight, fat, and lean mass as in cachectic mice, but no change in grip strength, indicating that anorexia is the primary driver of tissue wasting whereas muscle weakness arises through a food intake-independent mechanism. Moreover, we identified distinct circulating cytokines and metabolic hormones associated with the metastasis-driven cachexia. Conclusions Our results establish a metastasis-induced breast cancer cachexia model with a tightly matched control group, providing a platform for the field to identify metastasis-derived cachectic mediators and pathways.

https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.64898.title: PERTURBATION OF THE AMINO ACID STRESS RESPONSE PATHWAY EXPOSES A METABOLIC VULNERABILITY IN MULTIPLE AGGRESSIVE CANCER SUBTYPES
https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.64898.abstract: Cancer cells frequently experience nutrient limitation and depend on adaptive stress-response pathways to maintain metabolic homeostasis. Here, we show that pharmacological perturbation of amino acid stress signaling exerts broad anti-tumor activity across multiple aggressive malignancies, including acute lymphoblastic leukemia, acute myeloid leukemia, triple-negative breast cancer, ovarian cancer, and neuroblastoma. Sensitivity to pathway modulation is associated with a chronic stress-adapted metabolic state marked by constitutive amino acid response signaling, elevated NFE2L2 expression, and reduced mitochondrial abundance despite evidence of efficient oxidative metabolism. Mechanistically, we demonstrate that the ATP-competitive compound GCN2-IN-6 does not phenocopy genetic GCN2 suppression and exhibits context-dependent effects on the amino acid stress response. Nevertheless, tumors experiencing chronic metabolic stress remain exquisitely sensitive to disruption of this adaptive network, regardless of whether signaling is perturbed through canonical inhibition or paradoxical activation.
