The highest uptake was observed in the liver [SUV mean 13.06 ± 2.68 (day 7)], with no significant uptake in the spleen, normal lymph nodes, bone marrow, or salivary glands. Tumor biopsies confirmed radioactivity. 89 Zr-CB307 selectively accumulated in PSMA-positive tumor lesions without specific uptake in PSMA-positive normal or lymphoid tissues in patients with mCRPC.

https://aacrjournals.org/mct/article/25/.title: Mechanisms of Acquired Resistance Following Dual EGFR/MET Inhibition in MET -Amplified EGFR TKI–Resistant Lung Cancer
https://aacrjournals.org/mct/article/25/.abstract: Abstract Mesenchymal–epithelial transition factor ( MET ) amplification is an epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) tyrosine kinase inhibitor (TKI) resistance mechanism that may be overcome by dual inhibition of EGFR and MET. However, acquired resistance after dual inhibition still occurs, and the mechanisms remain largely unknown. We analyzed resistance mechanisms after dual inhibition for MET amplification–mediated EGFR TKI resistance in lung cancer. Patient-derived cell lines were established before and after acquired resistance to dual inhibition, if possible. Potential resistance mechanisms were evaluated through signal pathway analysis and next-generation sequencing. Of 12 patients with resistance after EGFR/MET inhibition, 5 (42%) acquired oncogenic fusions (3 BRAF fusions, 1 ALK fusion, and 1 RET fusion), 1 (8%) developed EGFR T790M, 1 (8%) exhibited EGFR C797S, and 1 (8%) transformed to small cell. The EGFR T790M and ALK fusion responded to subsequent targeted therapies. Serial cell lines from a patient with EGFR L858R and MET amplification (PE5345), after resistance to osimertinib and capmatinib through gradual escalation of drug exposure in vitro (PE5345 os/cp R) and after clinical resistance to osimertinib and capmatinib (PE5867), were propagated. Novel acquired general transcription factor IIi– BRAF fusions emerged in PE5867. Osimertinib plus trametinib reversed resistance. PE5345 os/cp R overexpressed EGFR, which was inhibited by afatinib. Additionally, amivantamab induced significant antibody-dependent cell-mediated cytotoxicity (ADCC) against PE5345, PE5867, and PE5345 os/cp R. We found that resistance after dual inhibition is heterogeneous, but some might still be targetable. Amivantamab induced significant ADCC against both MET -amplified EGFR TKI-resistant cancer and resistant cells after dual EGFR/MET inhibition. Understanding resistance mechanisms may provide clues for subsequent therapy.

https://aacrjournals.org/mct/article/25/.title: Quantification of Antibody–Drug Conjugate Targets in Head and Neck Squamous Cell Carcinoma
https://aacrjournals.org/mct/article/25/.abstract: Abstract Antibody–drug conjugates (ADC) have shown clinical benefit in common solid tumors like breast cancer, lung cancer, and urothelial cancers but are just beginning to be investigated in head and neck cancer. We developed a quantitative immunofluorescence assay to reproducibly and accurately measure HER3 protein concentrations in formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded tissues. Using this assay, we measured HER3 protein concentrations in two head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC) tissue microarray cohorts containing 329 patients. Cell lines with mass spectrometry–measured protein concentrations were used to convert fluorescence signals to protein concentrations in amol/mm 2 . HER3, EGFR, and TROP2 showed a broad dynamic range in our cohorts with almost all of the cases above our assay’s limit of detection (LOD). Specifically, 100%, 97.5%, and 98.4% of cases have HER3, EGFR, and TROP2 levels above assay LOD. Interestingly, despite the previous demonstration of extremely low HER2 expression in HNSCC, 39.1% of cases showed HER2 expression above our assay LOD of 52.5 amol/mm 2 . When comparing between therapeutic targets, 97.2%, 99.3%, and 98.6% of cases are double-positive for HER3/EGFR, HER3/TROP2, and EGFR/TROP2, whereas only 34.2%, 34.6%, and 30.5% of cases are double-positive for HER3/HER2, EGFR/HER2, and TROP2/HER2. HER3, EGFR, and TROP2 are highly expressed in HNSCC. HER2 expression is relatively low in this HNSCC cohort compared with other ADC targets, but there are 39.1% of cases with detectable HER2 exceeding historic estimates. Overall, ADC target levels in HNSCC for approved ADCs suggest that patients with HNSCC may benefit from this class of drugs.

https://aacrjournals.org/mct/article/25/.title: GITR and GITR-L RNA Expression Levels Correlate with Better Survival and Response to Immunotherapy
https://aacrjournals.org/mct/article/25/.abstract: Abstract Glucocorticoid-induced tumor necrosis factor–related protein ( GITR ) is an immune stimulator; however, the correlation between GITR and GITR ligand ( GITR-L ) expression levels and patient outcomes is not yet characterized. This study explores transcript expression patterns of GITR and GITR-L in relation to outcomes in 489 patients with advanced/metastatic cancers. Given that survival curves for the different subgroups analyzed did not show proportional hazards, restricted mean survival time (RMST) analysis was utilized. In multivariate analysis accounting for RNA expression of other immune modulators, high GITR expression correlated with better RMST in all 489 patients and in the subset of 272 patients who did not receive immunotherapy (all P < 0.05), but not in the 217 patients who received immunotherapy. On the other hand, high GITR plus low/moderate GITR-L expression correlated with longer overall survival in patients who received immunotherapy (multivariate P < 0.05), but not in the patients who did not receive immunotherapy. No GITR -correlated progression-free survival associations were observed in patients who received immunotherapy. Finally, the immunomodulator proteins inducible T-cell costimulator and CD226 were associated with a significantly improved mean survival in patients with a high GITR plus low/moderate RNA expression pattern who received immunotherapy. Overall, these results suggest that high GITR RNA expression may be independently prognostic of better RMST in patients with advanced/metastatic cancers, but only the combination of high GITR plus low/moderate GITR-L expression is independently predictive of better RMST after treatment with immunotherapy.

https://aacrjournals.org/mct/article/25/.title: H3K9me3 Regulates IFNγ low Tex Cell Differentiation to Promote Colon Tumor Liver Metastasis
https://aacrjournals.org/mct/article/25/.abstract: Abstract Despite the breakthrough in immune checkpoint inhibitor (ICI) immunotherapy in human cancer, colon cancer, except for the small subset of microsatellite instable human colon cancer, does not respond to ICI immunotherapy. As liver metastasis accounts for more than 90% of human colon cancer cases and mortality, ICI efficacy is primarily a measurement of liver metastasis suppression. Using a colon tumor liver metastasis syngeneic mouse model, we determined that mouse colon tumor liver metastases not only do not respond to anti–PD-1 immunotherapy but also exhibit no susceptibility to tumor-specific cytotoxic T lymphocyte (CTL) adoptive transfer immunotherapy. Analysis of human colon cancer liver metastases single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) datasets revealed that histone methyltransferases of histone 3 lysine 9 trimethylation (H3K9me3) are upregulated in colon tumors and expressed in subsets of T cells in liver metastases of patients with human colon cancer. Targeted therapy with the H3K9me3-specific histone methyltransferase inhibitor F5446 suppresses colon tumor liver metastasis. scRNA-seq analysis revealed the accumulation of PD-1 + Tim3 + exhausted T (Tex) cells in mouse colon tumor liver metastases, and F5446 treatment increased the level of IFNγ high PD-1 low Tex cells. Furthermore, F5446 therapy increased IFNγ high intermediate Tex (Tex-int) cells in human colon cancer patient liver metastases–derived xenografts (PDX) and suppressed PDX growth in humanized mice. In patients with human colon cancer, response to pembrolizumab is associated with tumor-infiltrating IFNγ high Tex cells. Our findings determine that H3K9me3 promotes differentiation of Tex cells and targeting H3K9me3 is an effective approach to increase IFNγ high Tex-int cells to reinvigorate CTL functionality to suppress colon cancer liver metastasis.

https://aacrjournals.org/mct/article/25/.title: Selected Articles from This Issue
Potent Anti-Tumor Activity of the AXL-Targeted Antibody-Drug Conjugate, Mipasetamab Uzoptirine (ADCT-601), in Preclinical Models of Adenoid Cystic Carcinoma
https://aacrjournals.org/mct/article/25/.abstract: Abstract Adenoid cystic carcinoma (ACC) is a rare salivary gland malignancy with no FDA-approved systemic therapies and limited benefit from conventional treatments. Proteogenomic profiling has revealed consistent overexpression of AXL, providing a compelling rationale to pursue AXL as a novel therapeutic target. We investigated mipasetamab uzoptirine (ADCT-601), an AXL-targeting antibody-drug conjugate (ADC) with pyrrolobenzodiazepine dimer payload, in preclinical models of ACC. In vitro cytotoxicity was assessed in AXL-positive cell lines, and in vivo efficacy was evaluated using cell line xenograft and patient-derived xenograft (PDX) models. ADCT-601 demonstrated potent and selective cytotoxicity in AXL-expressing ACC cell lines. In xenograft models, a single administration at 0.5 or 1.0 mg/kg induced significant tumor regression, with complete tumor eradication observed at 1.0 mg/kg. Across a panel of ACC PDX models, ADCT-601 produced strong yet variable anti-tumor activity, with therapeutic response correlating with AXL expression levels. ADCT-601 demonstrates robust AXL expression linked to anti-tumor activity in preclinical models of ACC, establishing a proof of concept for targeting AXL in this rare cancer. These findings support clinical translation of AXL-targeting ADC as a novel biomarker-driven therapy for patients with ACC.

https://www.nature.com/articles/s41419-0.title: Prostaglandin promotes tumor growth via inhibiting tumor antigen presentation in triple-negative breast cancer
https://www.nature.com/articles/s41419-0.abstract: Hormones play important roles in various physiological and pathological activities of the human body. However, in triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC), the most intractable breast cancer subtype with limited therapeutic targets, what hormones exist and what role they play remained unclear. Here, using a large cohort of TNBC patients (n = 360), we discovered that the relative abundance of prostaglandin and its receptor prostaglandin E receptor 1 (PTGER1) mRNA expression were both related to poor prognosis. Mechanistically, this was achieved by the prostaglandin-PTGER1-KLK5 axis in tumor cells, which could induce an immune-inhibitory microenvironment by inhibiting tumor antigen presentation. We also found that PTGER1 promotes KLK5 transcription through transcription factor JUN, and KLK5 suppresses MHC-I expression and thus promoting immune evasion. Moreover, using preclinical models, we proved that inhibition of KLK5 could augment the immunotherapy efficacy in treating TNBC. Collectively, our findings offer novel insights into hormones and TNBC microenvironment, which may provide novel therapeutic targets for treating TNBC.

https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.64898.title: MET inhibition exploits conserved regulatory dependencies in malignant rhabdoid tumors
https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.64898.abstract: Malignant rhabdoid tumors (MRTs) are lethal, yet genomically simple childhood cancers characterised by universal SWI/SNF dysregulation. Despite this shared molecular framework, the regulatory programs sustaining MRTs and how they wire actionable dependencies, remain poorly defined. Here, we integrated single-cell multi-omic profiling and spatial transcriptomics across anatomically and molecularly diverse MRTs, generating a comprehensive multimodal MRT dataset at single-cell resolution. We leveraged this resource to identify candidate tumor-specific dependencies, which were subsequently functionally validated in vitro and in vivo in matched patient-derived models. We found that distinct malignant subpopulations are spatially patterned in complex environmentally shaped topologies, consistent with reciprocal interactions with stromal and immune compartments contributing to intratumoral transcriptional diversity. We identified recurrent transcriptional metaprograms conserved across patients and molecular subtypes, including a previously undescribed shared core rhabdoid program, as well as a metaprogram characterized by extracellular matrix interactions, and preferentially localized in tumor-stroma intermixed neighborhoods, supporting identification of niche conditioning cues. Mechanistically, we identified regulatory wiring driving these metaprograms, with the core shared rhabdoid programme coordinated by a circuit centred on TCF12, ZNF148 and CHD2. Guided by target nominations from our integrated analyses, we performed a curated drug screen using patient-derived MRT models and validated HGF/MET signaling as a selective vulnerability in extrarenal rhabdoid tumors. Pharmacologic MET inhibition was cytotoxic in sensitive models and induced a complete response in vivo using a clinically approved compound. Importantly, MET expression in primary tumors correlated with response, supporting biomarker-guided patient stratification for immediate clinical translation. Collectively, our findings define the molecular architecture of MRTs, reveal conserved regulatory programs beyond anatomical and molecular subtypes, and highlight a targetable signaling axis with immediate translational potential, establishing a framework for precision therapy in this lethal pediatric malignancy.

https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.64898.title: Glioblastoma model mouse rescue from mortality by brain-targeted catalytically-enhanced angiotensin-converting enzyme 2 mutant-antibody fusion protein
https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.64898.abstract: We have discovered that an engineered angiotensin-converting enzyme 2 (ACE2)-brain-targeted antibody fusion protein, referred to as ACE2dm-s1, improves survival of CT-2A xenograft glioblastoma (GBM) model mice when administered in combination with a small molecule STING agonist cancer therapeutic. Particularly striking about these survival results is that prior efforts that used losartan, a small molecule angiotensin receptor antagonist that acts on the same Renin-Angiotensin System (RAS) axis that is affected by the action of ACE2dm-s1, showed that this small molecule provided no survival benefit when used as an element of combination therapy in the same CT-2A GBM model used in our experiments. The improved CT-2A mouse survival, which was not observed for ACE2dm-s1 or STING agonist monotherapy, combines with our flow cytometry study results that revealed an ACE2dm-s1-mediated shift of brain immune cell populations toward an anti-tumoral composition to establish ACE2dm-s1's utility as a tumor microenvironment (TME) modulator that could serve as an adjuvant in increasing the efficacy of wide range of cancer treatment modalities including chemotherapeutic agents, immune checkpoint inhibitors, and CAR-T cells.

https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.64898.title: The Pregnane X Receptor (PXR) contributes to phenotypic plasticity and modulates the sensitivity to targeted therapies in melanoma
https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.64898.abstract: The challenge in treating advanced metastatic melanoma lies in the development of therapeutic resistance and the risk of recurrence. Understanding the mechanisms underlying tumor adaptation to treatment is therefore crucial, as they can directly influence therapeutic efficacy. Tolerance to targeted therapies may be influenced by drug transport and metabolism within tumors, processes regulated by numerous genes under the transcriptional control of the nuclear receptor PXR (Pregnane X Receptor, NR1I2). We revealed, for the first time, significant and heterogeneous expression of PXR in human melanoma samples. We previously showed that PXR can be activated by BRAF inhibitors (BRAFi), but not by MEK inhibitors (MEKi), which are currently used in combination for the treatment of BRAF-V600E-mutated melanoma. Here, we investigated whether PXR expression influences melanoma cell sensitivity to MAPK pathway inhibitors. Using BRAF-mutated human melanoma cell lines, we showed that stable PXR expression sensitizes cells to combined BRAFi/MEKi treatment. Transcriptomic analysis further revealed that PXR expression is associated with the upregulation of several phenotypic markers, with MITF identified as a major regulator in untreated PXR-overexpressing cells. These findings suggest that PXR promotes a shift toward a melanocytic phenotype, which is associated with increased sensitivity to BRAFi/MEKi treatment. Characterization of the PXR-associated transcriptional signature in melanoma may therefore have translational value for identifying patients more likely to benefit from targeted therapies and support the development of PXR as a predictive biomarker of therapeutic response.

https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.64898.title: Synthetic lethality of p97 inhibition and PSMC2-overexpressionovercomes bortezomib resistance in multiple myeloma
https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.64898.abstract: The aim of the present study was to analyze genomic profiles obtained from multiple myeloma (MM) patient tumors to identify prognostic classifiers of clinical response and survival following bortezomib monotherapy and then target key actionable classifiers that underly bortezomib resistance. We discovered higher levels of proteasome PSMC2 messenger RNA in myeloma cells from patients that did not respond to bortezomib and that higher PSMC2 expression correlated with inferior progression-free and overall survival. Pharmacologic screening revealed that CB-5339, an ATP-competitive inhibitor of the molecular chaperone p97/VCP that shuttles ubiquitin-conjugated substrates to proteasomes, was synthetic lethal in MM cells engineered to overexpress PSMC2. p97 co-immunoprecipitated with 26S proteasomes affinity-purified from PSMC2-overexpressing cells which exhibited greater activity and reduced bortezomib sensitivity relative to PSMC2-KO cells. Bortezomib treatment followed by in-situ cross-linking and western blotting revealed higher levels of K48- and K63-linkage-specific ubiquitin chains covalently bound to 26S proteasomes isolated from PSMC2-KO cells compared to proteasomes affinity-purified from PSMC2-overexpressing cells. Western blotting demonstrated higher levels of 19S RPs, 26S proteasomes, and a PSMC2-PSMC1-PSMD2 subcomplex in PSMC2-overexpressing cells relative to PSMC2-KO cells. CB-5339 and bortezomib co-treatment synergistically targeted tumor cells obtained from MM patients previously exposed to bortezomib therapy and reduced the in vivo growth of PSMC2-overexpressing myeloma xenografts in mice. Taken together, we have discovered a genetic vulnerability that provokes proteasome-intrinsic bortezomib resistance and validated the potential of synthetic lethality to guide therapeutic interventions. Our study reaffirms that transcriptomic heterogeneity in MM is a primary driver of prognostic variability.

https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.64898.title: Lineage tracing in rhabdoid tumor organoids and orthotopic xenografts reveals convergent transcriptional states
https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.64898.abstract: Malignant rhabdoid tumors (MRTs) are aggressive pediatric malignancies driven by loss of a single SWI/SNF subunit in an otherwise near-silent genome, yet they display extensive transcriptional heterogeneity. Whether this heterogeneity reflects the outgrowth of transcriptionally distinct clones, or states adopted independently of lineage, is unknown. Here we combined lentiviral lineage barcoding with single-cell RNA sequencing in two patient-derived renal MRT organoid models, followed through long-term in vitro culture and in a novel orthotopic xenograft setting. In both modalities, tumors and cultures became progressively restricted to a small number of lineages, and the clones that expanded were transcriptionally distinct from one another. Decomposing into gene expression programs showed that some transcriptional states were used broadly across lineages while others were confined to a few, and that lineages expanding independently, in separate cultures and separate animals, converged on the same restricted states. Individual lineages generally maintained their transcriptional identity across passaging and across anatomical sites, including in metastases, which arose from clones already expanded in the matched primary tumor. Which lineages came to dominate, however, differed between animals given the same starting population. Clonal outcome is therefore variable while the transcriptional states available to a tumor are drawn from a constrained and recurring repertoire.

https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.64898.title: Adaptation of breast cancer cells to serum-free defined medium reveals changes in proliferation, adhesion, and lipid metabolism
https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.64898.abstract: Cancer cell metabolic dependencies are strongly influenced by nutrient availability, yet conventional culture conditions contain non-physiological nutrient concentrations and poorly defined serum components that may obscure metabolic vulnerabilities. Here, we investigated the adaptation of three breast cancer cell lines to physiologically relevant, serum-free defined medium (DM). Using a stepwise reduction in fetal bovine serum (FBS), we evaluated proliferation, adhesion, morphology, and transcriptional changes in HER2-positive SK-BR-3, triple-negative MDA-MB-231, and ER-positive/HER2-positive BT-474 cells. The three cell lines differed substantially in their ability to adapt to serum-free conditions. MDA-MB-231 cells adapted readily, maintaining proliferation and adhesion without exogenous substrate coatings. SK-BR-3 cells also achieved sustained proliferation in serum-free DM, but required a serum-derived coating to maintain adhesion. In contrast, BT-474 cells failed to sustain adhesion and proliferation following complete serum withdrawal, although they remained proliferative in medium containing 1% FBS. Adapted cells retained characteristic HER2 or vimentin expression despite changes in morphology and proliferation. RNA sequencing revealed extensive transcriptional remodeling, including reduced expression of cell-cycle-associated programs in SK-BR-3 cells and enrichment of cholesterol homeostasis gene sets in SK-BR-3 and MDA-MB-231 cells. Expression of cholesterol regulatory genes, including SREBF2, HMGCR, and LDLR, increased across all three lines. Together, these findings highlight cell-line-specific adhesion requirements and shared metabolic responses to serum withdrawal, establishing a framework for developing defined culture systems to investigate cancer metabolic dependencies through genetic screening.

https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.64898.title: Whole methylome changes in Barrett's metaplasia, dysplasia, and cancer
https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.64898.abstract: The clinical management of Barrett's esophagus (BE) and the risk of esophageal adenocarcinoma (EAC) is dependent on the presence or absence of dysplasia. The histopathological diagnosis of dysplasia is unreliable however, and would benefit from additional diagnostic criteria. Here, we obtained EM-seq whole-genome methylation profiles from 86 samples across the BE/EAC disease spectrum, notably supplementing the scant existing methylation evidence for low-grade and high-grade dysplasia. While the bulk of methylation changes occur in the transition from normal squamous epithelium to intestinal metaplasia (non-dysplastic Barrett's esophagus), we identified a smaller set of changes that mark the onset of dysplasia and progression to EAC. Methylation changes were broadly independent of copy number variation. They were tightly anticorrelated with RNA-seq expression for some genes. Deconvolution of the bulk methylation signatures into constituent cell types revealed four sample groupings enriched with a particular cell type (squamous, columnar, lymphoid and erythroid cells), somewhat reflecting existing clinical classifications. We outline potential markers that could improve the diagnosis of metaplasia and dysplasia in EAC.

https://www.nature.com/articles/s41568-0.title: Astrocytes drive stroke-induced glioma progression
https://www.nature.com/articles/s41568-0.abstract: Ye et al. show that ischaemic stroke can drive glioma progression through microenvironmental remodelling of tumour-associated astrocytes.

https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-0.title: Alpha-aminoadipate in the saccharopine pathway promotes cancer metastasis through sumoylation of transcription machinery
https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-0.abstract: Despite studies linking metabolism and cancer, our understanding of the metabolite network that drives metastasis remains incomplete. Through a metabolic RNAi-based screen for cell invasion, we identify alpha-aminoadipate (2-AAA), the intermediate metabolite of aminoadipic semialdehyde synthase (AASS) in the saccharopine pathway, as a common pivotal factor in metastasis of human cancers. Metabolite-protein connectivity mapping reveals that 2-AAA binds to SAE1, a crucial component of the SUMO-activating enzyme E1, and enhances SAE1 recruitment to UBA2, facilitating sumoylation. 2-AAA-mediated sumoylation of the RNA polymerase subunit POLR2A then partially promotes cancer cell invasion by inducing the expression of metastasis-promoting genes, including SPG11 and KCTD7. Targeting AASS with cetalkonium chloride, a newly identified small molecule inhibitor against AASS, attenuates cancer cell invasion and tumor metastasis. Our study highlights the mechanism by which metastasis is mediated by metabolite-driven sumoylation and indicates AASS as an effective therapeutic target for mitigating metastatic cancer progression. The role of metabolism in metastasis remains unclear. Here, a metabolic RNAi-based screen for cell invasion and metabolite-protein connectivity mapping reveals a mechanism by which sumoylation driven by alpha-aminoadipate, the intermediate metabolite of aminoadipic semialdehyde synthase, drives metastasis.

https://www.nature.com/articles/s41419-0.title: Death pathway plasticity in therapy resistance: mechanistic switches and translational opportunities
https://www.nature.com/articles/s41419-0.abstract: Regulated cell death (RCD) programs in cancer have traditionally been framed as discrete pathways defined by signature effectors, including caspases (apoptosis), RIPK1–RIPK3–MLKL (necroptosis), gasdermins (pyroptosis), lipid peroxidation control nodes (ferroptosis), PARP1–AIF/MIF (parthanatos), and FDX1-dependent lipoylation stress (cuproptosis). Here, we advance an integrated view in which these programs function as a configurable decision network rather than isolated routes. Therapeutic and microenvironmental inputs, such as death ligands, chemoradiotherapy, targeted agents, PARP inhibition, copper ionophores, nutrient/oxidative stress, extracellular matrix detachment, and cytotoxic T-cell pressure, converge on shared hub modules that act as rheostats, routing cells toward distinct execution outcomes or into drug-tolerant persister states. This circuit-level framing explains context-dependent switching and mixed phenotypes, including caspase-8/c-FLIP control of apoptosis–necroptosis, caspase–gasdermin coupling of apoptosis–pyroptosis, and metabolic–redox tuning of ferroptosis susceptibility via SLC7A11–GPX4–ACSL4–FSP1 and autophagy-linked lipid/iron handling. We outline a biomarker and functional assay framework to map tumor death wiring from biopsies and organoid challenges, enabling rational combination strategies that exploit death program plasticity while anticipating resistance and inflammatory toxicities.

https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-0.title: Transformer-based endoscopic polyp detection with structural reparameterization and dynamic upsampling
https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-0.abstract: Accurate polyp detection is important for colorectal cancer prevention, while practical deployment requires reliable localization, manageable model complexity, and robust detection performance. This paper presents an improved RT-DETR-r18 detector for endoscopic polyp detection. The proposed C2f_RCB backbone construction embeds a UniRepLKNet-derived large-kernel reparameterization transformation within the C2f hierarchy, while the original DySample operator replaces the two nearest-neighbor upsampling layers in the top-down neck. A source-code audit shows that the K = 7 DilatedReparamBlock contains one 7 × 7 depthwise main branch and three auxiliary depthwise branches, namely 5 × 5 with dilation 1, 3 × 3 with dilation 2, and 3 × 3 with dilation 3. During deployment, these spatial branches are merged into an equivalent 7 × 7 depthwise convolution, and compatible normalization/affine terms are further folded into adjacent operators by the UniRepLKNetBlock deployment routine; SE, GELU, GRN normalization/scaling, channel projections, residual operations, and DySample remain explicit in the inference graph. Under the archived evaluation protocol, the complete model achieves 96.8% precision, 93.0% recall, 97.1% mAP@0.5, and 79.5% mAP@0.5:0.95, with 13.90 million parameters and 46.6 GFLOPs. These values were obtained from an expanded-file split later found to contain augmented variants of the same original samples across subsets and should therefore be regarded as preliminary until leakage-free retraining is completed. The current evidence supports a compact, localization-oriented trade-off, but not a standardized runtime advantage, clinical readiness, or leakage-free generalization.

https://www.nature.com/articles/s41588-0.title: Longitudinal single-cell profiling of breast tumors highlights immune and epigenetic mechanisms associated with sensitivity to aromatase inhibitors
https://www.nature.com/articles/s41588-0.abstract: Estrogen receptor (ER)-positive breast cancer treatment is based primarily on endocrine therapy. To dissect mechanisms of sensitivity to aromatase inhibitors in ER-positive breast cancer, we profiled tumor biopsies from 25 patients during neoadjuvant therapy using single-cell RNA sequencing, immune receptor sequencing and enhancer activity mapping. Malignant cells with high ER signaling and elevated activity of enhancers with ER binding sites were sensitive to treatment. Resistance was associated with androgen receptor signaling, dedifferentiation and epithelial–mesenchymal transition. Poor responders preferentially used the androgen receptor cis-regulome under treatment pressure. The baseline tumor microenvironment was associated with tumor downstaging. Poor responders exhibited a ‘hot’, yet ineffective immune landscape enriched for naive lymphoid and undifferentiated myeloid cells. Good responders showed an active immune microenvironment with sustained clonal expansion of T cells. Our longitudinal single-cell analyses elucidate the genetic, cellular and epigenetic mechanisms driving sensitivity and resistance to neoadjuvant aromatase inhibition in ER-positive breast cancer. This longitudinal single-cell study of estrogen receptor (ER)-positive breast cancer suggests that strong estrogen signaling, ER-linked enhancers and active T cell responses could predict sensitivity to aromatase inhibitors, whereas resistance involves androgen signaling though hormone-sensing enhancer activity.

https://www.nature.com/articles/s41416-0.title: Long-term fatigue based on the EORTC QLQ-C30 up to five years after radiotherapy and its trajectories in men diagnosed with non-metastatic prostate cancer in the international REQUITE study
https://www.nature.com/articles/s41416-0.abstract: Fatigue is a common symptom in cancer patients associated with impaired quality of life (QoL). Little is known about long-term fatigue trajectories in prostate cancer (PCa) patients. Using the European Organisation for Research and Treatment of Cancer Quality of Life Group Core Questionnaire (EORTC QLQ-C30), 1758 men treated with radiotherapy (2014–2016) for non-metastatic PCa prospectively reported fatigue up to five years later. Associations between pre-radiotherapy characteristics and clinically important fatigue (Score: ≥39/100) two years post-radiotherapy were investigated using logistic regression. Fatigue trajectories were explored using latent class growth analysis and multinomial regression. About 35% (608/1758) of patients experienced clinically important fatigue at least once from the start of radiotherapy up to five years later. Two years post-radiotherapy, 14% of patients reported fatigue, which was associated with pre-radiotherapy fatigue level (OR: 8.67), self-reported diabetes (OR: 1.94), BMI (OR: 1.07), and age (OR: 1.03). Long-term fatigue was strongly linked to pain, insomnia, pelvic symptoms, functional impairments, and reduced QoL. Four fatigue trajectories were identified, characterised by low (45%), moderate (42%), elevated and decreasing (8%), and (6%) increasing mean fatigue levels. Diabetes was associated with a 6 percentage point increase in the probability of experiencing an increasing fatigue trajectory. The findings emphasise the need for early identification of PCa patients susceptible to long-term fatigue. PCa patients with elevated pre-radiotherapy fatigue levels and diabetes may require closer monitoring in risk-stratified aftercare programmes.

https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-0.title: A spatiotemporal cancer cell trajectory underlies glioblastoma heterogeneity
https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-0.abstract: Cancer cells show highly heterogeneous and plastic states in glioblastoma, an incurable brain tumour1–5. However, how these malignant states arise and whether they follow defined cellular trajectories across tumours is poorly understood. Here we generated a deep single-cell and spatial multi-omic atlas of human glioblastoma that pairs transcriptomic, epigenomic and genomic profiling of 12 tumours across many regions. We identify that glioblastoma heterogeneity is driven by spatially patterned transitions of cancer cells from developmental-like states towards those defined by a glial injury response and hypoxia. This cellular trajectory regionalizes tumours into distinct tissue microenvironments and manifests in a molecularly conserved manner across tumours as well as genetically distinct tumour subclones. Consistently, using a new deep-learning framework to map cancer cell states jointly with clones in situ, we show that tumour subclones are finely spatially intermixed through glioblastoma tissue microenvironments. We validate this cellular trajectory by using somatic mutation-based hierarchies in vivo and an experimental patient-derived organoid model ex vivo. Finally, we show that this cancer cell trajectory is intimately linked to myeloid heterogeneity and unfolds across regionalized myeloid signalling environments. Our findings define a stereotyped trajectory of cancer cells in glioblastoma and unify glioblastoma tumour heterogeneity into a tractable cellular and tissue framework. A deep single-cell and spatial multi-omic atlas of human glioblastoma is generated, pairing transcriptomic, epigenomic and genomic profiling, and tracing glioblastoma tumour heterogeneity to a stereotyped and spatially patterned trajectory of cancer cells.

https://www.nature.com/articles/s41591-0.title: A tumor transcriptomic atlas across eight decades of life reveals distinct features of early-onset colorectal cancer
https://www.nature.com/articles/s41591-0.abstract: The incidence of early-onset colorectal cancer is rising, but whether it is biologically distinct from average-onset disease is unclear. Mapping of the transcriptome of colorectal tumors across the age continuum shows that tumors in younger adults contain more stromal cells and have increased expression of long non-coding RNAs and genes associated with epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition.

https://www.nature.com/articles/s41419-0.title: PD-L1 is associated with metabolic adaptation and mitochondrial remodeling in NSCLC cells
https://www.nature.com/articles/s41419-0.abstract: Tumor metabolism is governed by a complex network of processes that can influence immune evasion. Metabolic dysregulation in tumor cells can lead to the accumulation of metabolites that may influence immune cell function. However, the relationship between PD-L1 expression and tumor cell metabolism remains incompletely understood. Here, we report that PD-L1 expression in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) cells is associated with increased endocytic activity and altered metabolic flux, particularly in the tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle. PD-L1 expression is aleo associated with mitochondrial remodeling, including alterations in proteins involved in mitochondrial fusion and fission and in mitochondrial respiratory chain components. Integrated multi-omics analyses further identified differential H3K9me3 patterns associated with differences in PD-L1 expression status, including differential H3K9me3 patterns at the PTPRN2 locus. Collectively, our findings suggest that differences in PD-L1 expression status are associated with metabolic, mitochondrial, and epigenetic alterations in NSCLC cells.

https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-0.title: A novel ferro-aging-related gene signature for prognosis and targeted drug prediction in cervical cancer
https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-0.abstract: Cervical cancer (CESC) remains a leading cause of cancer-related mortality in women. Recent studies have identified ferro-aging as a genuine biological pathway in primates, representing an iron-dependent metabolic process. However, cellular ageing and the decline in overall physiological function play a crucial role in tumour progression. Based on this, we have established a prognostic model related to ferro-aging and evaluated its predictive and diagnostic value in cervical cancer. We integrated data from the The Cancer Genomics Atlas (TCGA), the Gene Expression Online Resource (GEO) and single-cell RNA sequencing datasets. Following the identification of ferro-aging-related gene (FARGs) based on the literature, we constructed a prognostic model using machine learning algorithms and analysed model features via Shapley-based interpretability (SHAP) analysis. The Scissor algorithm was employed to evaluate cell populations associated with high- and low-risk groups. Studies on intercellular communication and spatial transcriptomics revealed the process of tumour microenvironment remodelling. Finally, potential therapeutic compounds were identified through AI-assisted virtual screening and molecular docking. A total of eight FAR model genes were ultimately identified: DUOX1, E2F1, IL1B, KEAP1, MAP3K14, SLAMF8, TFRC and TNFAIP3. This study constructed and validated a novel risk profile model comprising these eight ferro-aging-related genes; this model demonstrated moderate prognostic discriminatory power in both internal and external cohorts, with the tumour microenvironment in the high-risk group exhibiting an immunosuppressive state. Using single-cell RNA sequencing to assess cellular heterogeneity, macrophages, epithelial cells and CD8+ T cells were identified as key factors in CESC progression. Pseudotime analysis was performed to visualize the expression levels of FARGs along the pseudotime axis and explore how FARGs participate in the dynamic process of EndMT. Spatial transcriptomics was employed to map the distribution and expression of FARGs within epithelial cells in the tumour microenvironment. Intercellular communication intensity was increased in the low-risk group, with epithelial cells in this group signalling to macrophages via the APP-CD74 pathway. Drug screening indicated that BRD-A56371469 is likely to bind to DUOX1. The FARG signature is a candidate prognostic indicator for CESC, meriting further exploration in prospective cohorts. In silico screening prioritized BRD‑A56371469 as a computational binding scaffold for DUOX1, warranting subsequent experimental validation.

https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-0.title: Ultrasound-responsive erythrocyte-fused vesicles for targeted theranostics of Wilms’ tumor
https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-0.abstract: Wilms’ tumor (WT) is the most common renal tumor of childhood. Despite clinical chemotherapy and radiotherapy showed favorable treatment-response, serious side effects caused by the absence of efficient targeted therapeutic fumulations remain a major challenge in clinical practice. Here, we identified neural cell adhesion molecule 1 (NCAM1) as a potential delivery target by bioinformatic analysis and selected an NCAM1-targeting peptide (NTP) as its specific ligand. Then, we prepared NTP-modified vesicles loaded with doxorubicin (DOX) and perfluorohexane (PFH) (NDP), which were fused with red blood cell (RBC) membranes to obtain NDP@RBC, where “@RBC” denotes fusion with RBC membranes. After administration, the RBC membrane prolonged the circulation time of NDP@RBC, with 10.95% of baseline fluorescence retained at 48 h, compared with undetectable levels for free DOX and NDP. The NTP significantly facilitated WT cell recognition and cellular uptake, with the mean fluorescence intensity at 2 h reaching 0.95 × 105 compared with 0.62 × 105or the non-targeted DP@RBC group. PFH encapsulated in the vesicles enhanced the ultrasound (US) imaging signal and mediated ultrasound-responsive drug release, with cumulative DOX release reaching 85% under ultrasound versus 13.3% without ultrasound at 60 min. In vivo animal experiments showed that NDP@RBC + US suppressed tumor growth, with a tumor growth inhibition rate of 80.22% compared with the PBS group and 19.27% compared with NDP@RBC alone. In summary, this work highlights the importance of targeted theranostics of WT.

https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-0.title: Von Hippel-Lindau (VHL) prevents excessive protein aggregation and mediates aggrephagy by modulating the liquidity of p62 condensates
https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-0.abstract: Loss of proteostasis can cause protein aggregation and trigger aggrephagy, yet how these biological processes are coordinated remains unclear. Here, we showed that p62 condensates transit from a gel-like to a more liquid-like state in response to proteotoxic stress. VHL was recruited to aggresomes and colocalizes with p62, which is crucial for p62 to perform its distinct functions in aggresome formation and autophagic degradation. Mechanistically, VHL binds to p62 through its IDR1 region and increases the liquid-like properties via IDR2 region. VHL depletion or disease-associated IDR2 mutations impair p62 condensate dynamics, leading to excessive accumulation of aggregated proteins and concomitant KEAP1 sequestration/NRF2 stabilization. A chimeric peptide linking the p62 PB1 domain to VHL IDR2 recapitulates VHL’s fluidity-promoting activity and suppresses tumorigenesis and protein aggregation. Overall, our findings reveal an HIF-independent tumor-suppressive role of VHL in regulating proteostasis and suggest a new treatment for cancer through the targeting of condensate dynamics. VHL shows an unexpected HIF-independent role in maintaining protein homeostasis under proteotoxic stress, namely, by increasing the liquidity of p62 condensates and orchestrating aggresome formation and subsequent aggrephagy.

https://www.nature.com/articles/s41419-0.title: Human cytomegalovirus reprograms breast cancer cells toward a triple-negative and metastatic phenotype
https://www.nature.com/articles/s41419-0.abstract: Breast cancer remains a leading cause of cancer-related mortality in women, with triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) representing the most aggressive subtype due to the absence of effective targeted therapies. Human cytomegalovirus (HCMV) has increasingly been implicated in tumor progression; however, its mechanistic contribution to breast cancer pathogenesis remains poorly understood. Here, we investigated whether HCMV promotes TNBC-associated phenotypic reprogramming through modulation of key prognostic receptors and tumor-associated cellular pathways. Using transcriptomic, proteomic, molecular, and functional analyses in luminal (MCF7) and HER2-positive (SKBR3) breast cancer models, we demonstrate that HCMV infection induces extensive host-cell reprogramming characterized by suppression of ESR1, PGR, and ERBB2 expression at both transcript and protein levels, resulting in a receptor-suppressed state with selected TNBC-associated molecular features. Mechanistically, HCMV immediate-early (IE) proteins and the viral miRNAs hcmv-miR-US25-2-3p, hcmv-miR-UL36-3p, and hcmv-miR-UL22A-3p mediated repression of ESR1 and PGR. In contrast, ERBB2 downregulation occurred indirectly through virus-mediated suppression of the EGFR/CyclinD1/CDK4/6 axis, resulting in stabilization of the RB/E2F4 repressor complex at the ERBB2 promoter. Beyond receptor suppression, HCMV infection induced extensive inflammatory, metabolic, and epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT)-associated remodeling consistent with a state of virus-driven phenotypic plasticity. Although infected cells displayed reduced proliferative and metabolic activity, they exhibited enhanced invasion, EMT-associated transcriptional reprogramming, and increased metastatic dissemination in zebrafish xenograft models. Elevated TGFβ signaling and partial EMT-like states likely contributed to this invasive phenotype. Collectively, our findings identify multiple viral mechanisms through which HCMV promotes TNBC-associated cellular reprogramming and metastatic behavior. These results support a previously unrecognized role for HCMV in driving aggressive breast cancer phenotypes and highlight HCMV-targeted therapeutic strategies as potential approaches for HCMV-positive TNBC.

https://www.nature.com/articles/s41698-0.title: MedGenAgent: a closed-loop agent for oncology CT foundation model pretraining
https://www.nature.com/articles/s41698-0.abstract: Oncology computed tomography (CT) foundation models require large, high-quality training datasets. However, the collection and annotation of such data are costly and time-consuming because tumors occur across multiple anatomical regions and have complex three-dimensional (3D) structures. Strict privacy constraints and institutional variation further limit the availability of large-scale oncology CT datasets. Here, we propose MedGenAgent, a closed-loop agent that supports oncology CT foundation model pretraining in data-constrained settings by iteratively constructing a lesion-rich, anatomically balanced 3D pretraining dataset. MedGenAgent incorporates a Specification resolver tool for structured task parsing and a central Orchestrator tool to coordinate the entire closed-loop agent workflow by leveraging both an Execution layer (including the MAISI synthesis model node for 3D oncology CT sample synthesis, the MedGemma vision-language model node for automated quality control, and the foundation model training node) and a Memory store tool for iterative, feedback-driven updates. Through the synergy of these tools, MedGenAgent synthesized 11,159 CT samples and retained 11,000 quality-controlled samples. By first leveraging this synthetic dataset for pretraining and then aligning with real-world data using only 4400 DeepLesion samples, representing 38.37% of the data used for baseline pretraining, the MedGenAgent-pretrained foundation model achieved performance comparable to the full-data baseline across three retrospective downstream tasks: lesion anatomical site classification, nodule malignancy classification, and cross-institutional NSCLC overall survival classification. Furthermore, automated quality control, independent physician assessment, and workflow analysis demonstrated the construction of a quality-controlled synthetic CT dataset while revealing regional variation in sample quality. Together, these results show that MedGenAgent can autonomously construct quality-controlled synthetic CT data that support the competitive performance of oncology CT foundation models when annotated real-world data are limited.

https://www.nature.com/articles/d41586-0.title: A death sentence for ‘sloppy’ cancers
https://www.nature.com/articles/d41586-0.abstract: The process of making protein from RNA can go awry in cancer cells. This malfunction might be harnessed to create an effective gene-therapy tool that targets tumours.

https://www.nature.com/articles/s42003-0.title: Glutathione S transferase assembled gold silver nanoclusters activate cGAS STING immunity in breast cancer
https://www.nature.com/articles/s42003-0.abstract: Breast cancer often returns or spreads after treatment, and therapies that can destroy tumors while also engaging the immune system are urgently needed. However, it remains difficult to design safe nanomaterials that both heat tumors under light and turn dying cancer cells into signals that support long-lasting antitumor immunity. Here we show that glutathione S-transferase guided self-assembly produces ultrasmall glutathione-stabilized gold-silver nanoclusters for laser-assisted breast cancer treatment. Under near-infrared light, these nanoclusters efficiently generate heat and oxidative stress, killing breast cancer cells and releasing immune-stimulating signals. The treatment activates the cGAS-STING immune signaling pathway, promotes dendritic cell maturation, increases tumor-killing T cell infiltration, and strengthens memory T cell responses. In mouse models of primary and metastatic breast cancer, the nanoclusters preferentially accumulate in tumors and suppress tumor growth, metastasis, and relapse with limited signs of toxicity. This protein-guided nanocluster strategy provides a potential route for combining localized light-based treatment with systemic antitumor immunity and may support the future development of safer and more durable cancer nanomedicines. GST-mediated self-assembly of gold-silver nanoclusters activates cGAS-STING signaling and remodels antitumor immunity, enabling photothermal-immunotherapy to inhibit breast cancer growth, metastasis and recurrence.

https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-0.title: Monitoring initial dose to navigate ARPI treatment outcomes (MINATO study)
https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-0.abstract: Androgen receptor pathway inhibitors (ARPIs: apalutamide, enzalutamide, darolutamide, abiraterone) are central to the first-line treatment of castration-sensitive prostate cancer (CSPC). Although their efficacy has been established in large-scale clinical trials, real-world evaluations of drug tolerability and related outcomes remain scarce. Using a large prescription database, this study analyzed the continuation of ARPIs in CSPC and the impact of dose reduction on time to castration-resistant prostate cancer (CRPC). This was a retrospective cohort study using a medical information database (MDV). Among patients with prostate cancer, those who initiated a first-line ARPI while in the CSPC state (no CRPC diagnosis) were included. First, as indicators of treatment continuation, same-drug dose reduction among patients starting at the standard dose and switching to another agent were evaluated from the date of first-drug initiation using the Kaplan-Meier method and the log-rank test; the timing of dose reduction and the distribution of the final administered dose were also described. Next, as an indicator of prognosis, the time from first-drug initiation to the first CRPC diagnosis was evaluated by first-line agent using the Kaplan-Meier method and the log-rank test. Time to CRPC was examined in two cohorts: a full-period cohort and a post-approval cohort comprising patients who initiated treatment on or after the approval date of darolutamide plus docetaxel (February 24, 2023). In addition, for apalutamide and enzalutamide, time to CRPC was compared by starting dose (full dose vs. reduced-dose start) and by the presence or absence of on-treatment dose reduction. The first-line agents were enzalutamide in 8,254 patients (50%), abiraterone in 4,896 (30%), apalutamide in 2,318 (14%), and darolutamide in 951 (6%). Regarding dose reduction, the proportion of patients reducing the dose among standard-dose starters was highest for apalutamide (28%), versus 10% for enzalutamide, 12% for darolutamide, and 7% for abiraterone (log-rank P < 0.001). Apalutamide dose reductions were concentrated within the first 0–6 months. The proportion maintaining the standard dose as the final dose was only 52% for apalutamide, compared with 70–87% for the other agents. In contrast, switching was infrequent for all agents, with no significant difference among them (P = 0.060). Next, in the full-period cohort, the time to CRPC differed significantly among the agents (overall log-rank P < 0.001) and was longest for apalutamide; the same ordering was observed in the post-approval cohort, in which all four agents were simultaneously available (P < 0.001). Of note, apalutamide had the highest proportion of censoring (76% in the full-period and 90% in the post-approval cohort), and follow-up was uneven across agents. With respect to dose, apalutamide showed no significant difference in time to CRPC by either starting dose or the presence or absence of on-treatment reduction (starting dose P = 0.74; 6-month landmark P = 0.12). Enzalutamide showed a difference by starting dose (P < 0.001) but no difference by the presence or absence of on-treatment reduction (landmark P = 0.72). Because the four agents are prescribed to different patient populations under Japanese reimbursement rules, these between-agent differences are descriptive and are not efficacy comparisons. This study evaluated the continuation and dose-reduction patterns of various ARPIs as first-line treatment for CSPC. It also evaluated the association between dose reduction and time to CRPC.

https://www.nature.com/articles/s41591-0.title: Perioperative ivonescimab with or without chemotherapy in resectable non-small cell lung cancer: a phase 2 trial
https://www.nature.com/articles/s41591-0.abstract: Resectable non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) carries a high risk of postoperative recurrence, underscoring the need for effective perioperative therapies. This nonrandomized, noncomparative phase 2 trial evaluated neoadjuvant ivonescimab monotherapy (cohort 1) or in combination with chemotherapy (cohort 2), followed by surgery and adjuvant ivonescimab. In cohort 2, the major pathological response (MPR) rate was 70.1% (47/67; 95% confidence interval (CI) = 57.7–80.7); the lower bound of the 80% two-sided CI exceeded the historical control rate of 41% and the primary endpoint was met. The MPR rate in cohort 1 was 60.0% (6/10; 95% CI = 26.2–87.8). Among patients who achieved MPR, 83.3% (5/6) in cohort 1 and 97.9% (46/47) in cohort 2 had residual viable tumor (RVT) of ≤5%, respectively. Grade 3 or higher treatment-related adverse events (AEs) occurred in 36.4% (4/11) patients in cohort 1 and 30.4% (24/79) of those in cohort 2, with no grade 3 or higher hemorrhage or treatment-related death. Treatment-related surgery delay occurred in one (1.3%) patient. Surgery-related AEs related to ivonescimab occurred in 10.0% (1/10) and 10.4% (7/67) patients in the two cohorts, respectively, with no grade 3 or higher events reported. These data support perioperative ivonescimab with or without chemotherapy as a promising strategy for resectable NSCLC. ClinicalTrials.gov identifier: NCT05247684 . In a nonrandomized phase 2 trial, patients with resectable non-small cell lung cancer received perioperative ivonescimab as monotherapy or with chemotherapy, leading to encouraging pathological response rates in both cohorts, and sustained circulating tumor DNA negativity throughout neoadjuvant therapy may be predictive of response.

https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-0.title: In vivo CAR-T double knockout screen maps synergistic antitumour gene pairs
https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-0.abstract: Chimeric antigen receptor (CAR)-T cell therapy has transformed the treatment of haematological malignancies, but its efficacy remains limited by multiple negative regulatory mechanisms intrinsic to T cells1–4. Here we perform a high-throughput in vivo CAR-T double-knockout (DKO) CRISPR screen, and identify multiple DKO gene pairs that are both effective and synergistic. The top pair, NR4A1–SOCS3 DKO, has multiple favourable immunological features. Whole-transcriptome profiling and in vivo single-cell RNA sequencing reveal that NR4A1–SOCS3 DKO specifically upregulates metabolic pathways in CAR-T cells, which show significantly higher metabolic fitness and mitochondrial activity. NR4A1–SOCS3 DKO CAR-T cells and T cells exhibit exceptionally potent antitumour efficacy and long-term tumour control across different tumour models without compromising safety features. NR4A1–SOCS3 DKO outperforms several benchmark single-gene and dual-gene modifications in T cells and CAR-T cells5–9. These data demonstrate high-throughput in vivo CAR-T DKO screening for rapid discovery of combination targets, and establish NR4A1–SOCS3 as a promising pair of intracellular checkpoints to engineer high-performance CAR-T therapies against cancer. Using high-throughput in vivo CAR-T double knockout screening, synergistic gene combinations to improve CAR-T cell therapy are revealed.

https://www.nature.com/articles/s41588-0.title: The Participant Engagement and Cancer Genome Sequencing Network to accelerate research in rare and understudied cancers
https://www.nature.com/articles/s41588-0.abstract: The genomic characterization of cancers has considerably advanced research and clinical practice. However, critical gaps remain, including limited knowledge of tumor profiles in rare cancers and populations understudied in genomic research and insufficient integration of genomic, clinical and epidemiologic data. This Perspective highlights the Participant Engagement and Cancer Genome Sequencing (PE-CGS) Network, established by the US National Cancer Institute to address knowledge gaps in rare and understudied cancers. PE-CGS comprises five research centers supported by a coordinating center and guided by an external advisory panel. Collaborations across PE-CGS are grounded in shared values of participant-centeredness, engagement, access, collaboration and innovation. Activities emphasize participant engagement throughout the research process, including the return of results and collection of clinical and epidemiologic data alongside paired tumor/germline sequencing. PE-CGS demonstrates how engagement, return of results and comprehensive data collection can be integrated to support participant-centered cancer genomics research and accelerate research in rare and understudied cancers. The Participant Engagement and Cancer Genome Sequencing (PE-CGS) Network integrates participant engagement, return of genomic results and comprehensive data collection to advance cancer genomics research involving rare and understudied cancers.

https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-0.title: Decoding the regulatory programs governing glioblastoma plasticity
https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-0.abstract: Glioblastoma is incurable and resistant to therapy despite genomic stability under treatment1–8, suggesting that non-genetic cellular plasticity is a central driver of progression. Whether such plasticity reflects stochastic state switching or is governed by predictable gene regulation has remained unclear9–13. Here we introduce scDORI (single-cell deep multi-omic regulatory inference)—a deep-learning framework that infers enhancer-driven gene-regulatory networks at single-cell resolution—and apply it to single-nucleus multiome profiles of more than one million cells from primary glioblastomas. Integrating computational inference with systematic perturbation screens across patient-derived models, we show that a structured regulatory program with an asymmetric interplay of activators and repressors governs cellular plasticity in glioblastoma. The resulting transition landscape is hierarchical and predictable, but permits cross-lineage trajectories that are absent from normal neurodevelopment. Within this landscape, low-plasticity states such as the neuronal-like state are not stable differentiation end points but actively maintained configurations, stabilized by a network of safeguard repressors that silence alternative fates. We identify MYT1L as the dominant member of this network, and show that it binds to and represses master regulators of every alternative state to consolidate neuronal-like identity. MYT1L restricted plasticity even under standard-of-care therapy and suppressed tumour growth and invasion in vivo. Conversely, loss of MYT1L reactivated plasticity and accelerated malignant features, indicating that low-plasticity identity requires continuous repression. These findings reframe malignant cell state stability as a balance between activation and continuous repression, and nominate safeguard repressors as candidate therapeutic targets that are distinct from differentiation-inducing activators, with potential relevance across cancers in which phenotypic switching drives therapy resistance. Multi-omic analyses of cells from patients with glioblastoma (GB) provide insight into the role of non-genetic cellular plasticity in disease progression, showing that state stability in GB cells is controlled by a network of interacting activators and repressors.

https://www.nature.com/articles/s12276-0.title: Stromal APOL4 defines a cancer-associated fibroblast state that organizes a chemosensitive niche in ovarian cancer
https://www.nature.com/articles/s12276-0.abstract: Despite initial high response rates to platinum-based chemotherapy in high-grade serous ovarian carcinoma, most patients eventually develop resistance, and the contribution of the tumor microenvironment to treatment outcomes has remained underexplored relative to tumor cell-intrinsic mechanisms. Combining patient-derived ex vivo carboplatin screening with bulk and single-cell transcriptomics, functional perturbation in cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs), and high-resolution spatial transcriptomics, we identified stromal apolipoprotein L4 (APOL4) as a biomarker of platinum sensitivity. The ex vivo classification showed directional concordance with clinical platinum response, and stromal APOL4 expression predicted favorable outcomes across multiple validation cohorts. APOL4 specifically marked a transcriptionally distinct CAF subtype (CAF-1) that extended beyond canonical CAF states and exhibited high matrix metalloproteinase and immune-activating cytokine expression. APOL4 knockdown attenuated the CAF-1 transcriptional program, and in 3D tumor–CAF co-cultures conferred carboplatin resistance to 12 of 14 ovarian cancer cell lines, providing causal evidence that stromal APOL4 supports platinum sensitivity in a tumor cell-extrinsic manner. NicheNet analysis revealed bidirectionally asymmetric communication: CAF-1 engaged non-stressed cancer cells through epithelial integrity-supporting axes, whereas other CAFs preferentially reinforced stressed, drug-tolerant cancer cells through canonical chemoresistance circuits. High-resolution Xenium spatial transcriptomics revealed a contact-restricted spatial association between CAF-1 proximity and reduced cancer-cell stress, defining a low-stress, immune-infiltrated niche that is spatially and compositionally distinct from the stress-enriched, immune-poor niche associated with CAF-2, with CAF-3 sharing features of both compartments. These findings identify stromal APOL4–CAF-1 as a prognostic biomarker and a functional contributor linking stromal matrix remodeling to platinum sensitivity and associated with an immune-infiltrated microenvironment, highlighting CAF-1-targeted strategies to enhance chemotherapy efficacy. In high-grade serous ovarian carcinoma, initial chemotherapy response is crucial, yet resistance often develops, highlighting the need for predictive biomarkers. This study identifies apolipoprotein L4 (APOL4) as a stromal marker linked to platinum sensitivity, addressing the complexity of tumor microenvironment influences on treatment outcomes. Researchers used patient-derived ex vivo drug testing, transcriptomic profiling, and single-cell analyses to discover that APOL4-high tumors contain a specific cancer-associated fibroblast (CAF-1) subpopulation with enhanced matrix remodeling and immune-rich environments. These CAF-1 cells facilitate drug penetration through increased matrix metalloproteinase activity, correlating with improved patient outcomes. APOL4 expression in stromal cells, rather than tumor cells, predicts carboplatin sensitivity, offering a potential biomarker for chemotherapy response. Future research could explore stroma-targeted interventions to enhance platinum efficacy and overcome resistance, providing new therapeutic avenues in high-grade serous ovarian carcinoma. This summary was initially drafted using artificial intelligence, then revised and fact-checked by the author.

https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-0.title: Uncertainty-aware lung CT slice classification using a lightweight CNN with selective referral
https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-0.abstract: Lung CT slice classification may support image-level decision assistance, but deterministic neural networks do not explicitly indicate when a prediction is unreliable. This study presents a lightweight uncertainty-aware convolutional neural network (CNN) for three-class classification of benign, malignant, and normal CT slices, integrating Monte Carlo (MC) Dropout, validation-selected selective referral, and Grad-CAM visualization. After removing 43 exact duplicate files, 1,054 IQ-OTH/NCCD images were analyzed using an image-level split of 842 training, 106 validation, and 106 test images (seed 42). Because reliable patient identifiers could not be recovered, the study is considered an internal image-level proof-of-concept rather than patient-independent diagnostic validation. With 50-pass MC Dropout, the model correctly classified 105/106 test slices, achieving 99.06% accuracy (exact 95% CI: 94.86–99.98%) and a weighted F1-score of 99.04%. The single misclassified benign slice was predicted as normal and exhibited high predictive uncertainty. Selective referral was based on the scalar uncertainty score $${\text{U}} = {\text{max}}\left( {1 - {\text{Confidence}},\,{\text{H}}_{{{\text{norm}}}} ,\,{\text{MI}}_{{{\text{norm}}}} ,\,{\text{VR}}} \right)$$ , with a threshold selected as the 80th percentile of validation-set U values $$\left( {\tau_{U} = 0.174166} \right)$$ , without using test labels or test performance. This operating point accepted 88/106 slices (83.02% coverage) and referred 18/106 (16.98%), with an observed accepted accuracy of 100% (95% CI: 95.89–100%) and an observed selective risk of 0% (95% CI: 0–4.11%). Calibration analysis yielded a 10-bin equal-width expected calibration error of 0.0295, a multiclass Brier score of 0.0137, and a negative log-likelihood of 0.0385. Deep Ensemble and Ensemble MC Dropout each correctly classified all 106 test slices, although these results remain subject to the same image-level data limitation. Simulated low-contrast and Gaussian-noise perturbations reduced accuracy and increased referral, indicating responsiveness of the uncertainty score to distributional degradation. A separately retrained binary lightweight CNN variant on the Chest CT-Scan Images Dataset correctly classified all 286 Cancer-versus-Normal test slices (100%; 95% CI: 98.72–100%), but its validation-selected referral rule accepted only 134/286 slices (46.85%) and referred all 25 Normal test slices. Therefore, the second-dataset experiment should be interpreted as a dataset-specific image-level benchmark rather than direct external validation of the primary three-class model. These findings support further patient-wise, multi-center evaluation of uncertainty-aware CT-slice classification and selective referral.

https://www.nature.com/articles/s41418-0.title: NFE2L1 promotes cisplatin resistance by attenuating ferroptosis through SLC27A2-mediated fatty acid metabolism in ovarian cancer
https://www.nature.com/articles/s41418-0.abstract: Approaches that promote ferroptosis have emerged as promising therapeutic strategies for chemotherapy-resistant cancers; however, the mechanisms regulating ferroptosis during acquired therapeutic resistance remain incompletely understood. Using RNA sequencing, we identified that Nuclear Factor Erythroid-2 Related Factor 1 (NFE2L1) is upregulated in cisplatin-resistant ovarian cancer (OC) cells and patient tissues, as well as in ferroptosis-resistant models. Genetic knockdown of NFE2L1 resensitized cells to cisplatin both in vitro and in vivo. Notably, this effect was largely reversed by ferroptosis inhibitors, which significantly rescued cell survival following NFE2L1 depletion under cisplatin treatment. Further experiments demonstrated that modulating NFE2L1 expression affects the response to ferroptosis inducers by regulating iron accumulation and lipid peroxidation. Mechanistically, NFE2L1 silencing increased the transcription of long-chain fatty acid transport protein 2 (SLC27A2/FATP2). Chromatin immunoprecipitation and dual-luciferase reporter assays showed that NFE2L1 bound directly to the SLC27A2 promoter, where it competitively inhibited the recruitment of the transcription factor SP1. As a key member of the long-chain acyl-CoA synthetase family, FATP2 promotes the uptake and activation of long-chain fatty acids, processes that have been implicated in the regulation of ferroptosis. Subsequent LC–MS-based lipidomic analysis revealed that NFE2L1 reprogrammed intracellular fatty acid metabolism, characterized by increased polyunsaturated fatty acid (PUFA) levels and decreased monounsaturated fatty acid (MUFA) levels within phosphatidylethanolamines (PEs), thereby increasing cellular susceptibility to ferroptosis. Consistent with these findings, supplementation with exogenous unsaturated fatty acids modulated NFE2L1-mediated ferroptosis sensitivity. Collectively, our findings reveal a novel NFE2L1/SLC27A2 axis that drives cisplatin resistance in OC by suppressing ferroptosis, and suggest a potential therapeutic strategy for treating cisplatin-resistant ovarian cancer.

https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.64898.title: Squalene as a Candidate Signalling Molecule: Computational Evidence for a Predicted KEAP1 Interaction and Implications for Stress-Induced Altruistic Stem-Cell Niche Protection
https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.64898.abstract: Stem and progenitor cells exposed to cytotoxic stress must preserve both their own viability and the functional integrity of their surrounding niche. Previous investigations from our laboratory have described stress-adapted altruistic stem-cell phenotypes and demonstrated the cytoprotective potential of squalene in normal haematopoietic and mesenchymal progenitor cells through preservation of glutathione homeostasis. More recent studies have associated hypoxia-driven changes in squalene metabolism with intracellular squalene accumulation and protection against lipid peroxidation, while independent experimental evidence has implicated NRF2 in squalene-mediated cytoprotection. However, the molecular basis through which squalene may engage the NRF2 regulatory pathway remains incompletely understood. Here, we investigated the structural feasibility of a potential interaction between squalene and the KEAP1 Kelch domain using molecular docking across three human KEAP1 crystal structures (PDB IDs: 6TYM, 6SP4 and 5CGJ). The docking protocol was evaluated through native-ligand redocking, yielding RMSD values of 0.826, 0.277 and 0.303 A, respectively. Squalene was consistently accommodated within the canonical hydrophobic cavity, with predicted docking scores of 7.905, 7.513 and 6.756 kcal/mol. The predicted interaction environment was predominantly hydrophobic and involved residues including Arg415, Arg380 and Asn414, without conventional hydrogen-bond formation. These findings support the structural feasibility of squalene accommodation within the KEAP1 Kelch domain and provide a testable hypothesis connecting stress-responsive squalene metabolism with potential KEAP1 NRF2 regulation. However, docking alone does not establish direct binding, physiological accessibility, KEAP1 inhibition or functional NRF2 activation. Further biophysical, molecular-dynamics and cellular investigations are required to establish the biological significance of the predicted interaction.

https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.64898.title: Optimization of a Subcutaneous Epithelioid Hemangioendothelioma Xenograft Model for Evaluation of Preclinical Therapeutics
https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.64898.abstract: Epithelioid hemangioendothelioma (EHE) is an ultra-rare vascular sarcoma characterized by an unpredictable clinical trajectory and lack of established standard-of-care treatment regimens. Despite the pressing need for effective therapeutic strategies, the scarcity of clinically relevant preclinical models remains a major barrier to drug development. To address this challenge, we used a patient-derived human EHE cell line to optimize and validate a subcutaneous xenograft model in mice. Optimization of cell-inoculation density revealed that injection of high cell densities was associated with adverse systemic responses and primary tumour growth kinetics unsuitable for longitudinal drug screening. In contrast, inoculation of low, sub-million cell densities generated reproducible xenografts that followed classical sigmoidal growth kinetics, providing a suitable therapeutic window for comparative treatment studies. Subsequent histopathological analysis confirmed that the tumours were highly proliferative and retained key features of EHE pathology, including expression of the EHE-associated markers ERG and CAMTA1. Treatment response validation further demonstrated sensitivity to mTOR inhibition, a characteristic preserved from the original patient-derived sample. Treatment with nab-sirolimus significantly suppressed tumour growth and reduced phosphorylation of ribosomal protein S6, consistent with suppression of downstream mTORC1 signalling. In this study, the optimized CDX model retains key EHE features and provides an extended observation window with sustained growth of untreated controls, supporting longitudinal assessment of antitumour activity and pharmacodynamic responses. This platform provides a practical framework for evaluating and comparing candidate therapies for EHE.

https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.64898.title: Early Progression Cells mark a stem-like state associated with pancreatic cancer initiation and progression
https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.64898.abstract: Pancreatic cancer is deemed to progress from microscopic pancreatic intraepithelial neoplasia (PanINs). However, low grade PanINs are frequently detected in the general population without presentation or increased risk of developing cancer, suggesting that many PanINs never progress to tumours. What precisely characterises PanINs that develop into tumours is insufficiently understood. Using a mouse model where pancreatitis-induced tissue injury promotes pancreatic cancer from rare KrasG12D cells, we identify Early Progression Cells (EPCs) as a new entity, a novel population of cancer stem-like cells. Transcriptomic analyses illustrate EPCs as stress-adapted, inflammation responsive stem cells that also upregulate gene programmes indicative of microenvironment remodelling. Using identified EPC protein markers, we show that EPCs are prevalent in early metaplastic stages and in PanIN progression from low grade to high grade but are rarer in tumours. PanIN- and tumour-derived sphere and organoid assays demonstrate that EPCs possess all characteristics of stem cells in vitro and are dependent on Nupr1 stress response pathways for survival and growth. We identify APP-CD74 as a novel cell-cell interaction pathway between EPCs and neighbouring epithelial cells in PanINs and tumours. Inhibition of CD74 activity in vitro induces high-grade PanIN organoid death, suggesting EPCs are critical for high-grade PanINs. Using spatial transcriptomics of human samples, we detect gene signatures of EPCs in distinct regions of human PanIN and PDAC tissues, including APP-CD74 interactions, providing compelling evidence that EPCs are relevant to human disease. Further understanding of EPC biology will likely uncover new knowledge on why rare PanINs progress towards tumours.
