https://www.nature.com/articles/s41419-0.title: UBE2T upregulation underlies the metastasis-associated chemoresistance of breast cancer that can be reversed by BET inhibitors
https://www.nature.com/articles/s41419-0.abstract: Most primary breast cancers are sensitive to chemotherapy and some of them can achieve pathological complete response (pCR) by neoadjuvant chemotherapy. However, metastatic breast cancers are almost impossible to reach pCR with chemotherapy and thus are incurable diseases. The mechanisms of metastasis-associated chemoresistance remain poorly understood. Using paired primary and metastatic triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) models, we identify that UBE2T is responsible for metastasis-associated chemoresistance by promoting PHLPP ubiquitination and AKT phosphorylation, enhancing tumor stemness in metastatic breast cancer. Overexpressed NFYA is the transcription factor that upregulates UBE2T expression. Analysis of clinical samples shows that the NFYA/UBE2T/p-AKT axis was highly activated in metastatic breast cancer. More importantly, bromodomain and extraterminal domain proteins (BET) inhibitors are found to significantly reduce UBE2T transcription, restoring the sensitivity of metastatic breast cancer to chemotherapy both in vitro and in vivo. These findings suggest that BET inhibitors could reverse the metastasis-associated chemoresistance by targeting aberrantly upregulated NFYA/UBE2T/p-AKT pathway in metastatic breast cancer, particularly in TNBC.

https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-0.title: Stage harmonized temporal survival comparisons in de novo metastatic breast cancer using SEER
https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-0.abstract: Temporal survival comparisons in cancer registries depend on how stage is harmonized across changing coding systems. We analyzed SEER 17 breast cancers diagnosed in 2000–2023 using a year-specific TNM-priority M-stage algorithm. The primary cohort comprised 35,262 de novo M1 cases diagnosed in 2010–2023 with complete covariate and outcome data. Contemporary (2014–2023) versus Transition (2010–2013) diagnosis was associated with lower breast cancer-specific mortality before adjustment (hazard ratio [HR], 0.870; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.845–0.897) and after demographic and organ-site adjustment (HR, 0.844; 95% CI 0.819–0.870). Transition-target inverse probability weighting produced a similar estimate (HR, 0.853; 95% CI 0.827–0.879). A strict TNM analysis was unchanged, whereas the prior any-positive-stage rule yielded a near-null crude estimate. Because proportional hazards were not constant, the overall HR is an average association; adjusted HRs were 0.879 during 0–24 months and 0.801 after 24 months. The 36-month overall-survival restricted mean difference was 0.66 months (95% CI 0.34–0.99). These observational findings show that stage harmonization materially influences temporal comparisons and do not identify effects of imaging or treatment.

https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-0.title: Explainable machine learning estimates clinically significant prostate cancer risk in men with PSA 4–20 ng/mL
https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-0.abstract: Men with prostate-specific antigen (PSA) values of 4–20 ng/mL often have overlapping risks of benign disease, clinically insignificant prostate cancer, and clinically significant prostate cancer (csPCa). We retrospectively studied 859 men who underwent pathological evaluation; 76 had csPCa. Twelve prediction algorithms were assessed with 500 bootstrap resamples. In every resample, LASSO feature selection, hyperparameter tuning, and model fitting used only the bootstrap training sample, and performance was estimated from patient-level out-of-bag predictions. C5.0 had the highest AUROC point estimate (0.843, 95% CI 0.801–0.886), an AUPRC of 0.421, and a Brier score of 0.066. Calibration was broadly concordant at low-to-moderate predicted risks but uncertain in the sparse high-risk tail. At a 0.10 risk threshold, the model would avoid 544.8 biopsies per 1,000 men while missing 10.5 csPCa cases per 1,000. In an algorithm-matched comparison, the full C5.0 and clinical/PSA-only C5.0 models achieved AUROCs of 0.843 and 0.827, respectively (paired difference 0.0157, 95% CI − 0.0086 to 0.0395). The incremental benefit of additional blood-based predictors was therefore uncertain. C5.0 may support pre-biopsy triage, but multicenter external validation, recalibration assessment, and prospective impact studies are required before clinical use.

https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.64898.title: Pervasive chromothripsis drives pleural mesothelioma to impact gene function and patient survival
https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.64898.abstract: Pleural mesothelioma (PM) is a tumour type showing high structural complexity but the full spectrum of variants present and their impacts are poorly understood. We comprehensively describe the mutational landscape of mesothelioma, exploiting a large (N=443) cohort profiling the tumour genome and transcriptome in parallel. We find that the majority of candidate driver variants are mediated by copy number alterations (CNAs) and discover high frequencies of complex rearrangements across most tumours, dominated by chromothripsis (74% of tumours) and chromoplexy (59%). Chromothripsis contributes to significant CNA hotspots to delete known PM tumour suppressor genes such as CDKN2A, NF2 and BAP1, thought to be among the earliest events in PM development; and the presence of chromothripsis is associated with significantly worse patient survival. We also discover multi-faceted crosstalk between the mitochondrial and nuclear genomes during PM evolution, involving alterations to both genomes, and mitochondrial expression changes associated with subtypes and chromothripsis.

https://www.nature.com/articles/s41420-0.title: WDR54 stabilizes the fatty acid transporter SLC43A3 via the deubiquitinase OTUB1 to drive HNSCC progression
https://www.nature.com/articles/s41420-0.abstract: Metabolic reprogramming drives head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC), yet the underlying mechanisms remain elusive. Here, we identify WDR54 as a critical oncogenic driver. Clinical analyses reveal WDR54 is overexpressed in HNSCC and correlates with poor patient survival. Mechanistically, WDR54 interacts with the deubiquitinase OTUB1, enhancing its capacity to deubiquitinate and stabilize the fatty acid transporter SLC43A3. This prevents SLC43A3 proteasomal degradation, inducing lipid metabolic reprogramming essential for HNSCC proliferation and invasion. Furthermore, pharmacological intervention with dihydroergotamine effectively disrupts this WDR54-OTUB1-SLC43A3 axis, significantly suppressing HNSCC tumor growth in vivo. Collectively, our findings elucidate a previously unrecognized signaling axis integrating protein deubiquitination with lipid metabolism, highlighting dihydroergotamine as a promising targeted therapeutic strategy for HNSCC.

https://www.nature.com/articles/s42003-0.title: Acquired resistance to vorinostat in cutaneous T cell lymphoma involves augmented ERK phosphorylation
https://www.nature.com/articles/s42003-0.abstract: Vorinostat is the first approved histone deacetylase inhibitor used in many countries for treating advanced cutaneous T cell lymphoma (CTCL). However, prolonged application of this drug leads to the development of resistance, presenting a significant challenge to therapy. To better understand the mechanisms through which CTCL cells gain resistance, we established a vorinostat-resistant clone of the human CTCL line HuT78 (HuT78VR). HuT78VR cells exhibited enhanced drug efflux ability with increased expression of the drug efflux pumps ABCB1 and ABCG2. Employing an integrated transcriptomics and proteomics approach, we identified molecular signatures of vorinostat resistance. Specifically, HuT78VR cells presented increased expression of metastasis-related genes (LAIR2, VIM, MMP-9, IFNG, FASLG, CCND1, and CDKN1A) with increased cellular invasiveness and defective apoptosis. Further scrutiny of differentially expressed genes and proteins revealed the involvement of mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) signaling. In line with this, HuT78VR cells gained cross-resistance to inhibitors of histone deacetylase and topoisomerase but remained sensitive to inhibitors of MAPK/ERK. Ulixertinib, an ERK inhibitor, re-sensitized HuT78VR cells to vorinostat in vitro as well as in cell-derived xenografts in mice. These findings expand the understanding of vorinostat resistance in CTCL and suggest that ERK inhibition is an effective therapeutic approach to overcome vorinostat resistance.

https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-0.title: Cachexia index as a prognostic marker in gastrointestinal cancer with nomogram development and external validation
https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-0.abstract: The cachexia index (CXI) integrates skeletal muscle, albumin and systemic inflammation. We assessed its prognostic value and developed survival nomograms in 822 patients with gastrointestinal cancer, with external validation in 3,101 patients. CXI thresholds were 90.80 for men and 106.52 for women. Low CXI was associated with poorer disease-free survival (DFS; follow-up-averaged adjusted hazard ratio 1.84, 95% confidence interval 1.45–2.33) and overall survival (OS; 1.94, 1.38–2.72). Five-year DFS was 50.4% versus 70.9%, and OS was 70.4% versus 87.0%, in the low- and higher-CXI groups, respectively. The nomograms incorporated CXI, weight loss, tumor site and TNM stage. Bootstrap-corrected C-indices were 0.738 for DFS and 0.799 for OS; external C-indices were 0.681 and 0.639. External areas under the curve at two, three and five years were 0.706, 0.689 and 0.692 for DFS and 0.829, 0.707 and 0.638 for OS. The association persisted after age and sex adjustment and exclusion of second primary malignancies. These findings support CXI as a prognostic marker and a component of survival risk stratification in surgically treated gastrointestinal cancer.

https://www.nature.com/articles/s41375-0.title: Maternal donor risk in haploidentical transplant with post-transplant cyclophosphamide: the role of recipient sex

https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-0.title: A tumor-associated K318N variant abolishes AGGF1 nuclear import by disrupting key nucleocytoplasmic transport motifs
https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-0.abstract: Aberrant nucleocytoplasmic transport is linked to tumorigenesis. AGGF1 exerts nuclear tumor-suppressing functions, yet how its nuclear import is regulated remains unclear. Through deletion mapping and point mutations, we identified three motifs (272–279, 317–328 and 509–519 aa) governing AGGF1 nucleocytoplasmic distribution. Knockdown of importin β1 and inhibition of importin α1 showed that the importin α1/β1 complex is the primary nuclear import receptor. GST pull-down assays revealed that 317–328 aa and 509–519 aa, but not 272–279 aa, are required for efficient binding to importin α1. None of the three motifs alone was sufficient to efficiently drive nuclear import, whereas the combined 272–328 aa region conferred robust nuclear import. The tumor-associated K318N variant, within 317–328 aa, is absent from gnomAD and causes profound, cell-type-independent cytoplasmic mislocalization that is not attributable to enhanced CRM1-mediated nuclear export or 14-3-3α/β-dependent cytoplasmic distribution. Consequently, K318N fails to bind nuclear p53, stabilize p53, or activate its transcription, impairing AGGF1 tumor-suppressing function. RNA-seq showed K318-dependent genes enriched in Rap1 signaling, cytoskeleton regulation, and cardiac muscle morphogenesis, suggesting a predominantly loss-of-function effect. These findings identify key motifs and the nuclear import receptor for AGGF1, and reveal how a single variant disrupts nuclear localization and p53 regulation, potentially contributing to tumorigenesis.

https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-0.title: A dual-stream Pyramid ViT–ConvFormer architecture leverages dynamic early stopping to classify diffuse large B-cell lymphoma
https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-0.abstract: Molecular stratification of diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL) based on MYC rearrangement status (confirmed via fluorescence in situ hybridization) guides frontline therapeutic selection. Although Vision Transformers (ViTs) effectively model global tissue context, lacking localized inductive biases extends training convergence. We developed PyConv, an asymmetrical hybrid architecture engineered for the three-class histopathological classification of MYC-rearranged ($$MYC+$$) DLBCL, non-rearranged ($$MYC-$$) DLBCL, and reactive lymph node (RLN). PyConv combines local ConvFormer blocks with global Pyramid ViT blocks via Multi-Head Cross-Attention (MHCA) fusion. We evaluated the network on a patient-stratified cohort of 180 whole-slide images (69,480 testing patches) against 12 baseline backbones at both patch and patient levels. PyConv achieved a patch classification accuracy and macro F1-score of 0.9962 [95% CI: 0.9884–0.9991 via patient-level clustered bootstrapping] and a macro AUROC of 0.9999. Patient-level probability pooling yielded 100% classification concordance on the held-out test cohort (18/18 patients), showing no statistically significant discriminative loss compared to top-performing baselines (e.g., ConvFormer, $$p = 0.9866$$) while integrating global stromal context. PyConv converged by epoch 20, reducing training duration by 68.7% compared to pure Pyramid ViT. PyConv provides an accurate, computationally efficient benchmarking framework for automated lymphoma classification. Although high patient concordance demonstrates internal feasibility, the model serves as an exploratory proof of concept requiring multi-center and multi-scanner validation before clinical translation.

https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-0.title: Multimodal deep learning with clinical metadata for skin lesion classification
https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-0.abstract: Accurate skin lesion classification often requires integration of lesion appearance with patient clinical information. Although multimodal artificial intelligence (AI) approaches have shown promise, many existing methods rely on computationally intensive fusion mechanisms or simple integration strategies that may inadequately capture interactions between imaging and clinical data. This study aimed to develop and evaluate a multimodal deep learning model that integrates skin images and structured clinical metadata for skin lesion classification and to compare its performance with image-based and prior multimodal baseline models. This retrospective diagnostic study evaluated dataset-specific model performance using 2 public datasets (PAD-UFES-20 and ISIC 2019) and 1 institutional dataset (PKU-Skin). PAD-UFES-20 included 2,298 clinical images with 21 structured clinical variables across 6 lesion classes. ISIC 2019 included 25,331 dermoscopic images across 8 diagnostic categories. PKU-Skin was an institutional dataset of 800 clinical images (643 patients) with corresponding clinical metadata collected at Peking University Shenzhen Hospital and represented a binary classification task involving psoriasis and basal cell carcinoma. Model development and evaluation were performed separately within each dataset. The primary outcome was correct lesion classification. The primary evaluation metric was balanced accuracy. Secondary metrics included sensitivity, specificity, precision, F1 score, and overall accuracy. On PAD-UFES-20, the proposed multimodal model achieved a balanced accuracy of 85.6%, compared with 75.1% for a prior multimodal baseline model, with sensitivity of 76.1%, specificity of 95.2%, F1 score of 78.1%, and overall accuracy of 78.3%. On ISIC 2019, the model achieved a balanced accuracy of 86.0%, F1 score of 84.3%, and overall accuracy of 84.5%. On PKU-Skin, the model achieved a balanced accuracy of 99.6% and overall accuracy of 99.2%; because this dataset represented a separate binary classification task, these results should be interpreted as supportive evidence from an institutional setting rather than formal external validation of a single fixed model. In these retrospective dataset-specific experiments, integrating structured clinical metadata with skin images was associated with improved skin lesion classification performance relative to comparator models. These findings support further evaluation of multimodal approaches for dermatologic decision support, particularly in prospectively collected and clinically matched external datasets.

https://www.nature.com/articles/s43018-0.title: Basophils boost early antitumor immunity by restraining Treg cells
https://www.nature.com/articles/s43018-0.abstract: Basophils are rare immune cells best known for their roles in allergies. We find that they also restrict early metastatic seeding by suppressing regulatory T (Treg) cells through histamine–HRH1 signaling and MCPT8-mediated cleavage of CD25, thereby enhancing antitumor immunity. Progressing tumors subsequently reprogram basophils into a distinct, less protective state.

https://www.nature.com/articles/s43018-0.title: Spatiotemporal control of CAR-T cell TNF release via tumor-targeted irradiation
https://www.nature.com/articles/s43018-0.abstract: Adoptive chimeric antigen receptor (CAR)-T cell therapies have limited efficacy in solid tumors because of poor infiltration and impaired effector function, whereas radiotherapy is constrained by radioresistance and metastatic spread. Here we show that integrating the spatial precision of ionizing radiation with the biological specificity of CAR-T cells enables localized delivery of the inflammatory cytokine tumor necrosis factor (TNF). We identified radiation-responsive genes in tumor-infiltrating T cells and engineered synthetic radioinducible promoters to drive TNF expression. Human CAR-T cells carrying this construct (riTNF CAR-T cells) secreted high levels of TNF upon irradiation, independently of antigen engagement. In human xenograft and murine tumor models, the combination of riTNF CAR-T cells and local irradiation produced greater tumor regression than either treatment alone or standard CAR-T cells with irradiation. This response was associated with high intratumoral, but not systemic, TNF levels, increased tumor necrosis and apoptosis, vascular disruption and greater CAR-T cell infiltration. These findings establish a platform for spatially and temporally controlled cytokine delivery from engineered CAR-T cells. Masoumi et al. engineered CAR-T cells with a radiation-inducible promoter controlling the expression and local release of the cytokine TNF upon tumor irradiation.

https://www.nature.com/articles/s41588-0.title: AI-guided cancer survival prediction could spare some children high-dose brain radiation
https://www.nature.com/articles/s41588-0.abstract: We developed a multimodal artificial intelligence (AI)-based model to generate time-dependent, individualized survival predictions for patients with childhood brain tumors. This may help better identify candidates for therapy de-escalation, maintaining survival while reducing lifelong treatment-related side effects.

https://www.nature.com/articles/s42255-0.title: Lactylation couples glycolysis with cell cycle progression in cancer cells
https://www.nature.com/articles/s42255-0.abstract: Aurora B is essential for mitotic progression, yet whether its activity is regulated by tumour metabolism remains unclear. Here we show that Aurora B functions as a sensor of glycolytic activity and is activated through lactate-dependent signalling. Mechanistically, increased lactate production during aerobic glycolysis promotes KAT2A-mediated lactylation of phosphoglycerate kinase 1 (PGK1) at K131. Lactylated PGK1 phosphorylates Aurora B at T232, leading to cell cycle progression. Disruption of this pathway, either by expressing a PGK1 K131R mutant or a PGK1 variant defective in Aurora B binding, leads to mitotic defects and cGAS–STING activation. These effects suppress tumour cell proliferation and inhibit tumour growth in mice. Furthermore, combining a peptide that disrupts the PGK1–Aurora B interaction with anti-PD-1 therapy enhances CD8+ T-cell infiltration and produces synergistic anti-tumour effects. Collectively, these findings uncover a critical role of glycolysis in governing tumour cell division. This study shows that Aurora B activation by lactylated PGK1 links glycolysis to mitotic progression and immune evasion in cancer.

https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-0.title: Real-world feasibility of a nutritional frailty score-guided multimodal supportive care pathway in patients with digestive cancer
https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-0.abstract: Frailty, malnutrition, and sarcopenia are highly prevalent in digestive oncology and adversely affect treatment tolerance, toxicity, and survival. The integration of multimodal, multidisciplinary supportive care may mitigate these risks, but feasibility and clinical impact in routine practice remain uncertain. We conducted two complementary single-center studies at a French cancer center. We developed a Nutritional Frailty Score to assess the risk of nutritional deterioration in patients receiving first-line chemotherapy for digestive cancers. ParcoursDig (NCT04478175) prospectively assessed the feasibility of systematic multimodal supportive care (dietitian, physiotherapist, palliative care) using risk stratification based on this score in patients with localized or advanced digestive cancers. PrePOP was a retrospective observational study of patients with pancreatic or esophagogastric cancers receiving perioperative chemotherapy and surgery. Outcomes included treatment completion, nutritional changes, toxicities, surgical complications, and survival. In ParcoursDig, only 44% of patients completed the full supportive care pathway (63% in sensitivity analysis), falling short of the predefined feasibility threshold. No significant improvements were seen in health-related quality of life or survival, highlighting real-world implementation challenges. In PrePOP, baseline malnutrition prevalence was 71% (31% severe). Malnutrition was clinically associated with higher rates of chemotherapy dose reduction but not with surgical complications or survival. Weight loss during systemic therapy was common, but early nutritional intervention appeared to prevent further deterioration for some patients. Muscle mass loss during follow-up correlated with poorer prognosis, emphasizing the need for longitudinal, muscle-specific assessment. In this exploratory, single-centre experience, unsupervised, low-intensity interventions did not achieve the predefined feasibility threshold or measurable clinical benefit. Supervised, high-intensity modalities (e.g., structured interval training) and individualized care trajectories with longitudinal follow-up warrant evaluation in larger, multicentre studies.

https://www.nature.com/articles/s44303-0.title: Evaluation of treatment response in patients with recurrent grade 4 glioma using hyperpolarized [1-13C]pyruvate MRI
https://www.nature.com/articles/s44303-0.abstract: Hyperpolarized (HP) [1-13C]pyruvate MRI allows for noninvasive assessment of dynamic metabolic activity in the brain and has potential for monitoring treatment response in gliomas. This exploratory study evaluated the ability of serial HP [1-13C]pyruvate MRI to detect treatment-related metabolism and evaluate early therapeutic response. Twenty patients with recurrent grade 4 glioma undergoing cytotoxic, antiangiogenic, and targeted chemotherapies underwent serial HP [1-13C]pyruvate MRI in conjunction with routine clinical MRI. Percentage changes were calculated from the group mean at each timepoint. The lactate/pyruvate ratio in the normal-appearing white matter (NAWM) increased by 14.3% at 1-month in the bevacizumab-treated group, whereas it decreased by 13.1% at 2-month in the everolimus-treated group. Within the T2-lesion, the NAWM-normalized lactate/pyruvate ratio increased by 24.3% in the bevacizumab-treated group and decreased by 7.6% in the everolimus-treated group. Among patients with shorter 6-month progression-free survival, the NAWM-normalized lactate/pyruvate increased by 18.2% from baseline to 2-month follow-up. This exploratory proof-of-feasibility study demonstrates that serial HP [1-¹³C]pyruvate MRI can detect measurable longitudinal metabolic changes in recurrent grade 4 glioma during treatment. Larger, prospective studies with more homogeneous treatment cohorts are needed to validate these observations and determine their clinical utility as imaging biomarkers of treatment response.

https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-0.title: MR imaging and spectroscopy reveals metabolic changes in glioblastoma driven by treatment with temozolomide and lonidamine
https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-0.abstract: Resistance to temozolomide (TMZ) limits the efficacy of treatment in glioblastoma (GBM) which is fuelled by a metabolic reprogramming of the cancer cells and alterations in the tumour microenvironment. Lonidamine (LND), a glycolytic and mitochondrial inhibitor, modulates tumour metabolism and can alter tumour response to treatment. This study investigated the effects of LND in combination with TMZ and used MR imaging and spectroscopy to evaluate metabolic and microstructural changes in a syngeneic GBM model. C57BL/6 mice bearing intracranial GL261 tumours (n = 66) were treated with saline, LND, TMZ, or LND + TMZ for five consecutive days. Longitudinal imaging (days 0, 3, 6) included T2-weighted MRI, diffusion weighted imaging (DWI), and conventional and lactate-edited ¹H-MRS. Tumour volume, survival, DWI parameters, MCT4 expression, and mitotic indices were assessed. In vitro, acute and chronic bioenergetic reprogramming of GL261 cells was assessed using the Seahorse extracellular flux analysis. Lactate is a not simply an end product of high glycolytic cancer cells, but it has also emerged as a molecule capable to shaping the tumour microenvironment. A significant decrease in lactate observed in the LND and LND + TMZ groups indicated a reduction in the steady-state lactate pool suggestive of reduced lactate production, utilization or altered glycolytic flux. However, lactate remained high in the control and TMZ-only groups. This metabolic shift in the LND treatment group was consistent with a marked reduction in MCT4 protein, the lactate transporter, in LND-treated tumours. In vitro bioenergetic profiling of GL261 cells revealed an acute decrease in mitochondrial respiration in response to LND, with partial recovery at later time points. Finally, even though not significant, an enhanced survival benefit of the treatment combination was observed, with no significant differences observed between the groups for tumour volume, DWI-derived parameters, or mitotic index after 6 days. LND induces early metabolic changes detectable by MRS. Although a limited therapeutic benefit of addition LND to TMZ was observed in the early stages of tumour development, its tumour-selective activity and effect on tumour microenvironment is promising and its long-term effects on tumour development should be investigated as part of an optimized combination strategy for TMZ treatment.

https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-0.title: Curcumin nanoparticles attenuate radiation-induced liver and kidney injury in rats: a histopathological evaluation
https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-0.abstract: Radiation therapy is a common treatment for a variety of malignancies. However, it can have harmful effects on healthy tissues. Curcumin, a compound derived from turmeric, has antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, and radioprotective properties, making it promising for reducing radiation-induced damage. In this study, we aimed to evaluate the radioprotective effects of curcumin nanoparticles (CurNPs) on the liver and kidneys of rats exposed to radiation. Thirty male Wistar rats were divided into six groups: control, radiation-only, CurNPs (2 mg/kg), CurNPs(4 mg/kg), CurNPs (2 mg/kg) + IR, and CurNPs (4 mg/kg) + IR. The radiation-only group was exposed to a single dose of 6 Gy of radiation, while the CurNPs-treated groups received a dose of CurNPs before radiation exposure. The liver and kidney tissues were collected and subjected to histopathological examination. Histopathological analysis revealed that the radiation-only group exhibited severe damage to the liver and kidney tissues, characterized by hepatocyte degeneration, inflammation, and tubular necrosis. In contrast, the CurNPs-treated group demonstrated a significant reduction in radiation-induced pathological changes, with preserved tissue architecture, decreased inflammation, and enhanced cell viability. In conclusion, our histopathological study demonstrates that both 2 mg/kg and 4 mg/kg CurNPs possess the potential to serve as a promising radioprotective agent for the liver and kidneys but no apparent difference between the two doses.. The use of CurNPs could help mitigate radiation-induced toxicity in cancer patients undergoing radiotherapy. These findings warrant further investigation and provide a foundation for developing innovative radioprotective strategies.

https://www.nature.com/articles/s41588-0.title: An information-theoretic framework for inferring T cell dynamics from single-cell RNA and T cell receptor sequencing
https://www.nature.com/articles/s41588-0.abstract: Single-cell T cell receptor (TCR) repertoire sequencing enables simultaneous profiling of gene expression and TCR sequences, providing a coregistered measure of T cell phenotypic diversity and clonal dynamics. However, principled probabilistic frameworks for joint modeling of clonotype and phenotype have remained limited. Here we introduce TCRi, a hierarchical Bayesian information-theoretic framework that infers the joint probability distribution between genetic clonotype and transcriptional phenotype from paired single-cell transcriptomic and TCR sequencing data. TCRi treats phenotype assignment as a probabilistic inference problem: a variational autoencoder embeds single-cell expression into a structured latent space, and a hierarchical Bayesian model learns clonotype-specific phenotype distributions through principled information-sharing across clonotypes, patients and covariates. From these distributions, TCRi computes information-theoretic quantities: clonotypic entropy, phenotypic entropy, phenotypic flux and mutual information between clonotype and phenotype. When TCRi was applied to four real-world datasets comprising 167,118 CD8 T cells from patients with cancer treated with anti-PD-(L)1 immune checkpoint blockade, mutual information emerged as a robust discriminator of therapeutic response. T cells provide a unique setting for quantification of the relationship between genotype and phenotype. The authors introduce TCRi, an information-theoretic framework for this, and find mutual information to be a robust determinant of immunotherapeutic response.

https://www.nature.com/articles/s41416-0.title: Which is more effective at improving uptake of bowel cancer screening: text message reminders or patient navigation? Results from a three-arm RCT
https://www.nature.com/articles/s41416-0.abstract: Text message reminders (TMRs) and patient navigation (PN) increase bowel cancer screening uptake. To date, no studies have directly compared these interventions with one another. We conducted a three-arm randomised controlled trial with individuals, in London, who had not completed bowel cancer screening within 18 weeks of invitation. Participants were randomised to receive no reminder (usual care), TMRs at 19, 21, 23 and 25 weeks, or a TMR at 19 weeks, with telephone PN at 21, 23 and 25 weeks. The primary outcome was participation within 26 weeks of invitation. Differences were assessed using logistic regression. On an intention-to-treat basis (n = 3129), uptake was higher in the TMR and PN groups, compared with usual care (6.5% vs. 2.0%, p < 0.001; 7.5% vs. 2.0%, p < 0.001). There was no significant difference between TMR and PN groups. In the per-protocol analysis (n = 2294), uptake was significantly higher in the PN group than the TMR group (8.6 vs. 12.6%, p < 0.025). Subgroup analyses revealed telephone PN was significantly more effective than TMRs for men, specifically (14.5% vs. 6.7%, p < 0.001). While TMRs are no more effective than PN in general, implementing PN could help reduce disparities in uptake between men and women. ISRCTN17245519.

https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-0.title: A mixed-methods evaluation of a language model-powered breast cancer note augmentation tool for patients
https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-0.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have the potential to make clinical notes more understandable to patients, but tools must be tested with patients pre-deployment. We developed a patient-facing tool that uses an LLM (GPT-4-031) to generate “augmentations” to notes: simplified note text, defined medical terminology, frequently asked questions, extracted key information, and to-do items. We evaluated the tool with 200 healthy female participants and 8 notes. Compared to control, participants with access to augmentations had greater self-reported confidence (2.83 ± 0.05 augmentations, 2.18 ± 0.07 control, p<0.001) and scored higher on comprehension questions (0.63 ± 0.02 augmentations, 0.54 ± 0.04 control, p<0.001). We conducted interviews with 7 participants with a history of breast cancer and their own notes who described ease of use and perceived improvements in note understanding, but also reported concerns around LLMs. Three clinicians conducted an error analysis and found most errors to be minor and related to assumed context.

https://www.nature.com/articles/s41556-0.title: Positional replication fork instability drives PARP inhibitor cytotoxicity
https://www.nature.com/articles/s41556-0.abstract: Although poly(ADP-ribose) polymerase inhibitors (PARPi) show promise for treating homologous recombination-deficient cancers, the observed PARPi hypersensitivity in additional genetic contexts expands their potential use in precision oncology. Yet, the DNA lesions driving PARPi-induced cytotoxicity remain poorly defined. Here we uncover distinct replication-fork lesions in specific genomic regions as key determinants of PARPi cytotoxicity. Using CRISPR screens, we identify that loss of replication-coupled cohesin acetyltransferase ESCO2 confers PARPi hypersensitivity independently of homologous recombination deficiency. Quantitative single-molecule imaging reveals that ESCO2 loss promotes accumulation of G-quadruplex (G4) DNA structures at a subset of replication-associated sites, associated with PARP1 activation and engagement of fork protection factor TIMELESS to mitigate G4-induced stress. Notably, these G4 lesions localize to fragile pericentromeric regions and engage the G4 helicase DDX11. PARP inhibition disrupts this protective G4-processing response by preventing PARP1-dependent engagement of TIMELESS and DDX11, leading to G4 accumulation, DNA damage and chromosomal instability. Together, our findings define the G4–PARP1–TIMELESS–DDX11 axis as a critical safeguard of replication fork stability at hard-to-replicate loci and reveal ESCO2 as a therapeutic target for promoting synthetic lethality in PARPi-treated cancers. Through CRISPR screens and single-molecule imaging, Gupta et al. show that loss of the cohesion acetyltransferase ESCO2 leads to increased G-quadruplex formation at specific regions and drives PARP activation and PARPi hypersensitivity.

https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.64898.title: Response to azacitidine and the TIM-3 inhibitor, sabatolimab, in MDS and CMML is associated with distinct immune and antigen-presentation states
https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.64898.abstract: Targeting the immune checkpoint TIM-3 is of interest in myeloid neoplasms, yet the hematopoietic and immune changes associated with anti-TIM-3 therapy remain poorly characterized. We used single-cell RNA sequencing to profile bone marrow (BM) and peripheral blood from patients with myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS) and chronic myelomonocytic leukemia (CMML) treated with the hypomethylating agent azacitidine combined with sabatolimab, a monoclonal antibody targeting TIM-3, and integrated Human Cell Atlas reference datasets for comparison. CITE-seq profiling showed that TIM-3 was predominantly expressed on dendritic cells and NK cells, with variable expression across other populations, including CD34 cells and CD8 T cells. At baseline, we identified a population of CD34 myeloid-biased progenitors specific to MDS/CMML samples ("HSPC-like") characterized by inflammatory gene expression programs and features of impaired differentiation. In MDS, elevated baseline HLA class II expression across hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells (HSPCs), HSPC-like cells, and multiple myeloid populations was associated with response. Consistent with this finding, trajectory analysis suggested that nonresponders bypassed HLA class II-high states during myeloid differentiation. In MDS, the presence of distinct CD8 T-cell populations and increased interferon-response programs in CD8 T and NK cells at baseline was also associated with response. In both MDS and CMML, treatment among responders was associated with contraction of BM CD8 and CD4 T-cell populations characterized by type I interferon-responsive and inflammatory programs, including IFIT1, IFIT2, and TNF, along with expansion of a distinct GZMH/IFITM1-expressing cytotoxic CD8 T-cell population. Together, these findings identify baseline antigen-presentation and immune-response programs associated with therapeutic response and reveal coordinated remodeling of myeloid and lymphoid compartments during azacitidine/sabatolimab treatment in MDS and CMML.

https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.64898.title: BCL10 Gain-of-Function Impairs Germinal Center Participation by Naive B Cells and Cooperates with BCL6 to Drive Extrafollicular Diffuse Large B-Cell Lymphoma
https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.64898.abstract: BCL10 gain-of-function (GoF) mutations occur in diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL) cases of the BN2/C1 molecular subgroup. These alterations activate CARD11-BCL10-MALT1 (CBM) signaling and drive resistance to multiple drug classes, but their role in disease pathogenesis is incompletely understood. In particular, interactions between BCL10 GoF and additional DLBCL oncogenes are undefined. Here, we show BCL10 GoF in naive B cells blocks their participation in germinal center (GC) reactions and permits transformation to DLBCL with a non-GC B-cell phenotype. Most clinical cases with BCL10 GoF also carry translocation of the BCL6 proto-oncogene, and we show that co-activation of these two lesions together promotes pronounced oncogenic synergy. Detailed single-cell analyses of underlying premalignant B-cell populations revealed expansion of extrafollicular memory B cells whose gene-expression program remains prominent in resulting lymphomas in both the mouse and corresponding human tumors. We therefore define a novel role for BCL10 activating mutations in enabling BCL6 lymphomagenesis.

https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-0.title: Deep learning-based pediatric colorectal polyp classification: evaluation of training strategies, robustness, and generalization
https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-0.abstract: Although automated analysis of colorectal polyps during colonoscopy has the potential to support clinical decision-making, pediatric colorectal polyp classification remains challenging because of limited annotated datasets and variability in endoscopic appearance. This study systematically evaluates a pediatric colorectal polyp classification framework employing a two-phase transfer learning strategy across multiple pretrained convolutional neural network architectures. Controlled ablation experiments were conducted on the CP-CHILD-A and CP-CHILD-B datasets using five independent random seeds. For ConvNeXt-Small, the two-phase protocol improved accuracy from $$98.88\% \pm 0.54\%$$ to $$99.77\% \pm 0.16\%$$ on CP-CHILD-A and from $$89.21\% \pm 4.23\%$$ to $$99.88\% \pm 0.27\%$$ on CP-CHILD-B compared with training from scratch. Duplicate and near-duplicate analyses followed by inference-only sensitivity evaluation showed minimal changes in performance. Cross-dataset evaluation demonstrated strong transfer between CP-CHILD-A and CP-CHILD-B, while external evaluation on Kvasir revealed substantial domain shift. Evaluation on the independent VIM-Polyp dataset showed high positive-case recall, although this dataset comprised an adult, positive-only cohort. Overall, the findings support the effectiveness of two-phase training within the evaluated CP-CHILD setting while highlighting the importance of dataset diversity, patient-level separation, and independent pediatric validation before clinical deployment.

https://www.nature.com/articles/s41388-0.title: RHBDL2 promotes cancer stemness and chemoresistance in triple-negative breast cancer through EGFR/PI3K/AKT/mTOR/c-Myc pathway
https://www.nature.com/articles/s41388-0.abstract: Chemoresistance remains a major challenge in the treatment of triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC). However, the mechanisms underlying chemoresistance remain poorly understood. In this study, we identified that higher levels of Rhomboid-Like 2 (RHBDL2) expression were associated with chemoresistance and poor prognosis in patients with TNBC. Notably, the knockdown of RHBDL2 suppressed cancer stemness and chemoresistance by inhibiting CD44+/CD24− breast cancer stem cells (BCSCs) in TNBC cells. RNA sequencing analysis revealed that the EGFR/PI3K/AKT/mTOR/c-MYC signaling pathway was involved in this process. Mechanistically, we observed that RHBDL2 activated the EGFR/PI3K/AKT/mTOR/c-MYC signaling pathway by binding to EGFR. Knockdown of RHBDL2 inhibited the expression of EGFR on the TNBC cell membrane, thereby deactivating the downstream signaling pathway, and ultimately inhibiting TNBC progression and chemoresistance. Remarkably, our in vivo experiments demonstrated that knockdown of RHBDL2 effectively inhibited tumor growth in xenograft tumor models. Collectively, our study uncovers the roles and mechanisms of RHBDL2 in TNBC chemoresistance and proposes targeting RHBDL2 as an innovative therapeutic strategy to overcome chemoresistance in TNBC.

https://www.nature.com/articles/s41418-0.title: ENPP1 inhibits the cGAS–STING pathway to mediate immune evasion in EGFR-TKI–resistant non–small cell lung cancer
https://www.nature.com/articles/s41418-0.abstract: Third-generation EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs), such as osimertinib, have demonstrated promising clinical efficacy in the treatment of EGFR-mutant non–small cell lung cancer (NSCLC). Despite substantial progress with EGFR-TKIs, the development of acquired resistance remains a major clinical challenge. Notably, the addition of immune checkpoint blockade after TKI resistance has not resulted in significant survival benefits compared to chemotherapy. In this study, we performed a comprehensive transcriptomic analysis of established osimertinib-resistant tumor models and found that the expression of the ectonucleotide phosphodiesterase ENPP1, a key regulator of extracellular cGAMP signaling, was significantly upregulated in resistant tumors compared to the parental TKI-sensitive NSCLC tumors. Mechanistically, upregulated ENPP1 in resistant cells promoted the hydrolysis of extracellular cGAMP, suppressing the cGAS–STING pathway in immune cells and subsequently impairing immune cell activation and function, thereby promoting immune suppression and tumor progression. Genetic depletion or pharmacological inhibition of ENPP1 enhanced immune cell–mediated cytotoxicity against TKI-resistant tumor cells. Furthermore, the use of ENPP1 inhibitors both in vitro and in vivo enhanced immune cell activity and antitumor efficacy in TKI-resistant lung cancers with high ENPP1 expression. Importantly, these observations were further validated by paired clinical tumor samples, which demonstrated increased ENPP1 expression following the development of acquired EGFR-TKI resistance. Collectively, our study highlights a critical role for ENPP1 in mediating immune evasion through suppression of the cGAMP–STING pathway in the tumor immune microenvironment, supporting ENPP1 as a promising therapeutic target to enhance immunotherapy efficacy in EGFR-TKI–resistant NSCLC.

https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-0.title: CT radiomics for predicting thoracic vertebral compression fractures after radiotherapy in esophageal squamous cell carcinoma: a two-center retrospective study
https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-0.abstract: To develop and externally evaluate an exploratory CT radiomics-based model for patient-level risk stratification of thoracic vertebral compression fracture (VCF) after radiotherapy in patients with esophageal squamous cell carcinoma (ESCC). This retrospective two-center study included 551 patients with pathologically confirmed ESCC who underwent radiotherapy. Patients from institution 1 were randomly assigned to a training cohort (n = 321) or an internal validation cohort (n = 138), whereas patients from institution 2 were included in an external validation cohort (n = 92). Radiomic features and CT attenuation values were averaged across all eligible irradiated thoracic vertebrae on pretreatment CT for each patient. Candidate predictors were identified using univariable Cox regression, followed by Akaike information criterion–based Cox model selection in the training cohort. Six prediction models were developed: vertebral CT attenuation, radiomics, radiotherapy, clinical–radiotherapy, clinical–radiotherapy–CT attenuation, and radiomics-integrated models. Model performance was evaluated using the concordance index (C-index), time-dependent area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (time-dependent AUC), calibration curves, decision curve analysis, net reclassification improvement, and integrated discrimination improvement. During a median follow-up of 0.92 years (interquartile range, 0.58–1.50 years), 77 of the included patients developed post-radiotherapy thoracic VCFs, including 47, 21, and 9 events in the training, internal validation, and external validation cohorts, respectively. Age, alcohol consumption, radiotherapy fractions, vertebral CT attenuation, and Radscore were retained in the final radiomics-integrated model. The integrated model demonstrated discrimination for patient-level VCF risk, with C-index values of 0.888, 0.796, and 0.847 and 24-month AUCs of 0.903, 0.716, and 0.863 in the training, internal validation, and external validation cohorts, respectively. Bootstrap validation yielded an optimism-corrected C-index of 0.854. Although the external C-index comparison between Models 6 and 5 was statistically significant (p = 0.018), the 24-month NRI and IDI were not (p = 0.186 and p = 0.067, respectively). Calibration and decision-curve findings warrant cautious interpretation given the limited number of external events. CT radiomics showed promising predictive performance for post-radiotherapy VCFs in patients with ESCC and may provide additional information for individualized risk stratification. The radiomics-integrated model may have potential to support the identification of patients at higher VCF risk, although its incremental value and clinical utility require further validation in larger independent cohorts, particularly given the nonsignificant 24-month NRI and IDI results in the external validation cohort.

https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-0.title: Novel formula for improving the oral bioavailability of paclitaxel using P-glycoprotein inhibitors
https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-0.abstract: Paclitaxel (PCL), a taxane derivative with potent antimitotic properties, is ubiquitously utilized as a remedy for various cancers. PCL’s therapeutic utility via the oral route is limited by poor water solubility and low permeability, resulting in inadequate bioavailability. This limitation restricts the development of effective oral formulations, particularly for conditions such as gastric cancer. The current research aimed to evaluate the effects of P-glycoprotein (P-gp) inhibitors, specifically piperine (PIP) and silibinin (SBN), on the pharmacokinetic parameters of orally administered PCL. An in-silico drug-protein docking study was performed to evaluate interactions between PCL and selected P-gp inhibitors. PCL was administered orally at a dose of 40 mg/kg, either as a single treatment or in combination with PIP or SBN at 10, 20, and 40 mg/kg. Plasma samples were obtained at predetermined sampling intervals, followed by Liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry (LC-MS) analysis using an H-ESI source. Compared with PCL administered alone, combination treatment significantly enhanced key pharmacokinetic indices, including peak plasma concentration (Cmax) and area under the concentration–time curve (AUC). After administration of PCL with 10 mg/kg of PIP 1.67 and 1.09 fold increases in Cmax and AUC, 20 mg/kg of PIP 1.79 and 1.16 fold increases in Cmax and AUC, and 40 mg/kg of PIP 2.04 and 1.51 fold increases in Cmax and AUC. After administration of PCL with 10 mg/kg of SBN 1.36 and 1.03 fold increases in Cmax and AUC, 20 mg/kg of SBN 1.73 and 1.69 fold increases in Cmax and AUC, and 40 mg/kg of SBN 2.29 and 2.22 fold increases in Cmax and AUC. Additionally, the elimination half-life (t1/2) of PCL was extended, indicating prolonged persistence of the drug in circulation. It can thus be concluded that PCL, along with PIP or SBN, exhibits increased absorption through P-gp modulation. These findings emphasise the promising potential of incorporating such bioenhancers into the development of effective oral PCL formulations to improve cancer therapy. An AGREE score (0.69) indicates the eco-friendliness of the bioanalytical method.

https://www.nature.com/articles/s41419-0.title: Dipyridamole analogs uncouple two dipyridamole activities: induction of cancer cell death and inhibition of platelet aggregation
https://www.nature.com/articles/s41419-0.abstract: Statins, well-known for their cholesterol-lowering effects, have shown promise in inducing tumor-specific cell death by disrupting the mevalonate (MVA) pathway, a metabolic route critical for cancer cell proliferation and survival. However, their anticancer efficacy is hampered by a compensatory feedback mechanism involving the sterol regulatory element-binding protein 2 (SREBP2). When statins deplete cellular cholesterol, SREBP2 activation induces expression of genes involved in the MVA pathway, which counteract the anti-tumor effects of statin treatment. Our previous work revealed dipyridamole (DP), an established antiplatelet agent, as an enhancer of statins’ anticancer effects by inhibiting the SREBP-induced feedback response. Despite this advance, the broad pharmacological profile and antiplatelet activity of DP limit its applicability in the treatment of cancer patients. To address this limitation, we employed high-content image analysis to screen a library of 44 DP analogs for their ability to potentiate statin-induced pro-apoptotic activity in prostate and breast cancer cell lines. Concurrently, we evaluated these analogs for their impact on platelet aggregation. Remarkably, we identified five DP analogs that exhibited enhanced efficacy as potentiators of statin-induced apoptosis compared to DP, with undetectable antiplatelet aggregation activity. These data show these two DP activities can be successfully uncoupled using a medicinal chemistry strategy. This uncoupling is essential for reducing potential adverse effects on blood coagulation, particularly in cancer patients who are often at higher risk for bleeding compared with patients without cancer or patients undergoing surgery. This study not only demonstrates the feasibility of selectively enhancing statin efficacy through DP analogs but also paves the way for developing novel chemical entities that target SREBP in cancer, offering a promising strategy for safer, more targeted cancer therapies. This research contributes to advancing the understanding of MVA pathway modulation as a therapeutic strategy for cancer treatment.

https://www.nature.com/articles/s41698-0.title: IL1B⁺ Tumor-associated macrophages arise from inflammatory cancer-associated fibroblasts niches and are correlated with head and neck squamous cell carcinoma recurrence
https://www.nature.com/articles/s41698-0.abstract: Tumor-associated macrophages (TAMs) and cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs) are major components of the tumor microenvironment (TME), influencing tumor immunity, cancer progression, and treatment responses. Interactions between CAF and TAM subpopulations have only recently been investigated, revealing complex mechanisms that may shape tumor immunity and therapeutic outcomes. In this study, we performed single-cell RNA sequencing and spatial transcriptomics on primary patient-derived HPV-negative head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC) tumors to characterize cellular heterogeneity and stromal-immune crosstalk. We identified five TAM and four CAF subsets, with IL1B+ TAMs and IL-iCAFs forming a distinct, spatially co-localized inflammatory niche. In vitro co-culture experiments revealed that IL-iCAF-derived paracrine signals induced transcriptional features associated with the IL1B⁺ TAM state. Clinically, high infiltration of IL1B⁺ TAMs correlated with poorer survival and higher recurrence risk, likely driven by increased inflammatory signaling from IL1B+ TAMs that promotes regulatory T cell recruitment and exhaustion. Together, our findings identify a spatially organized inflammatory niche involving IL-iCAFs and IL1B⁺ TAMs and suggest that fibroblast-derived signals may contribute to the acquisition of inflammatory TAM features. These findings provide a basis for further investigation of IL-iCAF–TAM interactions and the potential clinical relevance of IL1B⁺ TAMs in HPV-negative HNSCC.

https://www.nature.com/articles/s41419-0.title: USP14-mediated deubiquitination stabilizes integrin β1 to sustain malignant progression and chemotherapy resistance in osteosarcoma
https://www.nature.com/articles/s41419-0.abstract: Osteosarcoma patients with metastasis or chemotherapy resistance typically have a poor prognosis, yet the precise mechanisms underlying these adverse clinical outcomes remain elusive. In this study, we analyzed tissue proteomic data from our osteosarcoma cohort to compare protein expression profiles between metastatic and non-metastatic cases, as well as subgroups with low versus high chemotherapy-induced tumor necrosis rates. Our clinical analyses revealed that elevated ubiquitin-specific protease 14 (USP14) expression was associated with lung metastasis, a lower tumor necrosis rate, and shorter overall survival. Functional experiments in vitro and in vivo demonstrated that USP14 knockdown robustly suppressed the proliferation and metastatic potential of osteosarcoma cells. Mechanistically, USP14 interacted with and stabilized integrin β1 via deubiquitination, thereby activating the FAK/SRC axis and inducing inhibitory  phosphorylation of GSK3β. This signaling cascade blocked β-catenin ubiquitin-dependent degradation to promote β-catenin accumulation, nuclear translocation, and subsequent activation of TCF/LEF-mediated transcription of downstream oncogenes, ultimately driving osteosarcoma progression. Moreover, chemotherapy upregulated USP14 expression, thereby promoting chemoresistance. Pharmacological inhibition of USP14 with IU1 synergistically enhanced the chemosensitivity of osteosarcoma cells to doxorubicin, effectively restraining tumor growth and metastasis. Collectively, our findings delineate a core USP14-driven oncogenic cascade governing osteosarcoma progression, highlighting USP14 as a promising therapeutic target to improve chemotherapy efficacy and clinical outcomes for osteosarcoma patients.

https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-0.title: Dose- and strategy-dependent effects of anti-angiogenic therapy on tumor growth and microenvironment remodeling
https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-0.abstract: To investigate how anti-angiogenic therapies influence tumor growth and tumor microenvironment remodeling in colorectal cancer, and to evaluate treatment-associated differences across dosages, therapeutic agents, and combination strategies. A murine colorectal cancer model established with MC38 cells was used to compare anti-angiogenic treatments across different doses, therapeutic agents, and combination regimens. Tumor growth was monitored, and microenvironmental changes were assessed using hematoxylin and eosin staining, reticulin staining, immunohistochemistry, and ELISA to characterize vascular, stromal, immune, and inflammatory alterations. All anti-angiogenic treatments inhibited tumor growth, with combination regimens showing greater efficacy than monotherapy. Fruquintinib exhibited a clear dose-dependent effect. Distinct treatment-associated remodeling patterns were observed, with bevacizumab associated with relatively organized vascular and stromal features, while the tested small-molecule TKIs were associated with more heterogeneous structural alterations. The low-dose combination strategy promoted coordinated vascular and immune microenvironment remodeling while maintaining antitumor activity. Anti-angiogenic treatments produced distinct tumor microenvironment remodeling patterns, with treatment-dependent changes in vascular and stromal organization. Optimizing dosing and combination strategies may help balance antitumor activity with coordinated microenvironmental remodeling. These findings provide a basis for further evaluation of anti-angiogenic strategies across additional colorectal cancer models.

https://www.nature.com/articles/s43856-0.title: Overview of models for predicting risk of developing ovarian cancer: a systematic review
https://www.nature.com/articles/s43856-0.abstract: Ovarian cancer is the deadliest gynaecological malignancy, and most cases are diagnosed at an advanced stage. There is no population-wide screening; models for predicting risk of ovarian cancer could be useful in decreasing mortality. We aimed to provide the first comprehensive overview of models for predicting the risk of developing ovarian cancer and their performance, risk of bias, and applicability. We performed a systematic search through MEDLINE and Embase to identify articles in which models for predicting risk of developing ovarian cancer were developed and/or validated. Model characteristics and measures of predictive ability were extracted and summarised for each model. The Prediction model Risk of Bias Assessment Tool (PROBAST) was used to assess risk of bias and applicability. We identified twenty-eight studies representing twenty-one ovarian cancer risk prediction models. Fifteen risk prediction models were developed or validated in the general population, while six were developed for high-risk populations, defined by family history, and one for patients with endometriosis. Twenty-three studies that reported discrimination and/or calibration had moderate-to-good performance. Risk prediction models with the best predictive ability reported an area under the receiver-operating characteristic curve (AUC) of 0.86 (95% confidence interval (CI) 0.84–0.87) for 2-year and an AUC of 0.77 (95% CI 0.76-0.78) for 10-year ovarian cancer risk in the general population. Several models for predicting short- and long-term risk of ovarian cancer have been published, of which a few have been validated in other populations. Some have limited predictive performance. Some models may be suitable for use in primary care or specialty clinics; however, assessment of their utility and validation in diverse cohorts is warranted. We aimed to identify in the published literature all models that have been developed to predict risk of developing ovarian cancer, and any studies that have been done to evaluate how well such models predict in another population.  From the identified articles, we extracted information on the models developed or evaluated, as well as any information on their ability to accurately predict the risk of developing ovarian cancer in the future.  We identified 28 articles and 21 models. Some were good at predicting the risk of ovarian cancer, but before they can be considered for use in practice, they would need to be evaluated in the population in which the prediction is to be made. If performing well, they may be useful for identifying individuals at a high risk of developing ovarian cancer who may benefit from early detection and prevention strategies or from enrolment into studies assessing the benefit of new such strategies. Ardasheva et al. provide an overview of models developed to predict the risk of developing ovarian cancer which may be used to identify individuals at a high risk.

https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-0.title: Silibinin enhances the antitumor effect of radiotherapy in melanoma cells and potentiates immunogenic cell death-associated markers
https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-0.abstract: Melanoma is an aggressive skin malignancy with limited response to radiotherapy (RT). This study investigated whether silibinin enhances RT-induced cytotoxicity and immunogenic cell death (ICD) in melanoma cells. Human A375 and murine B16-F10 melanoma cells were treated with silibinin, RT, or their combination. Cell viability and combination index (CI) values were evaluated. Apoptosis was quantified by flow cytometry, and caspase-dependent apoptosis was further investigated by measuring cleaved caspase-3 levels using ELISA with or without Z-VAD-FMK. ICD induction was evaluated by calreticulin (CRT) surface exposure and extracellular release of high-mobility group box 1 (HMGB1) and heat shock protein 70 (HSP70). Combination of silibinin with RT exhibited moderate synergistic anticancer effects in A375 and B16-F10 cell lines, as indicated by CI values < 1. Combination treatment significantly decreased cell viability and increased apoptosis compared with monotherapies. Increased cleaved caspase-3 levels were attenuated by Z-VAD-FMK, confirming caspase-dependent apoptosis. ICD markers, including CRT exposure HMGB1/ HSP70 release, were elevated in both cell lines and further enhanced by combination therapy. Silibinin promotes RT-induced apoptosis and ICD-associated markers. These finding support further investigation of silibinin as a potential adjunct to RT in melanoma cell lines.

https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-0.title: Dingxiang Guanshitong suppresses ESCC progression by modulating TAK1/NF-κB/GLUT1-associated glycolytic reprogramming
https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-0.abstract: Esophageal squamous cell carcinoma (ESCC) is a highly aggressive tumor with poor clinical outcomes and limited treatment options. Dingxiang Guanshitong (DGST), a traditional Chinese herbal formulation, has shown potential activity in ESCC, but its molecular mechanisms require further clarification. The current study aimed to evaluate the therapeutic impact and underlying biological actions of DGST on ESCC. Network pharmacology was used to identify candidate DGST constituents and targets, followed by KEGG pathway enrichment analysis. Antitumor effects of DGST was examined in a 4-nitroquinoline 1-oxide (4NQO)-induced ESCC mouse model using H&E staining, immunohistochemistry, TUNEL assay, and flow cytometry. Proteomics analysis identified differentially expressed proteins and enriched pathways. In TE-1 cells, TAK1 knockdown/overexpression stable lines were constructed by lentiviral transduction, and pathway involvement was evaluated using immunofluorescence, luciferase reporter assays, CCK-8, Transwell, scratch assays, qRT-PCR, western blotting, and metabolic indicator assays. DGST showed dose-associated suppression of ESCC tumor progression, cell proliferation, migration, and invasion, while promoting apoptosis. Proteomics suggested that DGST affected glycolysis and NF-κB-related pathways. DGST treatment was associated with reduced phosphorylation of TAK1, IκBα, and p65, lower GLUT1, HK2, PFKP, and LDHA expression, decreased ATP levels, and increased MPC1 as well as mitochondrial complex indicators. TAK1 knockdown enhanced the effects of DGST, whereas its overexpression reversed these effects. DGST may inhibit ESCC progression by modulating TAK1/NF-κB/GLUT1 axis-mediated glycolytic reprogramming. The findings elucidate the potential therapeutic value of DGST in the treatment of ESCC and provide mechanistic insights for its clinical application.

https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-0.title: miR-20a promotes cell proliferation and migration by targeting DLC1 in nasopharyngeal carcinoma
https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-0.abstract: The role of miR-20a in nasopharyngeal carcinoma (NPC) and its relationship with the tumor suppressor DLC1 remain incompletely understood. We analyzed miR-20a expression in public datasets and clinical samples, assessed cell proliferation and migration, and examined target regulation using a dual-luciferase reporter assay. Tumor growth was evaluated in a subcutaneous xenograft model. miR-20a was elevated in NPC tissues and cell lines, and higher expression was associated with poorer survival in a public dataset. miR-20a overexpression promoted cell proliferation and migration, altered epithelial–mesenchymal transition-associated markers, increased MMP-2, MMP-7 and MMP-9 protein levels, and enhanced xenograft growth. miR-20a inhibition increased DLC1 expression and the activity of a reporter containing the wild-type DLC1 3′ untranslated region, without significantly affecting the corresponding mutant reporter. DLC1 knockdown attenuated the inhibitory effects of miR-20a inhibition on colony formation and migration and counteracted associated protein changes. These findings support DLC1 as a functional mediator of miR-20a-associated malignant phenotypes in NPC and provide a rationale for further preclinical investigation of the miR-20a/DLC1 axis.

https://www.nature.com/articles/s41392-0.title: Antibody-drug conjugates: unpacking toxicity profiles and optimized designs for enhanced safety and antitumor efficacy
https://www.nature.com/articles/s41392-0.abstract: Antibody-drug conjugates (ADCs) have expanded treatment options across multiple malignancies, but their clinical benefit remains constrained by heterogeneous and sometimes serious toxicities. These toxicities rarely arise from a single component; instead, they reflect the association between target biology, molecular architecture, systemic exposure, and tissue susceptibility. We first examine the structural basis of ADC toxicity by discussing the distinct contributions of the antibody–target axis, linker, payload, drug loading, and conjugation strategy to systemic exposure and tissue toxicity. We distinguish organ-selective “on-target, off-tumor” injury from target-independent toxicity and further characterize two major off-target routes: context-dependent uptake of intact ADCs through Fcγ receptor-mediated or pinocytosis-dominant pathways, and spatially distinct exposure to released payload arising from premature systemic release or localized bystander diffusion. Furthermore, we summarize a multidisciplinary management framework, ranging from prophylactic measures to graded interventions across complex scenarios such as treatment rechallenge and combination therapy. Finally, we discuss strategies to widen the therapeutic window through exposure-response-guided dosing, next-generation molecular engineering, and emerging conjugate platforms. Artificial intelligence and computational approaches may further extend safety optimization from drug design to patient stratification and real-world surveillance. By linking molecular design, spatial exposure, and clinical management, this review provides an integrated framework to improve ADC safety while preserving antitumor efficacy.

https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.64898.title: BNCT Triggers Immunogenic Cell Death in B16 Melanoma Without Accompanying T-Cell Infiltration--Implications for Combination Immunotherapy
https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.64898.abstract: Objective: Boron neutron capture therapy (BNCT) is a targeted radiotherapy with highly selective tumor killing; its potential to induce immunogenic cell death (ICD) and modulate the tumor immune microenvironment has attracted attention. However, whether BNCT-induced immune activation can overcome the T-cell exclusion barrier of immunologically "cold" tumors and translate into intratumoral effector T-cell infiltration remains unclear. Methods: A B16 melanoma model was established in C57BL/6 mice. Mice were assigned to CK, N10/N20 (neutron irradiation alone for 10 or 20 min), BPA, and BNCTN10/BNCTN20 groups (BPA 500 mg/kg plus 10 or 20 min irradiation) to evaluate tumor suppression and survival. In a separate cohort (CK, N20, and BNCTN20), the most efficacious regimen (BNCTN20) was compared with CK on days 3 and 7: H&E staining; immunohistochemistry/immunofluorescence for gamma-H2AX, HMGB1, cleaved caspase-3, PD-L1, CD8+, and granzyme B; ELISA for cytokines and chemokines; and ICP-OES for 10B distribution. Results: BNCT significantly suppressed tumor growth. When CK tumors reached the humane endpoint (~2000 mm3), N20 tumor volume was half that of CK (TGI ~ 49.8%), whereas BNCTN20 reached only one tenth (TGI ~ 88.9%, p < 0.001), with prolonged survival (p < 0.001). BNCT induced gamma-H2AX-associated DNA damage, HMGB1 release, and cleaved caspase-3-mediated apoptosis; upregulated PD-L1; induced a Th1-type response (elevated IFN-gamma/TNF-alpha, reduced IL-10); and enhanced CXCL9/10 signaling. However, intratumoral CD8+ T-cell infiltration and granzyme B expression did not increase, indicating that this activation was not translated into a local effector T-cell response. Conclusions: BNCT inhibited tumor growth and prolonged survival while inducing ICD and a systemic Th1 response; nevertheless, systemic activation failed to translate into local CD8+ T-cell infiltration, while PD-L1 was upregulated, a "strong direct killing but blocked immune translation" profile in the B16 cold tumor. PD-L1-associated adaptive immune resistance may limit this conversion, providing rationale for combining BNCT with immune checkpoint blockade.

https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.64898.title: Targeting NF-κB prevents Schwann cell reprogramming and plexiform neurofibroma initiation in mouse model of Nf1
https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.64898.abstract: Plexiform neurofibromas arise in approximately half of all individuals with Neurofibromatosis Type I (NF1). Genetic lesions apart from NF1 pathogenic variants are not present in NF1 mutant Schwann cells, suggesting that tumorigenesis may instead require cellular rewiring. To identify putatively re-wired tumor cells, we used multiplex imaging and flow cytometry to delineate markers that distinguish tumor Schwann cell from non-tumor Schwann cells. We identified tumor Schwann cells as CD44+;CD49f+ cells that show increased transcription of epithelial to mesenchymal plasticity (EMP)- associated genes. CD44+;CD49f+ expression was induced by treating Nf1-/- Schwann cells with stressors or by direct NF-{kappa}B pathway activation via IKK2; treated Schwann cells increased secretion of NF-{kappa}B targets and immune cell chemoattractants CCL2 and CCL3. In established tumors, MEK inhibition plus NF-{kappa}B blockade diminished tumor cell proliferation, tumor Schwann cells, immune cell populations, tumor cytokines and tumor number. Notably, transient single agent NF-{kappa}B pathway blockade was sufficient to significantly delay tumor formation in mice. Thus, Nf1 loss in Schwann cells is followed by NF-{kappa}B activation and cellular reprogramming that drives tumor initiation and targeting NF-{kappa}B activation can reduce NF1-deficient tumor formation.

https://www.nature.com/articles/s41571-0.title: Unprecedented OS with the addition of tarlatamab to first-line maintenance therapy for ES-SCLC
Sacituzumab tirumotecan–pembrolizumab has efficacy in PD-L1-negative NSCLC

https://www.nature.com/articles/s41698-0.title: Pollutant-induced activation of the AHR–NF-κB–C/EBPβ axis in colorectal cancer
https://www.nature.com/articles/s41698-0.abstract: This study identified environmental pollutants associated with activation of the AHR–NF-κB–C/EBPβ signaling axis and examined their effects in colorectal cancer (CRC). ToxCast indicators and TCGA-COAD/READ RNA-seq data were integrated to construct a pollutant-response matrix; an SVM model prioritized phenmedipham for mechanistic testing. In vitro, phenmedipham increased AHR, p-p65, and C/EBPβ expression and pro-inflammatory cytokine secretion, whereas pathway-component silencing attenuated these effects. In vivo, phenmedipham increased colonic tumor burden and histopathological damage; pathway inhibition mitigated these phenotypes. Immunological analyses indicated impaired dendritic-cell activation and T-cell effector responses. These results provide preclinical evidence that phenmedipham can modulate inflammatory signaling and tumor-associated phenotypes in the tested models. They do not establish human carcinogenicity, CRC risk, or population-level exposure–disease causality; epidemiological validation is required.

https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-0.title: MSwinALL-Net: a multi-stage Swin Transformer network for acute lymphoblastic leukemia classification
https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-0.abstract: Acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) is a form of blood cancer that requires timely and precise diagnosis for effective treatment. The conventional method relies on manual examination of blood smear images which is a slow and inconsistent process due to cellular diversity and the limited availability of trained professionals. A Swin Transformer based architecture named MSwinALL-Net is proposed to overcome these challenges by incorporating a multi-stage shifted-window mechanism to capture both fine-grained local and global contextual features for identifying subtle abnormalities in leukemia cells. GAN based augmentation was used to synthesize high quality blood smear images. The proposed model outperforms transfer learning approaches by achieving an accuracy of 98.74%, precision of 1.0, recall of 0.99, F1-score of 0.99 and an AUC of 1.0 showing its potential for reliable, automated ALL diagnosis. The model's robustness and generalization are further validated through 5-fold cross-validation on benchmark leukemia datasets where the model outperformed recent transformer based models like ConvNeXt-Tiny and EfficientNetV2 which exhibited unstable and near random performance. These results highlighted MSwinALL-Net's effectiveness and reliability for automated ALL diagnosis in clinical applications. Future enhancement could incorporate more advanced generative frameworks such as StyleGAN and CycleGAN to further enhance synthetic image quality along with explainable AI techniques for providing interpretability and clinical transparency in real-world deployment.

https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-0.title: Ultrafine PVP-stabilized platinum nanoparticles for megavoltage X-ray radiosensitization of MCF-7 cells: synthesis, characterization, and free quercetin co-treatment
https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-0.abstract: Ultrafine polyvinylpyrrolidone-stabilized platinum nanoparticles (PVP-Pt NPs) were produced using a single-step hydrothermal route and investigated as candidate nanoradiosensitizers for megavoltage X-ray treatment of MCF-7 breast cancer cells. Their performance was examined both independently and during concurrent treatment with free quercetin (Que). Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) showed approximately spherical Pt nanoparticles, while quantitative TEM image analysis yielded particle diameters of approximately 3–6 nm with a mean diameter of ~ 4.5 nm. Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) showed a smooth and homogeneous surface without pronounced agglomeration or cracking, consistent with a stabilizing role of PVP in limiting particle coalescence. X-ray diffraction showed reflections consistent with crystalline face-centered cubic (FCC) platinum with the Fm-3 m space group. FTIR spectroscopy showed spectral features consistent with possible interactions between PVP functional groups and Pt species. The optical response was evaluated by UV–visible spectroscopy. The cytotoxic and radiation-associated effects of PVP-Pt NPs, free Que, and concurrent PVP-Pt + Que treatment were evaluated at concentrations of 0.1, 1, 10, and 100 µg/mL, with and without megavoltage X-ray irradiation at 2 and 4 Gy. Without irradiation, significant reductions in MTT-derived cell viability were observed for PVP-Pt and concurrent PVP-Pt + Que treatment at 10 and 100 µg/mL, whereas the overall effect of free Que concentration was not statistically significant. Among the investigated formulations, PVP-Pt NPs produced the greatest reduction in MCF-7 cell viability following irradiation. At 10 µg/mL mean MTT-derived cell viability was approximately 45.4% under 2 Gy and 38.6% under 4 Gy irradiation. These findings support further investigation of ultrafine PVP-Pt nanoparticles as candidate nanoradiosensitizers for enhancing radiation-associated cytotoxicity in MCF-7 breast cancer cells.
