https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-0.title: Cancer-associated fibroblasts as architects of tumor immune geography and lymphoid organization
https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-0.abstract: Cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs) shape how immune cells are organized within tumors and either support or hinder the formation of immune niches associated with clinical outcomes and treatment response known as tertiary lymphoid structures (TLSs). Some CAF states support immune-cell recruitment and TLS establishment, whereas others create dense, fibrotic environments that restrict immune organization. Importantly, the presence of TLSs does not by itself indicate antitumor immunity. Their function depends on surrounding CAFs, extracellular matrix, and blood and lymphatic vessels. In this Review, we argue that the TLS-CAF axis is a key determinant of antitumor immunity, highlighting a potential therapeutic opportunity for selective stromal reprogramming. Cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs) are a heterogeneous population of stromal cells that participate in the formation of tertiary lymphoid structures (TLSs). Here, the authors review the current knowledge on how CAF subsets shape the organization and function of immune cells within TLS and discuss the clinical implications of these CAF-TLS interactions.

https://www.nature.com/articles/s41408-0.title: Clinical characteristics, treatment, and long-term outcomes in 987 patients with splenic marginal zone lymphoma to inform treatment and surveillance strategies
https://www.nature.com/articles/s41408-0.abstract: Splenic Marginal Zone Lymphoma (SMZL) is an indolent non-Hodgkin lymphoma subtype. Due to its rarity, evaluation of real-world data is necessary to inform clinical practice. In this study, adults diagnosed with SMZL between 2000 and 2018 from North America, Europe, and Australia were included and followed until death or last visit. Data were extracted from medical records and regional/national registries. In total, 987 patients with median age of 68 years were included. The 10-year overall survival (OS) estimates were 59% (95%CI: 55-63) from first-line treatment and 49% (95%CI: 43-57) from second-line treatment. First-line splenectomy (n = 434) and rituximab monotherapy (n = 121) were associated with an Inverse Probability of Treatment Weighting (IPTW)-adjusted 5-year failure-free survival (FFS) of 52% for splenectomy versus 42% for rituximab; HR 0.70 (95%CI: 0.44-1.13) and adjusted HR for OS of 1.09 (95%CI: 0.59-2.01). The 10-year cumulative risk of transformation from diagnosis was 15% (95%CI: 12-18) with 5-year post-transformation OS of 38% (95%CI: 29-49), and 23% (95%CI: 13-41) for transformation after previous chemotherapy. Lower rates of transformation were seen in patients receiving frontline rituximab. While frontline therapy with either splenectomy or rituximab monotherapy had similarly favorable outcomes, patients had a persistent risk of progression and transformation andsurvival after transformation was poor.

https://www.nature.com/articles/s41419-0.title: ZNF598 promotes glioblastoma progression and temozolomide resistance by facilitating MFN1-mediated mitochondrial quality control
https://www.nature.com/articles/s41419-0.abstract: Glioblastoma (GBM) is the most aggressive primary brain tumor and frequently develops intrinsic or acquired resistance to temozolomide (TMZ). Mitochondrial quality control (MQC) is essential for tumor cell survival and therapeutic adaptation, yet its upstream regulatory mechanisms in GBM remain poorly defined. Here, we identify zinc finger protein 598 (ZNF598), an E3 ubiquitin ligase with RNA-binding capacity, as a critical regulator of MQC and TMZ resistance in GBM. Analysis of public datasets revealed that ZNF598 expression is significantly elevated in TMZ-resistant GBM cells and human glioma tissues, correlating with adverse patient prognosis. Functionally, ZNF598 knockdown suppressed GBM cell proliferation, induced apoptosis, and disrupted mitochondrial homeostasis, as reflected by reduced ATP production and mtDNA copy numbers, elevated reactive oxygen species, loss of mitochondrial membrane potential, and mitochondrial fragmentation. ZNF598 silencing suppressed tumor growth in subcutaneous and intracranial orthotopic xenograft models and markedly enhanced TMZ sensitivity in vitro and in subcutaneous xenografts. Mechanistically, ZNF598 associated with mitofusin 1 (MFN1) mRNA and maintained its stability, thereby sustaining MFN1 expression and MFN1-mediated mitochondrial fusion. Notably, this regulation was independent of the E3 ubiquitin ligase activity of ZNF598, as the catalytically inactive ZNF598C29A mutant restored MFN1 mRNA stability, MFN1 protein abundance, and mitochondrial function in ZNF598-depleted cells. Restoration of MFN1 partially rescued mitochondrial dysfunction and apoptosis induced by ZNF598 knockdown. Furthermore, screening of the Genomics of Drug Sensitivity in Cancer dataset identified the BET inhibitor RVX208, which rapidly reduced ZNF598 mRNA and protein levels, phenocopied the mitochondrial dysfunction and apoptosis caused by ZNF598 suppression, and increased TMZ responsiveness at least partly through ZNF598 downregulation. These findings establish ZNF598 as a pivotal upstream regulator of MFN1-mediated MQC and a key determinant of TMZ response in GBM, highlighting the ZNF598–MFN1 axis as a promising therapeutic target for overcoming TMZ resistance.

https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-0.title: SkinFusionNet: MobileNetV2 and vision transformer hybrid deep learning model with automated skin cancer classification
https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-0.abstract: Skin cancer is one of the most widespread and potentially fatal diseases worldwide, with millions of new cases diagnosed every year. Detecting malignant skin lesions early and accurately is crucial for improving patient survival and can also help reduce the overall cost of treatment. Nevertheless, the conventional methods of diagnosing are usually time-consuming, subjective, and dependent on the skills of a clinician, thus not providing homogeneous results. In order to solve such shortcomings, this paper presents an original hybrid deep learning model, SkinFusionNet (SFN), as an automated skin lesion classifier based on dermoscopic images. The suggested SFN model is a synergetic integration of the advantages of MobileNetV2 and Vision Transformer (ViT) architectures the ability to extract local features efficiently by using MobileNetV2 and the ability to learn long-range contextual dependencies by ViT. The manipulation of both fine-grained lesion textures and larger image structures by such integration results in the high diagnostic ability of SFN at a wide range of imaging settings. The model was trained and tested on the 2018 ISIC dataset which had been augmented and balanced to equalize malignant and benign samples at 3,000 and 3,000, respectively. With SFN, outstanding performance was observed with 95.44 per cent accuracy, 95.48 per cent precision, 95.44 per cent recall and a Dice score of 0.9544, which is high compared to current CNN based and hybrid models like ResNet, DenseNet and MobileNet variants. Grad-CAM visualizations were used to mark important areas of the images that had an impact on model predictions to increase clinical trust and interpretability to offer important information about the decision-making process. The findings have shown that SFN can be an effective, interpretable and high-performance framework used in the initial detection of skin cancer. It can be easily deployed in the real world due to its lightweight nature and good ability to generalize, especially in healthcare settings that have limited resources. The given strategy is an important move on the way to making explainable AI a part of dermatological diagnostics, which would make the process of skin cancer screening faster, more credible, and more accessible.

https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-0.title: The discovery and validation of genes associated with lactylation in papillary thyroid cancer
https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-0.abstract: Thyroid cancer is the most common endocrine malignancy. Lactic acid and acidification of the tumor immune microenvironment are key processes promoting carcinogenesis. This study was to identify genes related to lactylation in papillary thyroid cancer (P​TC) and explore potential regulatory mechanisms. Lactylation-associated genes were identified by combining differential expression and regression analyses, and these genes were subsequently used to construct a risk model. Functional enrichment analysis, immune microenvironment profiling, and drug sensitivity assessment were then performed. In addition, lactylation-associated genes scores were evaluated at the single-cell level, and key cell populations were identified. Finally, the expression of lactylation-associated genes was assessed in clinical samples. After multiple rounds of selecting, MTTP, FOSB, and JUN were identified as candidate lactylation-associated genes. A risk model was then constructed to classify PTC patients into a high risk group (HRG) and a low risk group (LRG), with HRG patients showing poorer prognosis. The “primary immunodeficiency” signaling pathway was associated with HRG and LRG. Significant differences were observed in the infiltration levels of endothelial cells and neutrophils between the HRG and LRG. Erlotinib_1168 were predicted to be more sensitive in the LRG, whereas Camptothecin_1003 and Vinblastine_1004 were predicted to be more sensitive in the HRG. Finally, single-cell analysis identified six cell types, among which T/natural killer cells, myeloid cells, B cells, thyrocytes, and myeloid cells were prioritized as candidate key cells by AUCell scoring of lactate-related gene set and the three-gene prognostic signature for subsequent pseudotime analysis. Experimental results show that, compared to the control group, MTTP, FOSB, and JUN were downregulated in tumors. MTTP, FOSB, and JUN were identified as lactylation-associated genes in PTC, offering preliminary clues for further investigation of targeted therapies.

https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-0.title: A compact integrated platform for real-time live-cell imaging and photodynamic therapy: design and experimental demonstration
https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-0.abstract: Real-time integration of live-cell imaging and photodynamic therapy (PDT) addresses a critical experimental gap between treatment delivery and longitudinal observation of cellular responses. We present a compact, incubator-compatible platform that integrates inverted bright-field microscopy, automated X–Y scanning, and a uniform 630-nm PDT illumination module within a single experimental workflow, allowing the same cell culture to undergo repeated imaging and PDT without transfer between separate incubation, treatment, and imaging setups. The optical module provides a 1.5 mm² field of view at 2.2 μm resolution. The integrated mechanical and electronic architecture enables automated scanning and repeatable acquisition of predefined imaging regions. To experimentally demonstrate the dual functionality of the platform, A375 melanoma cells treated with 5-aminolevulinic acid (5-ALA, 10–500 µM) underwent fractionated PDT and longitudinal imaging over 72 h. Complementary MTT assays confirmed a time- and dose-dependent decline in viability, while longitudinal image analysis quantified treatment-associated changes in cell confluency and individual-cell morphology over time. In addition, ROI overlap analysis demonstrated substantially improved preservation of imaging regions compared with a conventional workflow involving repeated manual sample transfer. By integrating treatment delivery and long-term imaging within the incubator, the platform provides an experimental infrastructure for continuous observation of the same cell populations during prolonged PDT protocols and other time-dependent cell-based studies.

https://www.cell.com/cancer-cell/fulltex.title: The neoantigen quality model: Is closer to self more non-self?
https://www.cell.com/cancer-cell/fulltex.abstract: T cells recognize antigens from pathogens and transformed cells. Yet what antigen is “ideal”? We propose a theoretical framework in which recognition is governed by T cell selection maximized near, not far from, self. Genomic errors generate antigens closer to self that paradoxically overlap with pathogen antigens and are immunogenic and non-self. We formalize this concept as the Neoantigen Quality Model, recasting antigen recognition as an adaptation to surveil the self and non-self living worlds.

https://www.cell.com/cancer-cell/fulltex.title: One structural class, one treatment? Firmonertinib in PACC-mutant NSCLC
https://www.cell.com/cancer-cell/fulltex.abstract: EGFR PACC-mutant non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) has limited treatment options. In this issue of Cancer Cell, Le et al. report preclinical profiles and promising systemic and intracranial efficacy of the broad-spectrum CNS-penetrant tyrosine kinase inhibitor firmonertinib in PACC-mutant NSCLC, supporting its further clinical development in this challenging mutation class.

https://www.cell.com/cancer-cell/fulltex.title: How far are we from multi-omics states to therapeutic targets in microsatellite-stable colorectal cancer?
https://www.cell.com/cancer-cell/fulltex.abstract: In this issue of Cancer Cell, Sadanandam et al. integrate multi-omics profiling of microsatellite-stable colorectal cancer with patient-derived models, identifying focal adhesion kinase and phosphoinositide-dependent kinase 1 as promising therapeutic targets. The study advances multi-omics discoveries toward functional precision oncology and potential treatment strategies to guide clinical translation.

https://www.cell.com/cancer-cell/fulltex.title: Finding MES: A hidden cell state in neuroblastoma
https://www.cell.com/cancer-cell/fulltex.abstract: In this issue of Cancer Cell, Patel et al. integrate bulk and single-cell/single-nucleus RNA sequencing with spatial transcriptomics and spatial proteomics across neuroblastoma patient-derived xenografts and annotated tumors to reveal adrenergic and mesenchymal signatures, identify distinct tumor cell populations in vivo, and demonstrate associations with patient outcomes.

https://www.cell.com/cancer-cell/fulltex.title: Intrinsic resistance to KRAS inhibition: Interfering with interferon
https://www.cell.com/cancer-cell/fulltex.abstract: In this issue of Cancer Cell, Zhang et al. perform multi-omics profiling on a large collection of patient-derived pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma organoids to elucidate the mechanisms underlying intrinsic resistance to KRAS inhibition. This work identifies suppression of innate immune signaling through sustained MYC activity as the principal driver of intrinsic resistance.

https://www.cell.com/cancer-cell/fulltex.title: Chromatin plasticity and lineage repurposing: When gastric identity turns acidic
https://www.cell.com/cancer-cell/fulltex.abstract: Chromatin dynamics shape gastric cancer at every stage. In this issue of Cancer Cell, Wang et al. uncover a premalignant chromatin state primed for oncogenic activation alongside a pseudo-gastric subtype that hijacks acid secretion to evade antitumor immunity, revealing gastric proton pumps as a potential therapeutic target.

https://www.cell.com/cancer-cell/fulltex.title: Neutrophils are known by their neighbors in breast cancer
https://www.cell.com/cancer-cell/fulltex.abstract: In this issue of Cancer Cell, Xu et al. combine large-scale computational pathology, spatial omics, and functional experiments to examine neutrophil organization in triple-negative breast tumors. They identify two neutrophil niches with different clinical associations: tumor-proximal neutrophils are linked to favorable prognosis, whereas neutrophils near immune cells associate with immunotherapy response.

https://www.cell.com/cancer-cell/fulltex.title: Antibiotics and outcomes of cancer immunotherapy: An updated meta-analysis and clinical applications
https://www.cell.com/cancer-cell/fulltex.abstract: Antibiotic-induced dysbiosis is increasingly recognized as a driver of resistance to immune checkpoint inhibitors, yet its clinical impact across cancer immunotherapy has lacked a comprehensive, up-to-date assessment. Porcari et al. report an updated meta-analysis of 116 cohorts and nearly 98,000 ICI-treated patients, showing that antibiotic exposure is significantly associated with worse overall and progression-free survival, and outline stewardship and microbiome-based strategies to prevent and repair dysbiosis in this setting.

https://www.cell.com/cancer-cell/fulltex.title: Lung neuroendocrine cancer induces immunosuppressive macrophages via serotonin to drive resistance to the T cell engager tarlatamab
https://www.cell.com/cancer-cell/fulltex.abstract: Nomura et al. identify a neuroimmune mechanism of resistance to DLL3 × CD3-directed T cell engager and ICB therapy in SCLCs and LCNECs. They show that tumor-derived serotonin programs immunosuppressive macrophages through HTR7 signaling, dampening antitumor T cell responses and limiting immunotherapy efficacy, while revealing a therapeutically actionable vulnerability.

https://www.cell.com/cancer-cell/fulltex.title: A sex-specific platelet switch controls anti-tumor immunity in glioblastoma
https://www.cell.com/cancer-cell/fulltex.abstract: Sloan et al. show that platelets suppress anti-tumor immunity through PAR4 signaling in glioblastoma. Blocking PAR4 selectively benefits females by enhancing estrogen receptor β-dependent CD8+ T cell responses, uncovering a mechanism that links thrombosis, sex differences, and immunotherapy and suggesting new opportunities for precision cancer treatment.

https://www.cell.com/cancer-cell/fulltex.title: Chromatin accessibility trajectories reveal pre-cancerous epigenetic priming and an acid-driven immunotherapy-resistant gastric cancer subtype
https://www.cell.com/cancer-cell/fulltex.abstract: Wang et al. build a chromatin accessibility atlas of 650 gastric tissue samples spanning pre-cancer to advanced cancer, revealing a cancer-like epigenetic priming state in metaplasia that licenses tumor initiation. Advanced cancers segregate into three epigenomic subtypes; the pseudo-gastric subtype resists immunotherapy via FOSL2-driven H+/K+ ATPase expression that acidifies the microenvironment and suppresses CD8+ T cells—a phenotype reversed by the acid blocker vonoprazan.

https://www.cell.com/cancer-cell/fulltex.title: Spatial omics resolves adrenergic and mesenchymal cell states in neuroblastoma
https://www.cell.com/cancer-cell/fulltex.abstract: Patel et al. combine six spatial-omics platforms with single-cell/single-nucleus RNA sequencing across 54 neuroblastoma tumors to resolve a debate over malignant mesenchymal (MES) tumor cells. Using signatures from patient-derived xenografts, they identify MES tumor cells and show that a higher MES score predicts worse patient outcome.

https://www.cell.com/cancer-cell/fulltex.title: A stroma-sensing TGF-β blockade reprograms CAF-myeloid niches to induce durable tumor immunity
https://www.cell.com/cancer-cell/fulltex.abstract: Kang et al. show that anchoring a soluble TGF-β trap (FEBP-sTβRII) to FN-EDB-rich matrix overcomes fibrotic immune exclusion. This localized blockade drives IFN-γ-dependent CAF-myeloid reprogramming, enhances T cell infiltration, and establishes durable, cross-protective antitumor immunity.

https://www.cell.com/cancer-cell/fulltex.title: Decoding neutrophil spatial heterogeneity and clinical implications in breast cancer
https://www.cell.com/cancer-cell/fulltex.abstract: Xu et al. investigate neutrophil spatial heterogeneity by integrating AI-powered computational pathology and single-cell spatial omics in comprehensive breast cancer cohorts. They identify clinically relevant neutrophil spatial patterns and provide mechanistic insights into the underlying biology. Combining neutrophil spatial patterns with established biomarkers further refines patient stratification.

https://www.cell.com/cancer-cell/fulltex.title: Firmonertinib in advanced non-small cell lung cancer with epidermal growth factor receptor P-loop and αC-helix compressing mutations
https://www.cell.com/cancer-cell/fulltex.abstract: Le et al. show that the small molecule TKI firmonertinib has a unique structure to inhibit EGFR PACC mutations in non-small cell lung cancer. In the phase 1b FURTHER trial, patients had robust and durable responses to firmonertinib with tolerable side effects. These findings support advancing to a large, randomized trial.

https://www.cell.com/cancer-cell/fulltex.title: Multiomic characterization of microsatellite-stable colorectal cancer reveals distinct biology and targetable vulnerabilities
https://www.cell.com/cancer-cell/fulltex.abstract: Sadanandam et al. integrate multiomic, single-cell, and clinical data from ∼2,000 CRC tumors (∼4,500 multiomic profiles including 195,246 cells/nuclei) to define microsatellite stable (MSS) CRC complexity. Analyses identify replication stress, right-sidedness, glutaminolysis, and MYC-E2F-associated epigenetic programs as key features and FAK, PDK1/2, and proteasomal inhibition, combined with trametinib, as potential therapeutic strategies in MSS CRC.

https://www.cell.com/cancer-cell/fulltex.title: KRASG12D-targeted therapy sensitivity depends on interferon signaling activation in pancreatic cancer
https://www.cell.com/cancer-cell/fulltex.abstract: Zhang et al. show that intrinsic resistance to KRASG12D-targeted therapy in pancreatic cancer is driven by suppressed interferon signaling associated with sustained MYC activity. Activation of interferon pathways, particularly via IFN-β, resensitizes resistant tumors and synergizes with KRAS inhibitors, revealing interferon signaling as an actionable target.

https://www.nature.com/articles/s41573-0.title: Conditional biologics in cancer immunotherapy: mechanisms, applications and clinical progress
https://www.nature.com/articles/s41573-0.abstract: Immunotherapy has transformed cancer treatment, enabling durable responses and long-term survival in many patients. However, widespread use remains limited by refractory indications, immune-related toxicities and acquired resistance. Complications such as cytokine release syndrome, immune-related adverse events, infusion-related reactions and on-target, off-tumour toxicities have emerged as specific safety concerns. Approaches that can direct immunotherapy to the tumour microenvironment (TME), such as intratumoural administration, have only partially mitigated these risks and present additional logistical and technical barriers. Conditional biologics, in which proteins are engineered to become active in response to tumour-associated signals or in the TME, enable the uncoupling of efficacy from toxicity. By enhancing tumour accumulation, targeting activity to a particular cell type and minimizing off-target effects, conditional activation offers a potential strategy to expand the therapeutic window of cancer therapeutics. This Review provides a comprehensive overview of the mechanisms, applications, challenges and future directions of this approach, while assessing completed and ongoing clinical trials. Conditional biologics (CBs) — protein therapeutics engineered to selectively activate within the tumour microenvironment — have the potential to increase the potency and limit the off-target adverse effects of cancer immunotherapies. This Review describes the design principles and activation mechanisms of CBs, assesses those being investigated in the clinic, and addresses ongoing challenges and future directions for the field.

https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-0.title: Prospective evaluation of urinary cytology in the VI-RADS 3 grey zone: association with muscle invasion in bladder tumors
https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-0.abstract: VI-RADS 3 lesions represent a diagnostic grey zone for predicting muscle invasion in bladder cancer. We aimed to evaluate the association between preoperative urinary cytology and pathological muscle invasion and to assess its diagnostic performance in patients with VI-RADS 3 bladder tumors. In this prospective single-center cohort study, patients who underwent TURBT between September 2023 and September 2025 were evaluated. Among 241 consecutive patients, 57 with preoperative VI-RADS 3 lesions and available urinary cytology were included. The primary outcome was pathological muscle invasion (≥ T2). Given the few events, analyses were unadjusted: Fisher’s exact test, absolute difference in proportions, odds ratio (OR), and sensitivity, specificity, positive (PPV) and negative predictive values (NPV) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs). Muscle-invasive disease was detected in 5/57 patients (8.8%). Urinary cytology was positive in 12/57 (21.1%) and negative in 45/57 (78.9%). The rate of positive cytology was significantly higher in patients with muscle-invasive disease compared to non–muscle-invasive cases (80.0% vs. 15.4%, p = 0.006). Muscle invasion occurred in 4/12 (33.3%) patients with positive and 1/45 (2.2%) with negative cytology (absolute difference 31.1% points, 95% CI 9.5–58.8% points). Sensitivity was 80.0% (95% CI 28.4–99.5), specificity 84.6% (71.9–93.1), PPV 33.3% (9.9–65.1) and NPV 97.8% (88.2–99.9). In this cohort, positive urinary cytology was associated with muscle invasion in VI-RADS 3 tumors. Whether cytology adds diagnostic value beyond mpMRI or improves clinical decision-making requires validation in larger multicenter studies.

https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-0.title: Isthmin-1, meteorin-like, and neuregulin-4 as potential diagnostic novel biomarkers for colorectal cancer in Thi-Qar Governorate, Iraq
https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-0.abstract: Colorectal cancer (CRC) is one of the leading causes of cancer complications and deaths globally. Unfortunately, we have limited tests for early diagnosis of the disease. Nevertheless, novel integrative metabolic and inflammatory markers, including Isthmin-1 (ISM1), Meteorin-like (Metrnl), Neuregulin-4 (NRG4), which have the ability to formulate novel diagnostic strategies and broaden the knowledge of CRC. In a case-control study of 180 individuals, three groups were assessed: patients with CRC, individuals with benign colorectal disease (BCD), and healthy controls (HC), with 60 individuals in each category. ELISA was performed to assess the levels of these markers in individuals’ blood. Statistical results showed clearly higher ISM1 levels in CRC patients (8.91 ± 2.14 ng/mL); BCD and HC showed 5.76 ± 1.63 ng/mL and 4.83 ± 1.41 ng/mL, respectively (p < 0.001). Metrnl values were lowered by 62.8 ± 15.7 pg/mL in CRC patients, versus 88.5 ± 19.4 pg/mL in BCD and 96.3 ± 20.1 pg/mL in HC (p < 0.001). NRG4 values were equally low in CRC patients, averaging 1.74 ± 0.52 ng/mL, although this was lower than in HC (p < 0.001). The ROC analysis was promising for the three markers, with AUC of 0.912 for ISM1, 0.895 for Metrnl, and 0.887 for NRG4. In addition, ISM1 was positively associated with tumor stage and tumor size (r = 0.61, 0.53), yet Metrnl and NRG4 had the opposite effect. This study demonstrates that elevated ISM1 levels, in conjunction with decreased Metrnl and NRG4 levels, are significantly associated with CRC and its severity. These biomarkers provide more accurate predictions, which may contribute to enhancing our understanding of early CRC detection and identifying risk factors.

https://www.nature.com/articles/s12276-0.title: Dynamic SMAD–RUNX2 complexes orchestrate breast cancer bone metastasis
https://www.nature.com/articles/s12276-0.abstract: Bone metastasis of breast cancer is a multistep process involving detachment from the primary tumor, homing and adhesion to bone, clonal survival, and osteolysis, driven by dynamic interactions between tumor cells and the bone microenvironment. Although Runt-related transcription factor 2 (RUNX2) has been recognized as a downstream effector of SMADs in bone metastatic programs, our study has revealed that SMAD–RUNX2 complexes also regulate the intrinsic functions of SMADs, thereby acting as active amplifiers of TGFβ and BMP signaling. We further characterized the distinct roles of the SMAD1–RUNX2 and SMAD2/3–RUNX2 complexes across the bone metastatic cascade using cancer cells overexpressing either wild-type RUNX2 or RUNX2 variants in response to treatment with TGFβ and BMP. SMAD–RUNX2 complexes were found to play microenvironment-dependent roles during bone metastasis. The TGFβ-induced SMAD2/3–RUNX2 complex promoted osteotropic migration and secondary dissemination, whereas the BMP-activated SMAD1–RUNX2 complex increased cancer cell adhesion and survival in the bone microenvironment, with both complexes increasing osteolytic lesion formation. Mechanistically, the competitive binding of SMAD2/3 and SMAD1 to RUNX2 appeared to underlie the crosstalk between the TGFβ and BMP pathways. Together, these findings demonstrate a dynamic interplay among SMAD1, SMAD2/3, and RUNX2 that integrates TGFβ and BMP signaling during bone metastasis, highlighting the potential for developing context-dependent therapeutic strategies. Bone metastasis is a significant complication of breast cancer, severely impacting patients' quality of life and survival. This study explores the roles of SMAD1–RUNX2 and SMAD2/3–RUNX2 complexes in breast cancer bone metastasis. Researchers used breast cancer cells with wild-type or mutated RUNX2 to analyze the effects of these complexes under TGFβ and BMP treatments. They found that SMAD2/3–RUNX2 promotes cancer cell migration to bone, while SMAD1–RUNX2 enhances cell adhesion to bone. These complexes differentially regulate gene expression related to metastasis, with SMAD2/3–RUNX2 facilitating dissemination and SMAD1–RUNX2 supporting bone colonization. The findings highlight the role of RUNX2 as a transcriptional amplifier in TGFβ and BMP signaling, suggesting potential therapeutic targets for managing bone metastasis. Future research could focus on disrupting SMAD–RUNX2 interactions to develop treatments for bone metastasis. This summary was initially drafted using artificial intelligence, then revised and fact-checked by the author.

https://www.nature.com/articles/s41416-0.title: Long-term fatigue dimensions in the Multidimensional Fatigue Inventory (MFI) up to five years after radiotherapy and their trajectories in men diagnosed with non-metastatic prostate cancer in the international REQUITE study
https://www.nature.com/articles/s41416-0.abstract: Fatigue is a common, multidimensional symptom in cancer patients. Little is known about fatigue dimensions and their trajectories in prostate cancer (PCa). Using the Multidimensional Fatigue Inventory (MFI), 1097 men treated with radiotherapy for non-metastatic PCa (2014–2016) prospectively reported fatigue up to five years later. Prevalent fatigue was defined as scores ≥75th percentile in men aged ≥60 years in a German general population sample. Pre-radiotherapy patient characteristics were examined for their associations with general fatigue, physical fatigue, mental fatigue, reduced activity, and reduced motivation two years later using logistic regression models. Fatigue trajectories up to two years post-radiotherapy were explored using latent class growth analysis and multinomial regression. About 72% (785/1097) of patients reported being fatigued for at least one dimension in the MFI from before the start of radiotherapy up to five years later, with 45% (367/816) being fatigued two years post-radiotherapy. Pre-radiotherapy fatigue level (OR: 4.7–9.0), depression (OR: 2.5), diabetes (OR: 1.8–2.2), hypertension (OR: 1.6–1.8), and BMI (OR: 1.8–2.2) were statistically significant predictors of long-term fatigue two years post-radiotherapy across dimensions. Depression, BMI, and pelvic radiotherapy were associated with experiencing a high fatigue trajectory. Early fatigue assessments, in addition to self-reported comorbidities and BMI, showed additional benefits beyond symptom detection by providing prognostic value for poorer long-term fatigue outcomes. Multidimensional fatigue assessments could guide tailored symptom management strategies, targeting specific dimensions to address associated impairments in quality of life and functioning.

https://www.nature.com/articles/s41590-0.title: Mechanosensitive YAP–RUNX1 signaling drives TH1 cell dysfunction and tumor immunosuppression
https://www.nature.com/articles/s41590-0.abstract: Tissue stiffening is a predominant malignant physical alteration in cancer progression, yet its effect on specific immune subsets within the tumor microenvironment is not well defined. Here we show that elevated tissue stiffness subverts tumor-infiltrating type 1 helper T (TH1) cells to drive immunosuppression in pancreatic cancer. Mechanistically, stiffness triggers integrin-mediated mechanotransduction to activate YAP, which translocates to the nucleus and cooperates with RUNX1 to transcriptionally upregulate a set of dysfunction-associated genes. These reprogrammed TH1 cells acquire a distinct dysfunction-associated secretory phenotype, which in turn drives M2-like polarization of macrophages and amplifies local immunosuppression. Notably, inhibiting YAP expression or disrupting YAP–RUNX1 interaction reverses the dysfunctional state of TH1 cells and restores antitumor immunity. These findings delineate a mechano–immunological mechanism by which tumor stiffness subverts TH1 cell functions, indicating a possible therapeutic avenue to alleviate immunosuppression and potentiate immunotherapy efficacy in stiff tumors. Solid tumor stiffness can limit the ability of immune cells to enter and kill tumor cells. Here the authors show that this stiffness activates YAP signaling in type 1 helper T cells, making them dysfunctional and thereby leading to a more immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment.

https://www.nature.com/articles/s41375-0.title: Mesenchymal stromal cells drive immune escape in MDS and sAML through metabolic rewiring of NK cells
https://www.nature.com/articles/s41375-0.abstract: Myelodysplastic neoplasms (MDS) are clonal hematopoietic stem cell disorders that frequently progress to secondary acute myeloid leukemia (sAML). Besides intrinsic genetic changes, the disease’s development is heavily influenced by the bone marrow (BM) microenvironment, especially mesenchymal stromal cells (MSCs). In this study, we present a comprehensive characterization of how unhealthy MSCs affect natural killer (NK) cell anti-leukemic function in MDS and sAML. Using integrated ATAC-seq and RNA-seq profiling, we show that MDS/sAML-derived MSCs induce profound chromatin remodeling in NK cells, marked by reduced promoter accessibility and downregulation of genes essential for stress response and survival. Functionally, pathological MSCs fail to deliver the protective support normally provided by healthy MSCs, instead driving mitochondrial fragmentation and apoptosis in NK cells, ultimately suppressing their cytotoxic activity. Together, these findings reveal a previously unrecognized loss of supportive capacity in pathological MSCs that hampers NK-cell fitness. Therapeutic approaches that bolster mitochondrial resilience in NK cells may help counteract this microenvironment-induced impairment and strengthen immune surveillance in MDS and sAML.

https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-0.title: Prevalence of autoimmune disease and associated 5-hydroxymethylcytosine cell-free DNA patterns in appendiceal neoplasms
https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-0.abstract: Autoimmune diseases (AID) are associated with increased risk of developing gastrointestinal cancers, but their relationship with appendiceal neoplasms (AENs) remains unexplored. We performed a multi-institutional retrospective review of 179 AEN patients, identifying 44 (24.6%) with a history of AID, most commonly suspected Hashimoto’s thyroiditis (14.0%). 5-hydroxymethylcytosine (5hmC), an epigenetic marker involved in gene regulation and immune function, offers a promising tool for studying tumor biology. Plasma samples from 68 patients were analyzed using Nano-hmC-Seal (5hmC-Seal) technology to generate genome-wide 5hmC profiles from cfDNA. 5hmC profiling identified 58 candidate differentially hydroxymethylated regions (DhMRs) and 80 candidate differentially hydroxymethylated genes (DhMGs) between AID and non-AID patients based on nominal p-value and effect-size thresholds. These included. several oncogenes, proto-oncogenes, and tumor suppressor genes such as MNT, FYN, ERG, and KAT6B. Functional pathway analysis involving differentially hydroxymethylated regions or genes revealed significant hydroxymethylation of immune-related and oncogenic pathways in patients with autoimmune disease, including intestinal immune network for IgA production, along with the IgE high-affinity receptor, FcεRI, and MAPK and ErbB signaling pathways. These findings suggest that autoimmune conditions might contribute to a distinct epigenetic landscape in appendiceal cancers, supporting further investigation into immune-mediated mechanisms of tumorigenesis.

https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-0.title: Helicobacter pylori infection as a prognostic factor in gastric cancer: Impact of comorbidities on overall survival
https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-0.abstract: Helicobacter pylori infection is a risk factor for gastric cancer, but its impact on prognosis remains underexplored in high-prevalence settings such as Brazil. This study aimed to estimate overall survival in patients with gastric adenocarcinoma and H. pylori infection and identify comorbidities associated with prognosis in a Brazilian multicenter cohort. This was a prospective multicenter cohort study in three Brazilian centers (North, Midwest, Southeast). Sociodemographic, clinical, and histopathological variables were analyzed among patients tested for H. pylori. Frequencies were compared via Pearson's chi-square test. The probability of overall survival was estimated via Kaplan‒Meier analysis, and associations with prognostic factors were assessed via Cox regression (stepwise forward, p < 0.20). H. pylori-positive patients had greater survival (65%) than H. pylori-negative patients did (51%), but the difference was not significant. Infection is associated with tumors in the body/antrum and initial stage. In the multiple model, stage III/IV disease and a Charlson Comorbidity Index score ≥ 3 were associated with increased mortality regardless of infection status. Among the negative patients, those with vascular disease had an increased risk of death (HR = 1.67; p = 0.05). Among positive patients, those with peptic ulcer (HR = 6.53; 95% CI 1.44–29.54; p = 0.01) and diabetes (HR = 3.81; 95% CI 0.99–14.70; p = 0.05) tended to have increased mortality. In this Brazilian multicenter cohort, H. pylori infection was associated with a worse prognosis in patients with gastric adenocarcinoma. Vascular disease increased mortality among negative patients, whereas peptic ulcer and diabetes tended to increase mortality among positive patients. Assessing comorbidities and H. pylori status should be considered in the prognosis and therapeutic management of these patients.

https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-0.title: In Vivo T2 mapping for early treatment response assessment in esophageal cancer: a prospective study
https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-0.abstract: To evaluate the feasibility and reproducibility of in vivo T2 mapping in esophageal cancer (EC) and explore its role in early treatment response assessment during nonsurgical multimodal therapy. This prospective study consecutively enrolled patients with pathologically confirmed EC who were undergoing nonsurgical multimodal therapy from February 2024 to February 2026. In vivo T2 mapping MRI was performed before treatment initiation and again prior to the second treatment cycle. Image quality and measurement reproducibility of T2 mapping were evaluated. Quantitative parameters, including pre- and post-treatment T2 values, absolute change (ΔT2), and percentage change (ΔT2%), were calculated. Apparent diffusion coefficient (ADC)-derived parameters were also assessed as established diffusion-based quantitative imaging biomarkers for comparison and multiparametric analysis. Treatment response was assessed using predefined clinical response criteria, and patients were classified into responder and non-responder groups. Between-group differences in T2-derived parameters were analyzed. Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve analysis and multivariable logistic regression were performed to evaluate treatment response using clinical-adjusted and imaging-based models. Thirty-four patients were identified as responders (CR/good PR), and twenty-two as non-responders (IR/SD/PD) based on clinical response evaluation. T2 values decreased significantly after early treatment compared with baseline (p < 0.05). The magnitudes of ΔT2 and ΔT2% were significantly greater in responders than in non-responders. No significant differences were observed in absolute T2 values between the two groups either before or after treatment. The area under the curve (AUC) was 0.738 for ΔT2 and 0.754 for ΔT2% in predicting treatment response. The optimal cutoff values for ΔT2 and ΔT2% were − 5.44 ms and − 6.52%, respectively. In the clinical-adjusted model, ΔT2% remained significantly associated with treatment response after adjustment for age, sex, tumor location, and American Joint Committee on Cancer (AJCC) clinical stage. The imaging-based model showed a higher AUC than ΔADC alone (0.834 vs. 0.823), but the difference was not significant (DeLong test, p = 0.554). In vivo T2 mapping demonstrated good measurement reproducibility in EC. Both ΔT2 and ΔT2% were associated with treatment response, whereas the incremental value of combining ΔT2% with ΔADC requires further investigation.

https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-0.title: TMEM45A promote triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) related depression via the AKT/mTOR signaling pathway
https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-0.abstract: Patients diagnosed with triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) frequently experience depression, a comorbidity that substantially compromises quality of life and survival outcomes. This study aimed to characterize the functional role and underlying regulatory mechanisms of TMEM45A in triple-negative BC related depression (TN-BCRD). First, we validated the regulatory effects of TMEM45A in 4T1 cells. An in vitro TN-BCRD model was established using HT22 hippocampal neurons co-exposed to 4T1 cell-derived conditioned medium and corticosterone. The siRNA of TMEM45A was transfected into 4T1 cells to investigate the effect of tumor cell-expressed TMEM45A on the TN-BCRD phenotype and the AKT/mTOR signaling pathway. For in vivo validation, we established 4T1 tumor-bearing mice model and examined the effects of tumoral TMEM45A on tumor growth, depression-like phenotypes, and hippocampal AKT/mTOR signaling. TMEM45A is significantly overexpressed in TNBC tissues. Knockdown of TMEM45A induced apoptosis and inhibited migration and invasion in 4T1 cells, while it promoted proliferation and reduced apoptosis in HT22 cells. TMEM45A knockdown also attenuated the activity of AKT/mTOR signaling and reduced the secretion of pro-inflammatory factors in HT22 cells under BCRD conditions. In vivo mice experiments demonstrated that TMEM45A knockdown in 4T1 cells suppressed the tumor growth and rescued depression-like behaviors in tumor-bearing mice. TMEM45A serves as a key regulator of TN-BCRD, and its targeted inhibition may represent a promising therapeutic strategy for this condition.

https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-0.title: Eligibility gap scoring across first-line targeted and immunotherapy trials and real-world cohorts in metastatic renal cell carcinoma
https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-0.abstract: First-line treatment for metastatic renal cell carcinoma (mRCC) has shifted toward immune checkpoint inhibitor-based combinations, but pivotal trial populations may differ from patients treated in routine practice. We developed an eligibility gap (EG) score to visualize selected eligibility-related baseline characteristics across first-line mRCC studies. Phase III randomized controlled trials (RCTs), published real-world data (RWD) cohorts, and the original AGEHA-JPN cohort were analyzed. The EG score integrated median age, prior nephrectomy rate, and IMDC risk distribution on a 0–99.9 scale. Thirty-six datasets were included: 10 RCTs, 25 published RWD cohorts, and AGEHA-JPN. Median EG scores were higher in RCTs than RWD cohorts (74.0 vs 60.3; p < 0.001), mainly reflecting younger age and higher prior nephrectomy rates, whereas IMDC-domain scores were similar. Asian RWD cohorts had lower median scores than non-Asian RWD cohorts (50.7 vs 64.5). Sensitivity analyses using alternative domain and sample-size weighting preserved the RCT–RWD separation. The EG score provides a descriptive framework for contextualizing selected baseline differences between trial and real-world populations. However, it does not capture factors such as histology, comorbidity, or metastatic burden and is not a comprehensive measure of trial eligibility, generalizability, or prognosis.

https://www.nature.com/articles/s41698-0.title: E2F1 signatures stratify immunotherapy response and reveal YWHAQ vulnerability in esophageal squamous cell carcinoma
https://www.nature.com/articles/s41698-0.abstract: To improve biological interpretation of immune checkpoint inhibitor (ICI) response in esophageal squamous cell carcinoma (ESCC), we developed an E2F1 transcriptional regulation-related framework integrating spatial multi-omics and experimental validation. Single-cell and post-treatment spatial analyses localized E2F1-associated activity predominantly to malignant epithelial states. In ten ESCC Xenium specimens, paired patient-level analyses linked E2F1-high epithelial neighborhoods to lower CD8 effector T-cell and B-cell densities, a lower immune-active niche score, and higher epithelial CD274-positive fractions. In harmonized public ICI cohorts, E2F1.Sig functioned as an exploratory response-stratification signature, achieving the highest mean area under the curve (AUC) among evaluated immune signatures across validation and external testing cohorts. Separately, TCGA analyses supported prognostic associations of a 20-gene Hub-E2F1.Sig risk score. In ESCC, Hub-E2F1.Sig-based subtyping defined three immune microenvironmental states with distinct survival patterns. Cluster1 showed a more favorable immune contexture and better prognosis, suggesting its association with immune responsiveness. YWHAQ, a key Hub-E2F1.Sig gene, was associated with poor prognosis, and YWHAQ depletion reduced malignant phenotypes, increased cisplatin-associated apoptosis, and attenuated PD-1/PD-L1-associated immunosuppressive features in vitro and in vivo. Virtual screening identified 6’-Sialyllactose as an in silico candidate YWHAQ-binding compound. These findings support an exploratory E2F1-centered framework and nominate YWHAQ as an ESCC-focused therapeutic hypothesis.

https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-0.title: Redox, lipid, and metabolic changes associated with early tolerance to combination chemotherapy in two pancreatic cancer cell models
https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-0.abstract: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) shows limited responsiveness to chemotherapy and rapidly develops resistance, which can be facilitated by early adaptive tolerance to sub-lethal drug exposure. Here, we investigated changes associated with the development of early tolerance to a chemotherapy combination analogous in composition to FOLFIRINOX in MIA PaCa-2 and PANC-1 cells using a stepwise adaptation approach. Comparison of metabolic similarities and divergences between the two cell lines by dose-response analysis revealed limited, yet progressive and cell-specific, shiftsin drug sensitivity. At the consolidated stage, Nile Red imaging and targeted lipidomics revealed cell line-specific lipid remodeling, including elongation of membrane phospholipid acyl chains in both lines. PANC-1 cells show increased saturation of phosphatidylcholine and triacylglycerols and reduced polyunsaturation of phosphatidylethanolamine and phosphatidylcholine. Antioxidant profiling also shows model-dependent patterns: MIA PaCa-2 cells exhibit increased total catalase, total glutathione S-transferase, and glutathione reductase activities, whereas PANC-1 cells show reduced catalase activity together with increased total glutathione S-transferase activity. These changes are accompanied by increased cytosolic and mitochondrial oxidation-dependent fluorescence in MIA PaCa-2 cells and reduced mitochondrial oxidation-dependent fluorescence in PANC-1 cells. MIA PaCa-2 cells also showed reduced extracellular lactate production, while cellular energy charge remained unchanged in both models. Whether these adaptations can be exploited therapeutically remains to be tested; they nevertheless identify redox- and lipid-related pathways as candidates for functional studies aimed at preventing the transition from tolerance to stable resistance.

https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-0.title: Clinical application of deep neural networks in laser endomicroscopic molecular imaging for accurate assessment of lung nodules
https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-0.abstract: Needle-based near-infrared confocal laser endomicroscopy (NIR-nCLE) enables intraoperative imaging of pafolacianine-labeled cells within pulmonary lesions, but interpretation requires operator experience. We evaluated a machine-learning pipeline for classifying NIR-nCLE recordings as benign or malignant using final histopathology as the reference standard. Fifty patients undergoing pafolacianine-guided resection were prospectively enrolled, and 248 lesions were sampled. An AlexNet-based convolutional neural network classified individual frames, with lesions classified as malignant when the proportion of frames predicted to be malignant was ≥ 0.02. Lesion-level performance was assessed by stratified five-fold cross-validation using 121 analyzable recordings available in the retained de-identified archive, comprising 70 malignant and 51 benign lesions and 23,589 frames. All frames from each lesion were confined to a single fold; patient-level partitioning was not possible because patient-to-recording links were unavailable. Sensitivity was 98.6% (95% CI 95–100%), specificity was 72.5% (60–84%), positive predictive value was 83.1%, negative predictive value was 97.4%, accuracy was 87.6% (81–93%), and the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) was 0.97 (0.94–0.99). Logistic regression using mean fluorescence intensity alone achieved an AUROC of 0.97 (0.94–0.99) and an accuracy of 90.1%; a 100-unit feature-based neural network achieved an AUROC of 0.98 (0.95–1.00). In an internal exploratory intraoperative cohort of 10 additional patients, all nine malignant and 18 benign lesions were correctly classified before final pathological evaluation, yielding a sensitivity of 100% (95% CI 66.4–100%) and a specificity of 100% (81.5–100%). Automated classification of NIR-nCLE recordings demonstrated promising preliminary internal performance, with similar AUROC estimates for simpler fluorescence-based models. Independent external validation with patient-level separation is required before clinical use.

https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-0.title: Development of quinoline derivatives as dual EGFR/HDAC-2 inhibitors: design, synthesis, anticancer evaluation, and molecular dynamics simulations
https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-0.abstract: The quinoline scaffold is widely exploited in the design of new anticancer candidates. As a continuation of our previous work in the search for promising anticancer candidates, we designed novel quinoline-based compounds linked to a range of heterocyclic rings by applying a molecular hybridization strategy. In this work, the resulting quinoline derivatives were synthesized and evaluated for their anti-proliferative activity against three cancer cell lines, namely PC-3, HCT-116, and MDA-MB-231, in addition to one normal cell line, WI-38. Among these compounds, two derivatives (4) and (11) showed potent anti-proliferative activity against MDA-MB-231 breast cancer cells with IC₅₀ values of 4.91 and 8.25 µM, respectively. The same two derivatives also showed significant activity against the HCT-116 colon cancer cell line with IC₅₀ values of 6.38 and 9.44 µM, respectively. Mechanistic studies further showed that compound (4) potently inhibited EGFRWT (IC₅₀ = 0.084 µM) and mutant EGFR forms, as well as HDAC-2 with IC50 = 0.123 µM. All biological assays were performed in three independent experiments (n = 3), and all reported differences versus the untreated control were significant at a two-sided adjusted P < 0.05. Additionally, western blot analysis of compound (4) revealed downregulation of pEGFR, pERK, and pAKT, while RT-qPCR analysis showed upregulation of BAX and caspase-3, -7, and − 9 and downregulation of BCL-2 at the mRNA level. Cell-cycle analysis showed that derivative (4) induced arrest at the G1/S boundary. Taken together, all these results, along with molecular docking and molecular dynamics simulations, supported the stable binding within the ATP-binding site of EGFR and the zinc-binding pocket of HDAC-2.

https://www.nature.com/articles/s41573-0.title: Histone lysine demethylases in the third decade: biology and therapeutic prospects
https://www.nature.com/articles/s41573-0.abstract: Histone post-translational modifications, such as methylation, acetylation, phosphorylation and ubiquitination, have fundamental roles in regulating chromatin structure and gene expression. Histone methylation was once considered a static modification until the discovery of the histone lysine demethylase LSD1 (KDM1A), more than two decades ago. Since then, numerous KDMs in two main enzyme classes have been identified. Their diverse roles in regulating gene expression, metabolism, immune responses and disease pathogenesis have been extensively studied and small-molecule inhibitors have been developed. KDMs exert context-dependent functions as either oncogenes or tumour suppressors, which complicates their therapeutic targeting. As we enter the third decade of investigations into histone demethylation, unlocking the full therapeutic potential of inhibiting KDMs will require a deeper understanding of their biology, substrate specificity, interaction networks and regulatory crosstalk. In this Review, we discuss the functions of KDMs in metabolic and immune regulation and their roles in cancer and other diseases. We describe the landscape of KDM inhibitors, especially LSD1 inhibitors, which are the most advanced demethylase inhibitors in clinical trials. We highlight the need for more potent and selective KDM inhibitors, biomarkers of therapeutic response, novel combinatorial treatments and innovative drug discovery strategies. Histone lysine demethylases regulate gene expression and chromatin structure and help to integrate epigenetics with metabolic and immune responses. This Review discusses the diverse contributions of these demethylases to disease pathogenesis, particularly cancer, and the efforts underway to target them with small molecules.

https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.64898.title: Glycolysis and interferon transcription in melanoma immunotherapy
https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.64898.abstract: Glycolysis and interferon signalling have both been associated with responses to PD-1 blockade, but their joint transcriptional relationship with treatment outcome remains uncertain. We examined whether a state with high glycolysis and low interferon- response was associated with reduced disease control in melanoma. Fixed Hallmark gene sets were scored by single-sample gene set enrichment analysis in GSE91061, GSE78220 and an additional Liu cohort. Disease control analyses included 47, 26 and 100 patients. Conditional odds ratios for the joint state were 6.06 (exact 95% confidence interval, 1.04 to 65.61), 0.35 (0.026 to 3.11) and 1.03 (0.39 to 2.73), respectively. Holm-adjusted P values for the two initial comparisons were 0.073 and 0.365. The additional exploratory P value was 1.000. Continuous models and analyses that omitted each patient in turn did not provide consistent evidence of an adverse association. IFN scores were negatively correlated with DNA-derived tumour purity in 102 patients (Spearman {rho} = -0.671). Among 40 patients with paired biopsies, disease control was associated with higher on-treatment IFN scores after baseline adjustment, although the paired subset had lower baseline glycolysis than patients without paired profiles. In patient-level single-cell analyses, the baseline CD8 T cell correlation weakened when an alternative rank score used a common gene background. The defined joint state was not consistently associated with poorer disease control across cohorts. Bulk IFN scores were related to tumour purity, and cellular correlations were sensitive to scoring choices. These transcriptomic results do not measure pyruvate concentration, glycolytic flux or STAT1 pyruvylation.

https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.64898.title: Nutrient Availability as a Driver of Transcriptome Reprogramming in Osteosarcoma
https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.64898.abstract: Background: Gene expression in mammalian cells is intricately regulated by environmental and metabolic cues. Among these, nutrient availability represents a key feature of the tumor microenvironment and has recently emerged as a potent modulator of oncogenic signaling networks. In this study, we employed a cell-line model of osteosarcoma, a rare but highly aggressive bone malignancy affecting both humans and dogs. We demonstrate that altering the concentration of a single nutrient can profoundly reprogram gene expression in osteosarcoma cells, revealing a previously underexplored phenomenon: nutrient-dependent gene regulation. This finding highlights potential opportunities for therapeutic intervention and underscores the broader implications of metabolic regulation for personalized medicine and nutrition. Methods/Results: We performed bulk RNA sequencing of an established osteosarcoma cell line cultured under varying concentrations of two key nutrients, glucose and glutamine. Differential gene expression analysis revealed a pronounced nutrient-dependent transcriptional response. The identified genes were functionally associated with pathways involved in cancer, development, nervous system regulation, metabolism, cellular signaling, and immune responses. We identified seven distinct expression patterns, one of which exhibited a striking correlation with cell growth rate and resembled a FOS-like transcriptional signature. Notably, the proto-oncogene FOS was among the identified genes and displayed a strong growth-rate-dependent expression pattern. Conclusion/Impact: Our findings demonstrate that modulation of nutrient availability profoundly reshapes the gene expression landscape of osteosarcoma cells, revealing nutrient-responsive targets with potential therapeutic relevance. This work expands our understanding of metabolic regulation in cancer and suggests that nutrient-based interventions may provide a controllable means of influencing tumor progression. Beyond oncology, such approaches may also have broader implications for developmental biology, autoimmune disorders, and nervous system function. More broadly, this study highlights the potential of metabolic interventions as a strategy for targeted modulation of gene expression programs.

https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.64898.title: Psychoneuroimmunology of Viral Hepatitis and Hepatocellular Carcinoma: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.64898.abstract: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) and viral hepatitis (VH) are recognized primarily as hepatic diseases, yet they impose a substantial neuropsychiatric disorders (NPDs) encompassing depression, anxiety, cognitive impairment, and fatigue. Whether these manifestations reflect psychological reactions or biologically grounded psychoneuroimmune dysfunction remains poorly understood. Here, we present a pre-registered systematic review and meta-analysis (PROSPERO 2026 CRD420251081757) synthesizing evidence from 24 studies combining psychosocial outcomes with immune dysregulation markers across HCC and VH populations. Bibliometric and network analyses identified a growing psychoneuroimmunology research hub linking cytokine signaling, microglial activation, blood-brain barrier (BBB) disruption, and gut-liver-brain axis dysregulation to the neuropsychiatric phenotype of these diseases. Meta-analysis revealed a pooled hazard ratio (HR) of 1.92 (95% CI: 1.09-3.39) for adverse outcomes in HCC and a pooled HR of 2.28 (95% CI: 1.48-3.52) for depression associated to genetic variants in VH. TNF-a, but not IL-6, showed a tendency toward lower levels in VH patients with versus without NPDs, suggesting differential inflammatory roles. The literature, however, remains fragmented by heterogeneous designs and a paucity of longitudinal data. A psychoneuroimmunological approach, integrating immune, endocrine, neural, and psychosocial dimensions, is essential for capturing the full systemic impact of HCC and VH and should inform future mechanistic research and multidisciplinary clinical strategies.

https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.64898.title: Synthetic chromatin engineering for STAT1 reactivation toward restoring cisplatin sensitivity in breast cancer
https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.64898.abstract: Chemoresistant cancers acquire transcriptomic and epigenetic alterations through changes in transcription factor activity and chromatin accessibility. Integrative in silico analyses identified STAT1 as a recurrently suppressed transcription factor in cisplatin-resistant breast cancer. Using cisplatin-resistant triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) MDA-MB-231 cells, we further confirmed reduced STAT1 expression and activity, accompanied by defective nuclear translocation, indicating that suppression of STAT1 signaling contributes to cisplatin resistance in breast cancer. To restore STAT1 activity, we sought to promote its nuclear localization and transcriptional activation through chromatin engineering. Based on the identification of PHF6 as a direct STAT1-binding protein through in silico and in vitro analyses, we engineered Dual Reader 3 (DR3), a PHF6-derived synthetic chromatin regulator designed to enhance both STAT1 interaction and chromatin engagement through histone H2B ubiquitination. DR3 induced STAT1-associated transcriptional programs, including inflammatory and tumor-suppressive miRNAs. Mechanistically, DR3 physically promoted STAT1 nuclear translocation, activated STAT1 through a non-canonical S727-dependent mechanism independent of Tyr701 phosphorylation, and enhanced chromatin accessibility at STAT1-responsive regulatory regions through histone H2B ubiquitination. CUT&RUN analysis further revealed coordinated transcriptional and epigenetic remodeling associated with DR3-mediated STAT1 activation, including upregulation of HIPK2, which enhanced cellular sensitivity to cisplatin by strengthening the intrinsic DNA damage response. Finally, we investigated whether STAT1 reactivation could alleviate acquired cisplatin resistance. In vivo delivery of DR3 restored cisplatin sensitivity in resistant breast tumors. By coupling STAT1 nuclear translocation with chromatin remodeling, DR3 reactivated STAT1-dependent transcriptional programs and restored cisplatin sensitivity in breast cancer. Together, this study establishes transcription factor reactivation through synthetic chromatin engineering as a potential therapeutic strategy for overcoming chemoresistance in solid tumors.

https://www.nature.com/articles/s41392-0.title: Cancer drug resistance as a temporal process: cell plasticity, adaptive buffering, signaling pathways and therapeutic interception
https://www.nature.com/articles/s41392-0.abstract: Cancer drug resistance remains a principal barrier to durable cancer control, yet it is still often interpreted through endpoint-centred models that emphasise pre-existing resistant clones, incomplete drug exposure or late-acquired mechanisms. These explanations are essential but incomplete. The question is not only why resistant cells exist, but also how residual cells remain alive long enough to become resistant. Across tumour types and therapeutic modalities, treatment reshapes residual populations while it is acting, driving transitions through non-genetic heterogeneity, stochastic cell-fate variability, reversible tolerance, stress adaptation, microenvironmental support and eventually stable resistance. This Review develops a temporal framework in which resistance is resolved into a phase-structured trajectory organised around two mechanistic transitions: entry into adaptive buffering and later stabilisation into resistance hardening. Adaptive buffering is defined operationally as a transient, support-dependent survival state in which residual tumour cells preserve viability by recruiting physiological support systems while molecular and phenotypic reorganisation proceeds. It is not a single pathway or a synonym for drug tolerance, but a functional demand-capacity state whose dependencies change over time. We distinguish adaptive buffering from drug tolerance, persister states, dormancy, minimal residual disease and established resistance and discuss how buffering can be evaluated experimentally using perturbational, single-cell, spatial, computational and functional readouts. The framework suggests that informative biomarkers should assign residual populations to adaptive phases, so that therapy can intercept transient dependencies before adaptive states become hardened and clinically entrenched.

https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-0.title: Integrating metabolomics and proteomics uncovers core carbon metabolic dysregulation in Wilms’ tumor in children
https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-0.abstract: The unclear etiology, insufficient molecular classification strategies, and lack of validated therapeutic targets pose a critical barrier to precision treatment for Wilms’ tumor (WT) in children. Therefore, this study aimed to investigate metabolic dysregulations in WT by integrating metabolomics and proteomics. Metabolomic analysis of plasma samples from 36 WT patients and 36 healthy controls revealed 14 differentially abundant metabolites, including 5 upregulated and 9 downregulated. Proteomic analysis of 7 WT tissues and matched adjacent noncancerous tissues identified 3,378 significantly differentially expressed proteins, of which 1,783 were upregulated and 1,595 were downregulated. Integrated multi-omics analysis further identified three aberrant pathways associated with core carbon metabolism dysregulation: the citric acid cycle, ascorbate and aldarate metabolism, and propanoate metabolism. Collectively, these preliminary findings suggest that dysregulated carbon metabolism is associated with WT pathogenesis.
