https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-0.title: Machine learning model using contrast-enhanced CT for predicting overall survival in unresectable hepatocellular carcinoma treated with TACE plus targeted and immunotherapy: a multicenter study
https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-0.abstract: The aim of this study was to develop and validate a machine learning model based on contrast-enhanced CT (CECT) for predicting the overall survival (OS) in unresectable HCC patients treated with TACE combined with immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) plus molecular targeted therapies (MTTs). This study retrospectively reviewed 180 unresectable HCC patients who received TACE-ICIs-MTTs therapy from 4 medical centers. The study comprised of training cohort (n = 93), internal validation cohort (n = 39) and external validation cohort (n = 48). A series of analyses and kinds of models were conducted to build a Radscore. Then, models were constructed using Radscore and clinical variables selected through multivariate Cox regression analysis, evaluated by the Harrell’s concordance index (C-index) and the area under the curve (AUC). The radiomics-clinical model was further assessed by decision curve and calibration curve analysis. The Radscore was derived from 6 features selected by the optimal model (Lasso Cox + RSF with the highest C-index of 0.777). HBV infection and vascular invasion are clinical independent predictors of OS. The radiomics-clinical model demonstrated favorable performance. It achieved C-index values of 0.893(0.859–0.927), 0.758 (0.657–0.86) and 0.74 (0.624–0.856) in the training, internal validation, and external validation cohorts, respectively. In the external validation cohort, the AUCs achieved 0.731 (0.569–0.893), 0.7 (0.515–0.885), and 0.756 (0.569–0.943) for predicting 1-, 2-, and 3-year outcomes, respectively. The machine learning model based on CECT exhibited favorable performance in predicting overall survival in unresectable HCC patients treated with TACE-ICIs-MTTs, showing potential to identify likely responders and guide treatment decision-making.

https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-0.title: Heterogeneous chemotherapy-induced peripheral neuropathy trajectories and their associated factors in patients with gastrointestinal tumors: a cohort study
https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-0.abstract: Chemotherapy-induced peripheral neuropathy (CIPN) is a common and important nerve-related side effect of chemotherapy. However, researchers still know little about how CIPN changes over time in patients with gastrointestinal tumors. This prospective cohort study aimed to identify different CIPN patterns during chemotherapy and to examine factors related to these patterns. We recruited 233 patients with gastrointestinal tumors from a tertiary cancer center. All patients had a pathological diagnosis and received first-line chemotherapy with drugs known to cause peripheral nerve damage. At baseline, we collected demographic and clinical data. We also measured cancer-related fatigue with the Revised Piper Fatigue Scale, physical performance with the Short Physical Performance Battery, and self-management efficacy with the Strategies Used by People to Promote Health scale. We assessed CIPN symptoms with the Chemotherapy-Induced Peripheral Neuropathy Assessment Tool after the 1st, 3rd, 5th, and 7th chemotherapy cycles. We used latent class growth modeling to identify CIPN trajectory patterns. We used chi-square tests, analysis of variance, and logistic regression analyses to examine factors related to these patterns. We identified four CIPN trajectories: worsening CIPN symptoms (71 patients, 30.5%), mild stable CIPN symptoms (81 patients, 34.8%), improving CIPN symptoms (42 patients, 18.0%), and severe stable CIPN symptoms (39 patients, 16.7%). Age, smoking history, number of chronic diseases, chemotherapy regimen, standardized cumulative neurotoxic exposure index, cancer-related fatigue, physical performance, and self-management efficacy were related to CIPN trajectory membership. These findings highlight the heterogeneity of CIPN trajectories during chemotherapy and the factors associated with trajectory membership.

https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.64898.title: ERV-derived dsRNAs induce stress granules that drive neural crest fate to initiate melanoma
https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.64898.abstract: Melanoma arises when melanocytes are oncogenically reprogrammed into neural crest-like cells, but what initiates this switch is unknown. Here we show that endogenous retrovirus (ERV)-derived double stranded RNAs (dsRNAs) induce stress granules (SGs) that drive this fate change. In zebrafish, melanoma progresses through a stage-specific ERV switch: zferv marks precursor cells before crestin activates in tumor cells. Both elements generate dsRNA that triggers eif2ak2-dependent SGs within precursor lesions and through transformation. SGs are tumorigenic as G3BP1 overexpression accelerates melanoma onset, whereas mosaic, melanocyte-specific g3bp1/2 knockout delays it. Small molecule-mediated inhibition of G3BP1/2 eliminates precursor lesions and reduces tumor burden. Similarly, blocking dsRNA sensing prevents SG formation and lowers melanoma incidence. Human nevi and melanomas show analogous, stage-specific ERV programs and SG assembly. In human melanoma cells, SGs sequester and translationally repress SOX10-regulating mRNAs, including the tumor suppressor KMT2D. Mosaic knockout of kmt2d in vivo enhances SOX10-driven neural crest reactivation. Thus, an ERV-SG axis establishes an oncogenic translatome that enables melanoma fate, with diagnostic and therapeutic potential.

https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.64898.title: EGF and EREG regulate early oncoprotein-mediated tissue transformation in intestinal organoids.
https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.64898.abstract: Somatic mutations, coupled with abnormal extracellular signaling cues, promote tumor development. The abundance and affinity of EGF-family ligands for EGFR influence tissue development and play a central role in organoid culture by differentially regulating the balance between crypt proliferation and villus differentiation in mouse small intestinal organoids (mSIOs). To test how medium ligand composition affects early oncogenic transformation, we generated a Ptprg KO organoid line by CRISPR/Cas9 and two previously described organoid lines harboring synthetic bio-orthogonal expression systems for KRASG12V and {beta}-Ctn4A, activated by the membrane-diffusible ligands TMP or TMP-Cl. Measurements of crypt and villus region area showed that acute oncogenic activity did not alter organoid growth in media containing 50 ng/mL EGF; however, organoids grown without EGF consistently showed differential growth of the crypt region. Furthermore, EREG and sub-saturating EGF (0.5-5 ng/mL) treatments differentially affected crypt/villus development in each organoid line. Finally, we measured organoid morphology and found that crypt domain spatial distribution is independent of crypt area and requires EGF or EREG, highlighting the role of both proliferation and crypt organization in oncogenic tissue transformation.

https://www.nature.com/articles/s43018-0.title: Natural killer cell inflammatory circuits in antitumor immunity
https://www.nature.com/articles/s43018-0.abstract: Nature Cancer, Published online: 10 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s43018-026-01276-2 Huntington et al. provide an overview of the biology and role of natural killer (NK) cells in cancer, highlighting the importance of NK cell–dendritic cell cross-talk and NK cell metabolic fitness in regulating the antitumor immune response.

https://www.nature.com/articles/d41591-0.title: Next-generation KRAS G12C inhibitor improves survival in lung cancer
https://www.nature.com/articles/d41591-0.abstract: Phase 3 trial data show that the next-generation KRAS G12C inhibitor divarasib leads to longer progression-free survival than the first-generation inhibitors sotorasib and adagrasib in patients with non–small-cell lung cancer.

https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-0.title: A lactate-fatty acid loop drives prostate cancer bone colonization by mediating metabolic interplay between tumor cells and osteoblasts
https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-0.abstract: Bone metastasis is the major cause of morbidity and mortality in advanced prostate cancer, yet current therapies provide only limited clinical benefit. Here, we show that prostate cancer cells metabolically adapt to the bone microenvironment by utilizing bone-cell-derived lactate as an alternative nutrient source. Beyond fueling oxidative phosphorylation, lactate serves as carbon source for fatty acid synthesis. Among the resulting lipid products, oleic acid is secreted to reward osteoblast, establishing a reciprocal metabolic interplay that supports both tumor progression and pathological bone formation. Mechanistically, we identify MCT1 as the essential transporter mediating lactate uptake in bone-colonizing tumor cells. MCT1 expression is coordinately regulated by NFAT signaling and extracellular glucose availability at both transcriptional and post-translational levels. Genetic deletion and pharmacological inhibition of MCT1 markedly suppresses prostate tumor growth in bone. Together, these findings uncover a lactate-driven metabolic crosstalk, identifying MCT1 as a promising therapeutic target for prostate cancer bone metastasis. Bone metastases in advanced prostate cancer remain difficult to treat and are associated with poor outcomes. Here, the authors show that bone-colonizing prostate tumor cells exploit lactate uptake via MCT1 to fuel tumor growth and promote osteogenesis, identifying MCT1 inhibition as a potential therapeutic strategy.

https://www.nature.com/articles/s41591-0.title: A novel candidate biomarker for detecting premalignant and early ovarian cancer
https://www.nature.com/articles/s41591-0.abstract: New data suggest that the long noncoding RNA known as Tu-Stroma represents a promising new circulating biomarker for the detection of ovarian cancer at premalignant and early stages, for which sensitive screening methods currently are lacking.

https://www.nature.com/articles/s41419-0.title: TINAG suppresses renal cell carcinoma progression and angiogenesis by rebalancing mTORC1 signaling via integrin α3β1 receptor
https://www.nature.com/articles/s41419-0.abstract: The mammalian target of rapamycin (mTOR) signalling is crucial in promoting tumor growth and metastasis. Yet current mTOR inhibitors face limitations due to resistance and adverse effects. Inhibitors block the cytoplasmic signalling of mTOR, which may induce feedback loops that activate other cell proliferative signalling or reactivates mTOR itself, making it difficult to achieve complete inhibition of mTOR activities. In this study, we identified tubulointerstitial nephritis antigen (TINAG), a kidney-specific extracellular matrix protein, as an extracellular regulator of mTOR. Our data demonstrate that TINAG binds to integrin α3β1 transducing negative signals that suppress mTORC1 activity in tumor and endothelial cells, thereby reducing proliferation, migration, and angiogenesis. In both in vitro and in vivo models, TINAG protein exhibited pronounced inhibition on RCC growth and metastasis in wild-type RCC tumor and a sorafenib-resistant tumor model. Surprisingly, we also found the integrin α3β1 receptor with its canonical ligands did not promote cell growth, on the contrary, integrin α3β1 overexpression inhibited cell growth and migration. More interestingly, TINAG also exhibited an antiangiogenic potential, which functioned as a dual inhibitor on tumor cell and blood vessels simultaneously. Our finding reveals an extracellular mechanism regulating mTORC1 via TINAG-integrin interaction, suggesting TINAG as a novel tumor suppressor and promising dual targeting therapeutic candidate for RCC treatment.

https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-0.title: Fatty acid characteristics of high-fat diet-induced tumor tissue in the liver of mice
https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-0.abstract: Recent studies have highlighted the potential involvement of hepatic lipid characteristics in the development of liver cancer. Using a non‑invasive approach that integrates near‑infrared hyperspectral imaging (HSI) with machine learning, we previously established a method to visualize total lipid concentration, saturation level, and hydrocarbon chain length of fatty acids within a three‑dimensional feature space in mouse liver tissue. In the present study, to further elucidate the mechanisms underlying tumorigenesis, we expanded our dataset by adding eight additional tumor‑bearing mouse samples and separately analyzed cancerous and non‑cancerous regions within each hepatic lobe. Both gas chromatography and HSI consistently demonstrated that cancerous tissues exhibited elevated total lipid concentrations and were characterized by a notably higher abundance of oleic acid.

https://www.nature.com/articles/s42255-0.title: Microbiota-based modulation of intratumoral cholesterol metabolism for colorectal cancer treatment
https://www.nature.com/articles/s42255-0.abstract: Excess cholesterol accumulates in colorectal cancer (CRC) and promotes its progression, yet systemic cholesterol-lowering has limited benefits and safety concerns. Here we show that redirecting intestinal cholesterol metabolism through the gut microbiota generates a metabolite, 4-cholesten-3-one (4-C-3), which suppresses CRC growth. A screen of microbial cholesterol metabolites showed that 4-C-3 is depleted in faecal and tumour samples from patients with CRC. 4-C-3 suppresses tumour growth in CRC cell lines, patient-derived organoids and xenografts. Mechanistically, 4-C-3 suppresses two major oncogenic drivers of CRC by inhibiting epidermal growth-factor receptor activation and stabilizing mutant oncogenic KRAS in an inactive state, thereby overcoming KRAS-driven resistance to anti-epidermal growth-factor receptor therapy. As proof of concept, restoring 4-C-3 using either Oscillibacter ruminantium, a natural 4-C-3 producer reduced in CRC, or a non-pathogenic Escherichia coli engineered to convert intestinal cholesterol into 4-C-3, lowered intratumoral cholesterol and induced tumour regression in preclinical models without overt toxicity. These findings uncover a microbiota–cholesterol metabolic pathway that can be harnessed through microbiome engineering to selectively target CRC and overcome therapy resistance. Modulation of intratumoral cholesterol metabolism through delivery of a microbiota-derived metabolite is shown to induce colorectal cancer regression in mice.

https://www.nature.com/articles/s41591-0.title: Blood-based RNA biomarker for the early detection of ovarian cancer
https://www.nature.com/articles/s41591-0.abstract: Flower-Win/Lose signaling underlies a tumor–host fitness conflict in ovarian cancer, in which tumor-derived exosomal Tu-stroma reduces the fitness of surrounding host cells, favoring tumor expansion within host tissues. High-grade serous carcinoma (HGSC), the most prevalent histotype of epithelial ovarian cancer and leading cause of ovarian-cancer-related mortality, arises from serous tubal intraepithelial carcinoma (STIC), a noninvasive precursor typically identifiable only by histopathologic examination of excised fallopian tube tissue. Here we evaluated Tu-stroma, a tumor-associated long noncoding RNA enriched in serum extracellular vesicles (EVs), as a circulating biomarker in STIC and early-stage HGSC, representing the earliest histopathologically defined phases of disease. Tu-stroma was quantified in serum EVs from 506 individuals with histologically normal adnexa, benign-adnexal lesions, isolated STIC and HGSC across International Federation of Gynecology and Obstetrics (FIGO) stages I–IV. Normalized EV Tu-stroma ΔCT values were elevated in STIC (n = 43) and HGSC (n = 232) versus controls (n = 143) and benign-adnexal lesions (n = 88), including premenopausal women (controls = 57, benign = 34, STIC = 32, HGSC = 88). In paired receiver operating characteristic analyses, Tu-stroma showed higher discrimination than cancer antigen 125 (CA125) for STIC versus controls (area under the curve (AUC) = 0.99 versus 0.59, P < 0.001) and benign-adnexal masses (0.99 versus 0.31, P < 0.001), and for HGSC versus controls (AUC = 0.99 versus 0.96, P = 0.001) and benign-adnexal masses (0.98 versus 0.84, P < 0.001). Tu-stroma showed no systematic elevation across inflammatory or physiologic comparators (n = 116) or nonovarian malignancies (n = 160), each assessed against healthy controls (n = 100), supporting disease-context specificity. Modeled risk-enriched contexts yielded predictive values compatible with intended-use populations. These findings identify Tu-stroma as a candidate EV-RNA marker associated with pre-invasive and early HGSC biology. Prospective evaluation in consecutively enrolled real-world cohorts is required to validate diagnostic performance, predictive value and clinical utility. Tested in a cohort of 506 individuals, the RNA-based biomarker of microenvironment fitness Tu-stroma shows high performance in discriminating early-stage ovarian cancer from benign lesions, outperforming CA125.

https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-0.title: Prospective and genetic analyses implicate lower immunosurveillance in the aetiology of prostate cancer
https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-0.abstract: Tumour-promoting inflammation and immune evasion are key features of cancer, but prospective evidence linking specific immune pathways to prostate cancer risk remains limited. Here we show that circulating proteins involved in immune regulation may influence prostate cancer development. We analyse 368 immune- and inflammation-related proteins measured in blood samples from men in the European Prospective Investigation into Cancer and Nutrition (EPIC), including 1434 cases and matched controls, and combine these results with data from UK Biobank. While no proteins are associated with risk in EPIC alone after multiple testing correction, meta-analysis identifies several proteins linked to prostate cancer risk, including IL15 and FLT3LG, in particular, in blood taken long before diagnosis. Higher levels of immune surveillance-related proteins, particularly those involved in natural killer and T cell activity, are associated with lower prostate cancer risk, whereas genetic evidence implicates PARP1, SPINT2 and NME3 in increased risk. These findings suggest that immune pathways play a role in prostate cancer development and highlight potential targets for prevention. Role of specific immune and inflammation-related pathways and protein markers in the development of prostate cancer remains to be elucidated. Here the authors show evidence for potential protective role of dendritic cell mediated immunosurveillance, with protective associations with immune and inflammation related proteins measured more than seven years before diagnosis.

https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-0.title: Machine learning–based multiphase CT radiomics for differentiating hepatocellular carcinoma from hepatocellular adenoma in dogs
https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-0.abstract: Noninvasive differentiation between hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) and hepatocellular adenoma (HCA) is clinically important. Although computed tomography (CT) is widely used to evaluate hepatic masses, these entities often exhibit overlapping imaging features, limiting differentiation based on conventional CT findings alone. Given this limitation, we evaluated conventional CT features and developed radiomics-based machine learning (ML) models to differentiate HCC from HCA in dogs. Seventy-five dogs with histologically confirmed HCC or HCA that underwent triple-phase CT were retrospectively included. For conventional CT evaluation, regions of interest (ROIs) were manually segmented for each hepatic mass across all phases. In addition, 1,316 radiomic features were extracted from the segmented ROIs. SHAP (Shapley Additive Explanations)-based feature selection was applied, and the selected features were evaluated using multiple ML classifiers. Conventional CT analysis demonstrated limited qualitative differences between HCC and HCA. In contrast, radiomics-based ML analysis showed high cross-validated classification performance, particularly with random forest and boosted tree-based models. Washout-related intensity and texture features in the delayed phase were the most informative, and multiphase feature integration achieved the highest performance. In summary, radiomics-based ML analysis of triple-phase CT showed promising potential for differentiating HCC from HCA, suggesting that it may serve as a noninvasive adjunct for the preoperative diagnosis of canine hepatocellular tumors.

https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-0.title: At-home colorectal cancer screening participation, persistency, and connection to follow-up care: insights from a large multi-state system
https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-0.abstract: Colorectal cancer (CRC) is one of the most common sources of cancer incidence and mortality in the United States. Early detection is crucial for positive outcomes, but screening rates persistently fall short of public health goals. Low-barrier screening options like fecal immunochemical tests (FITs) have the potential to increase screening and reduce disparities across demographic groups, but they require annual testing and follow-up for abnormal results. The study used a retrospective, observational design to assess screening patterns for three types of FIT participation (i.e., initial, continued, and connection to follow-up care) in a multi-state health system. All age-eligible adult patients mailed a FIT from January 2019 to March 2025 were included (n = 158,128). The main measure for initial and continued participation was FIT return; the main measure for follow-up participation was having a colonoscopy within 12 months of receiving an abnormal FIT result. The majority (59%) of patients who received a FIT participated, and 73% of eligible patients participated in a second test. Among those with abnormal results, 59% had follow-up testing within a year. Initial, continued, and follow-up screening rates varied by race/ethnicity, language, payor, and geography. Findings highlight the potential benefits of low-barrier CRC screening like FIT for certain groups, as well as opportunities to engage all eligible patients across the CRC screening paradigm.

https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-0.title: Associations between nutritional indices and self-reported history of colorectal cancer in middle‑aged and older adults: a cross‑sectional study based on NHANES 1999–2020
https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-0.abstract: This study aimed to investigate the association between nutritional indices (i.e., the Geriatric Nutritional Risk Index [GNRI], Prognostic Nutritional Index [PNI], Advanced Lung Cancer Inflammation Index [ALI], and the Controlling Nutritional Status [CONUT]) and a self-reported history of colorectal cancer (CRC) using data from the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES) 1999–2020. Weighted multivariate logistic regression was employed to evaluate the associations of GNRI, PNI, ALI, and CONUT with a self-reported history of CRC. Restricted cubic spline (RCS) analysis was used to examine dose–response relationships. Subgroup analyses were performed to test for potential effect modifications. Propensity score matching (PSM) was applied to balance baseline characteristics in sensitivity analyses, ensuring the robustness of the results. Among 25,169 eligible participants, 327 (1.3%) had a self-reported history of CRC. Weighted logistic regression revealed that PNI (OR = 0.957, 95% CI: 0.925–0.990) was negatively associated with a self-reported history of CRC, whereas CONUT was positively associated (OR = 1.274, 95% CI: 1.156–1.404). Both GNRI and PNI demonstrated nonlinear negative relationships (P for nonlinear = 0.010 and 0.019, respectively). Exploratory subgroup analyses suggested potential effect modifications by diabetes for GNRI and by sex for CONUT. The inverse association was seemingly stronger in diabetic participants, and the positive association was seemingly stronger in females. Sensitivity analyses after PSM confirmed the stability of these findings. GNRI, PNI, and CONUT were associated with a self-reported history of CRC in middle-aged and older adults, suggesting a link between systemic immunonutritional status and a self-reported history of CRC.

https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-0.title: Integrated intracellular and secretome proteomics reveal compartment-specific responses to plasma-treated water solutions combined with doxorubicin in hypopharyngeal carcinoma
https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-0.abstract: Cold atmospheric Plasma-Treated Water Solutions (PTWS) carry reactive oxygen and nitrogen species and may enhance chemotherapy, but their effects on the tumour response remain unclear. We used SWATH-MS and DDA proteomics to characterise intracellular and secreted protein changes associated with Air (richer in nitrite) and oxygen (O₂) (richer in H2O2) PTWS combined with doxorubicin (DOXO) in FaDu Head and Neck Cancer cells and HaCaT keratinocytes. This discovery-based study aimed to identify treatment-associated proteomic signatures rather than causal mediators. Proteomic responses were formulation-, cell- and compartment-dependent. In FaDu cells, more than 80% of the secreted proteins modified by PTWS + DOXO were not modified by DOXO alone. Air PTWS + DOXO increased extracellular HSP70, HSP10 and RAB11B, whereas O₂ PTWS + DOXO predominantly reduced secreted protein abundance, with 25 of 33 modified proteins decreased, including cathepsin D, HSP27 and moesin. Both PTWS formulations reduced extracellular PRDX6, while HaCaT cells showed fewer and mainly adaptive changes. Secretome changes were only partly reflected by intracellular proteomics, providing complementary information on the treatment response. Overall, PTWS did not simply amplify the response to DOXO but modified it in a formulation- and cell-dependent manner. The identified secretome signatures provide hypotheses for future functional studies and should not be interpreted as direct evidence of tumour-microenvironment remodelling.

https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-0.title: Preoperative prediction of lymphovascular invasion in breast cancer using multicenter DCE-MRI radiomics and clinical features
https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-0.abstract: Lymphovascular invasion (LVI) is a key histopathological factor driving the metastatic process in invasive breast cancer; however, a definitive diagnosis is typically only possible postoperatively. Radiomics based on dynamic contrast-enhanced magnetic resonance imaging (DCE-MRI) has shown promise for the preoperative prediction of LVI. Nevertheless, existing studies are largely single-center, lack systematic comparisons of machine learning algorithms, and have insufficient external validation. This study developed and validated multicenter DCE-MRI radiomics models for preoperative LVI prediction, systematically compared ten machine learning algorithms, and quantified the incremental value of radiomics over clinical variables available before surgery. This retrospective multicenter study included 935 female patients with pathologically confirmed invasive ductal carcinoma from three institutions. All patients underwent preoperative 3.0 T DCE-MRI. After manual three-dimensional delineation of regions of interest on DCE-MRI images, 1,197 radiomic features were extracted with PyRadiomics after image resampling to 2 × 2 × 2 mm³ (B-spline interpolation), intensity normalization, and fixed-bin-width discretization. Feature selection (Mann-Whitney U test, Pearson correlation pruning with |r| > 0.9, and least absolute shrinkage and selection operator [LASSO] regression) was confined to the training cohort. Ten classifiers were compared: logistic regression (LR), support vector machines (SVM), k-nearest neighbors (KNN), random forests (RF), Extremely Randomized Trees (ExtraTrees), XGBoost, LightGBM, Gradient Boosting, AdaBoost, and multi-layer perceptron (MLP). A primary clinical model was built using only variables available before surgery (age, histological grade, Ki-67, MRI axillary lymph node status, and MRI tumor size); a sensitivity clinical model additionally included postoperative sentinel lymph node (SLN) status. Combined clinical-radiomics models and a nomogram were constructed, and all probability thresholds were fixed at the value maximizing the Youden index in the training set. Performance was assessed by the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) with the DeLong test, calibration intercept and slope, Brier score, and decision curve analysis (DCA) in a training set, an internal validation set, and two independent external test sets. In the multivariable analysis, SLN status (odds ratio [OR] 5.743, 95% confidence interval [CI]: 3.693–8.931, p < 0.001) and MRI tumor size (OR 1.413, 95% CI: 1.186–1.684, p < 0.001) were independently associated with LVI; because SLN status is established intraoperatively or postoperatively, the primary clinical model used only the five preoperative variables. Among the ten radiomics algorithms, LR and MLP showed the most stable cross-center performance (LR: AUC 0.841, 0.716, 0.632, and 0.586 in the training, internal validation, test 1, and test 2 cohorts, respectively), whereas complex ensemble methods overfit (Gradient Boosting: 0.991 in training vs. 0.696 and 0.532 externally; XGBoost: 0.894 vs. 0.613 and 0.453). The preoperative combined model achieved AUCs of 0.856, 0.721, 0.665, and 0.603, respectively, significantly outperforming the preoperative clinical model in the training, validation, and test 2 cohorts (DeLong p < 0.001, p = 0.013, and p < 0.001) but not in test 1 (p = 0.306), and significantly outperforming the radiomics model only in test 1 (p = 0.026). The incremental value of radiomics was significant in the training cohort (integrated discrimination improvement p < 0.001) but not in the external cohorts. Calibration slopes of the combined model declined externally (0.49, 0.28, and 0.21), indicating that probability estimates require local recalibration. In this multicenter study, LR and MLP were the most robust radiomics classifiers for preoperative LVI prediction, whereas complex ensemble algorithms were prone to overfitting on external validation. The preoperative combined model improved discrimination and clinical net benefit over the clinical model internally, but its external incremental value was inconsistent and its calibration deteriorated in the external cohorts. A sensitivity analysis using postoperative SLN status showed higher absolute performance, underscoring that genuinely preoperative tools trade performance for applicability. These findings emphasize rigorous multicenter benchmarking, recalibration before local deployment, and honest reporting of external performance in radiomics research.

https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-0.title: Adaptive saliency-guided signal representation for robust brain tumor MRI classification
https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-0.abstract: Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) analysis is often affected by acquisition noise, intensity inhomogeneity, and complex anatomical variations that complicate the extraction of discriminative signal patterns. Although deep learning methods have demonstrated strong performance in medical image analysis, many approaches treat images as visual patterns without explicitly modeling their underlying signal structure. This paper proposes an Adaptive Saliency-Guided Signal Representation (ASGSR) framework that explicitly models MRI data as structured spatial signals. The proposed framework formulates MRI classification as a task-conditioned signal-representation problem in which classification-derived spatial sensitivity determines the subsequent spatial transformation of the MRI signal. The resulting saliency-conditioned representation is subsequently characterized using multi-resolution and statistical operations before probabilistic classification. A Bayesian decision model is employed for classification with posterior-probability-based confidence estimation. Experimental evaluation on multiple publicly available brain MRI datasets demonstrates improved classification performance and robustness under the evaluated conditions compared with the selected convolutional and transformer-based baselines. The method achieves an average classification accuracy of 95.2% and an AUC of 0.97 across the evaluated datasets, while the derived spatial representation exhibits higher PSNR and SSIM under the defined representation-level evaluation protocol. These results indicate that the proposed signal-centric formulation can improve classification performance, robustness to the evaluated perturbations, and the spatial sensitivity representation of MRI inputs under the evaluated experimental conditions.

https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-0.title: Identification of the SNHG14/hsa-miR-577/CLIC4 ceRNA axis reveals the association of CLIC4 with stromal activation and microenvironment remodeling in colorectal cancer
https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-0.abstract: Colorectal cancer (CRC) is a prevalent malignancy with complex molecular regulatory mechanisms. In this study, we analyzed transcriptomic profiles from The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) and identified differentially expressed mRNAs, miRNAs, and lncRNAs. Using integrative bioinformatics approaches, we constructed a CRC-specific ceRNA regulatory network to screen candidate regulatory molecules involved in CRC progression. Based on this framework, SNHG14/hsa-miR-577/CLIC4 was identified as key competing endogenous RNAs (ceRNAs) of interest for further investigation. Subsequent functional analyses suggested that CLIC4 was closely associated with tumor microenvironment remodeling and stromal activation-related biological processes. Gene set enrichment analyses (GSEA) revealed that increased CLIC4 expression was positively correlated with pathways and signatures associated with epithelial–mesenchymal transition (EMT), transforming growth factor-β (TGF-β) signaling, angiogenesis, and matrisome remodeling, thereby supporting its potential role in modulating the stromal characteristics of CRC. Moreover, ceRNA-based screening yielded potential upstream regulatory insights for CLIC4, establishing a foundational understanding of its post-transcriptional regulation in CRC. In summary, our findings underscore CLIC4 as a potential biomarker linked to stromal activation and microenvironmental remodeling in CRC, offering candidate regulatory insights for forthcoming mechanistic and translational investigations.

https://www.nature.com/articles/s41419-0.title: RSK2 and β-Trcp-mediated ubiquitination of FOXN3 impairs DNA damage and confers radioresistance in lung cancer
https://www.nature.com/articles/s41419-0.abstract: Aberrant DNA damage responses can result in genomic instability, thereby affecting the efficacy of radiotherapy. The transcription factor FOXN3 plays critical roles in cellular growth and proliferation, inflammation, and the response to injury; however, its involvement in lung cancer radioresistance remains unclear. Here, we revealed that reduced expression of FOXN3 was correlated with poor prognosis in lung adenocarcinoma patients and that FOXN3 depletion impaired the DNA damage response, thereby conferring radioresistance in lung cancer. Mechanistically, FOXN3 promoted BRCA1 transcription by binding to the BRCA1 promoter region, thereby increasing DNA damage. Furthermore, the protein kinase RSK2 and E3 ubiquitin ligase β-Trcp collaboratively interacted with FOXN3, facilitating its ubiquitination-mediated degradation via a conserved DSGYAS motif. Importantly, this cooperative degradation of FOXN3 attenuated DNA damage and promoted radioresistance in lung cancer cells. Our study provides a mechanistic foundation for targeting FOXN3-related pathways as a potential strategy to overcome radioresistance in lung cancer.

https://www.nature.com/articles/s41392-0.title: Spatial transcriptomics tumor microenvironment determinants of tyrosine kinase inhibitor response in renal cell carcinoma: results from a phase 2 clinical trial
https://www.nature.com/articles/s41392-0.abstract: Metastatic clear cell renal cell carcinoma (ccRCC) exhibits heterogeneous clinical outcomes, and limited biomarkers are available to predict response to targeted therapies. This study evaluated cell compartment-specific transcriptional biomarkers predicting clinical response to the tyrosine kinase inhibitor (TKI) sunitinib. In this phase 2 clinical trial (NCT00715442), 46 patients with metastatic ccRCC received sunitinib pre- and post-cytoreductive nephrectomy, with a primary endpoint of time-to-progression (TTP) and secondary endpoints of overall survival (OS) and sunitinib toxicity. To investigate spatial dynamics of therapeutic response to sunitinib, we applied whole-transcriptome digital spatial profiling (DSP) to tumor tissue from responders and non-responders. For 46 trial patients, median TTP was 8.2 months (95% CI: 6.1–19.3) and OS 36.3 months (95% CI: 19.7–70.5). Responders displayed a tumor microenvironment enriched in pro-inflammatory/immunostimulatory programs, while non-responders displayed enrichment of immunosuppressive programs with elevated PD-L1 expression in myeloid cells and exhausted CD8 + T-cell signatures. Sunitinib resistance mechanisms involving VEGF-dependent and independent angiogenic pathways were identified, revealing potential therapeutic targets. DSP-based machine learning models showed strong prognostic and predictive performance in sunitinib-treated patients in an external JAVELIN Renal 101 cohort, but attenuated performance in the avelumab plus axitinib cohort, indicating treatment-context specificity. Our findings highlight immune regulation as a key determinant of sunitinib response in metastatic ccRCC. Spatial profiling revealed potentially targetable mechanisms of TKI resistance involving SPP1-associated myeloid programs, CD8 + T-cell exhaustion, and angiogenic signaling, highlighting interactions between angiogenesis, lipid metabolism, and tumor immunity as determinants of therapeutic outcome.

https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-0.title: Prediction of the self-association of the nuclear inhibitor of DNA-binding and differentiation proteins
https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-0.abstract: The inhibitor of DNA binding and differentiation (ID) proteins (ID1–ID4) are members of the helix-loop-helix (HLH) family of transcriptional regulators that play a critical role in regulating cell cycle progression and cell differentiation. Their overexpression in various cancer types makes them promising therapeutic targets. It has been reported that ID4 acts as a tumor suppressor, as ID4 heterodimerizes with ID-1, -2, and -3 and promotes bHLH DNA binding, essentially acting as an inhibitor of inhibitors of differentiation proteins. In this work, we utilize advanced computational biophysics and bioinformatics tools to map the structural foundations of ID protein self-association. High-resolution models were generated and subjected to 100 ns Molecular Dynamics (MD) simulations to capture their conformational dynamics in physiological environments. Through protein–protein docking (HADDOCK) and interface analysis, aiming to characterize the binding hotspots of both homodimers and heterodimers, facilitating the development of inhibitors that can disrupt its pathological interactions. Results revealed that ID1 can self-dimerize and form a stable dimer with ID4. The dimerization is exerted by the HLH domain, and the dimers are stable compared to the monomeric isoforms. The ID1-ID4 dimer formation has an important role in lowering their concentration in the nucleus and hence affecting their function. Hence, the identified interaction pattern may have important implications for regulating their activity.

https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-0.title: Long term survival after mesometrial resection for cervical cancer from the Mesometrial Resection (MMR) Study
https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-0.abstract: The Leipzig School Mesometrial Resection Study (MMR Study) investigates whether surgical treatment based on stage-associated ontogenetic cancer fields and their corresponding lymphatic compartments can achieve durable locoregional tumor control without adjuvant radiotherapy. This ongoing, prospective, single-center observational cohort study enrolls patients with primary cervical cancer. Depending on ontogenetic tumor stage, patients undergo total mesometrial resection (TMMR) or extended mesometrial resection (EMMR) with therapeutic lymph node dissection. As all locoregional at-risk tissues are surgically removed, adjuvant radiotherapy is omitted. This long-term follow-up analysis included patients FIGO 2009 stages IB1–IIB. Between 1999 and 2020, 543 patients were included, with a median follow-up of 104 months. Disease stages were IB1 (60%), IB2 (11%), IIA1 (4.4%), IIA2 (1.7%), and IIB (23%). Nodal status was pN0 in 72.4% and pN1 in 27.6%. Ten-year recurrence-free survival (RFS) and overall survival (OS) were 84.0% and 84.1%, respectively. Stratified by nodal status, 10-year RFS was 92.6% for pN0 and 60.8% for pN1, while OS was 90.9% and 65.6%, respectively. Multivariable Cox regression showed favorable prognostic stratification for ontogenetic tumor staging compared with conventional pT staging (AIC 928.78 vs. 939.23). TMMR or EMMR with therapeutic lymph node dissection was associated with favorable long-term oncologic outcomes in this cohort. Ontogenetic tumor staging may improve prognostic assessment in cervical cancer.

https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-0.title: Aptamer-engineered extracellular vesicles enable targeted celecoxib delivery for in vitro breast and colon cancer therapy
https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-0.abstract: Cancer remains a leading cause of death worldwide, largely due to limitations in current therapies that often suffer from poor selectivity, systemic toxicity, and drug resistance. Innovative drug delivery platforms that can selectively target tumor cells while sparing healthy tissue are urgently needed to improve treatment outcomes. In this study, we address these challenges by developing a novel targeted delivery system using extracellular vesicles (EVs) loaded with celecoxib (Cel), a potent anti-inflammatory drug with anticancer properties, and functionalized with DNA aptamer AS1411 (Apt) to enhance tumor targeting. Celecoxib was efficiently encapsulated into EVs derived wharton’s jelly (WJ) mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs) via sonication. Subsequently, the EV surfaces were chemically conjugated with amine-modified Apt using EDC/NHS chemistry, creating a targeted nanosystem (Cel-apt-EVs) designed for enhanced recognition and uptake by cancer cells. Comprehensive in vitro analyses demonstrated that Cel-apt-EVs significantly improved cellular binding affinity and cytotoxicity in MCF-7 and HCT116 cancer cell lines compared to free celecoxib and non-functionalized EV formulations, while exhibiting minimal toxicity towards normal WI38 fibroblasts. Cell cycle analysis revealed that Cel-apt-EVs induced significant G0/G1 phase arrest in cancer cells, indicating inhibition of cell cycle progression. Furthermore, Annexin V/propidium iodide (PI)-based flow cytometry confirmed enhanced apoptotic cell death, with a marked increase in early and late apoptotic populations following Cel-apt-EVs treatment. Cel-apt-EVs effectively inhibited cancer cell migration in wound healing assays and markedly suppressed angiogenesis in the chick chorioallantoic membrane (CAM) model. These results highlight that aptamer-functionalized EVs provide a promising and biocompatible platform for precision delivery of celecoxib, improving anticancer efficacy while reducing off-target effects. This strategy offers new avenues for the development of safer and more effective targeted therapies in oncology.

https://www.nature.com/articles/s41568-0.title: 3D models to capture and perturb tumour heterogeneity in vitro
https://www.nature.com/articles/s41568-0.abstract: Tumour heterogeneity is a defining feature of cancer and a major obstacle to effective therapy as it drives metastasis, resistance and relapse. Experimental tumour models have largely exploited simplified, homogeneous systems that fail to capture the full biological and spatial diversity of real tumours. Recent advances in 3D models have considerably expanded our capacity to model different dimensions of tumour heterogeneity. These platforms also enable controlled perturbations of cancer-cell-intrinsic and microenvironmental features, including genetic programmes, therapy responses and transport, extracellular matrix composition and mechanics, oxygenation, perfusion, stromal and immune interactions, and tissue architecture. Such perturbations could reveal how different aspects of tumour heterogeneity shape disease progression and therapy response dynamics. However, how close we are to generating 3D models that not only recapitulate the dynamic, multiscale nature of human cancers but also enable systematic perturbations for mechanistic insights remains a key question. In this Review, we summarize the current landscape of 3D models and how effectively they capture tumour heterogeneity, what perturbations they enable, and how these capabilities can be matched to specific biological or therapeutic questions. We also discuss outstanding challenges in model fidelity, standardization, scalability, longitudinal analysis and clinical predictability. Tumour heterogeneity drives disease progression yet remains difficult to capture in experimental systems. In this Review, Fomina and McGuigan discuss how emerging 3D tumour models, including organoids, assembloids and microfluidic platforms, recapitulate distinct dimensions of tumour heterogeneity to enable mechanistic studies of cancer biology and drug response. They also outline future directions for improving model fidelity, scalability and translational utility.

https://www.nature.com/articles/s41420-0.title: Na+/Ca2+ exchanger 1 (NCX1) drives migration and vasculogenic mimicry in mesenchymal glioblastoma
https://www.nature.com/articles/s41420-0.abstract: Glioblastoma (GBM) is a highly aggressive brain tumor characterized by diffuse invasion, marked cellular plasticity, and poor prognosis, particularly in the mesenchymal subtype. The Na+/Ca2+ exchanger 1 (NCX1) has been implicated in glioblastoma motility, but its role in patient-derived mesenchymal GBM and vasculogenic mimicry (VM) remains unclear. Here, we investigated NCX1 function in GBM19, a primary mesenchymal glioblastoma stem cell-enriched culture. GBM19 cells displayed coordinated migration and formed Vascular Endothelial (VE)-cadherin-positive loop-like structures consistent with VM, whereas leading-edge cells showed a more migratory phenotype. NCX1 was enriched at the migratory front and was functionally active in both leading-edge and loop cells, as demonstrated by patch-clamp recordings and pharmacological inhibition with bepridil. NCX1 blockade impaired wound closure, disrupted actin organization, altered cell polarity and directional migration, reduced spheroid invasion, and prevented proper loop formation and closure. In vivo, VM-like tumor structures were positive for NCX1 and VE-cadherin. Transcriptomic analysis further showed a positive correlation between NCX1 and the VM-related regulator E74-like factor 2 (ELF2) specifically in mesenchymal GBM, where high ELF2 expression was associated with worse survival. These findings identify NCX1 as a regulator of migration and vasculogenic mimicry in mesenchymal glioblastoma and support its potential as a therapeutic target in aggressive GBM.

https://www.nature.com/articles/s41571-0.title: T cell redirection in high-risk smouldering multiple myeloma: can deep responses prevent progression to multiple myeloma?
https://www.nature.com/articles/s41571-0.abstract: The randomized phase II ImmunoPRISM trial has shown encouraging efficacy of the B cell maturation antigen-targeted bispecific T cell engager teclistamab in high-risk smouldering multiple myeloma, although several aspects constrain interpretation of the results. Herein, I discuss aspects that should be addressed in future research, such as patient selection, treatment duration, clinically relevant end points and adequate treatment in the control arm, to establish whether deep responses translate into durable prevention of progression with an acceptable benefit–risk profile.

https://www.nature.com/articles/s41577-0.title: Activated TILs are restricted by iron availability in pancreatic cancer
https://www.nature.com/articles/s41577-0.abstract: A preprint by Schoenfeld et al. investigates the relationship between iron restriction and the function of tumour-infiltrating lymphocytes in pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma.

https://www.nature.com/articles/s41388-0.title: B3GNT9-mediated O-glycosylation reprograms fatty acid metabolism in peroxisomes to promote invasion progression of peritumoral glioma cells
https://www.nature.com/articles/s41388-0.abstract: Glioblastoma (GBM) is a highly aggressive brain tumor characterized by rapid recurrence and invasion, particularly in the peritumoral brain zone (PBZ), a critical site for tumor spread. Through RNA-seq of tumor core and PBZ tissues from GBM patients, we identified B3GNT9 as significantly upregulated in tumor cells within the PBZ. Bioinformatics analysis revealed that elevated B3GNT9 expression is associated with poor prognosis. Functional studies in glioblastoma cell lines, patient-derived cells, and animal models showed that B3GNT9 overexpression promotes cell proliferation, migration, and invasion. Mechanistically, RNA-seq and in vitro experiments demonstrated that B3GNT9 enhances glioma invasiveness by regulating the fatty acid metabolism gene ACOX1. Quantitative proteomics further identified PPARD as a key transcription factor mediating the B3GNT9-ACOX1 signaling axis. B3GNT9 increases mucin-type O-glycosylation in glioblastoma cells, facilitating O-GalNAc glycosylation of PPARD, which enhances its transcriptional activity and drives ACOX1 expression. High-throughput metabolomics and cellular, organoid, and animal studies revealed that activation of the B3GNT9–PPARD–ACOX1 axis reduces intracellular eicosapentaenoic acid (EPA) levels, promoting GBM invasiveness. These findings highlight the critical role of B3GNT9 and O-glycosylation in GBM progression, suggesting that targeting the B3GNT9–PPARD–ACOX1 axis could offer a promising therapeutic strategy to suppress GBM invasion and recurrence.

https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-0.title: Metabolomic rewiring of energy, structural and signaling networks underlies triple negative breast cancer aggressiveness
https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-0.abstract: Triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) is highly prevalent in West Africa and associated with poor prognosis and limited therapeutic options. Targeted quantitative metabolomic and lipidomic profiling was performed on pretreatment tumor biopsies from Senegalese women with TNBC (n = 40) and hormone-dependent breast cancer (HDBC; n = 40). After exclusion of two PCA outliers, 39 samples per group were analyzed. Using the Biocrates MxP Quant 500 XL platform, 1019 analytes were assayed, and 655 metabolites were retained for statistical analysis. Sixty-nine metabolites differed significantly (p < 0.01, fold change ≥ 1.2), including eight after FDR correction (q < 0.05). OPLS-DA showed robust group separation (Q2cum = 0.56; CV-ANOVA p < 2.62 × 10−12). Machine learning classifiers achieved consistent discrimination (AUC ≥ 0.70), with Ridge regression performing best (AUC = 0.79). TNBC showed metabolic patterns consistent with increased glycolysis, fatty acid oxidation, glutaminolysis, and branched-chain amino acid catabolism, together with alterations potentially related to angiogenesis and extracellular matrix remodeling. Lipidomic differences included phosphatidylethanolamines, sphingolipids, and phosphatidylinositol species. Overall, tumor metabolomic and lipidomic profiling discriminated TNBC from HDBC and identified metabolic features associated with aggressive tumor biology in West African patients.

https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-0.title: Pan-cancer expression and clinical associations of HSD11B2 and its functional role in breast cancer cells
https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-0.abstract: Although HSD11B2 serves as a crucial enzyme governing glucocorticoid metabolism, its systemic roles across human malignancies have not been fully elucidated. Current evidence remains fragmented, and integrative pan-cancer investigations covering its expression control, clinical relevance, immune correlates and influence on breast cancer aggressiveness are still lacking. To fill this gap, we integrated multi-omics bioinformatic analyses with experimental validation at both the cellular and animal levels, thereby systematically assessing the diagnostic and prognostic significance, underlying molecular mechanisms and tumor-promoting activities of HSD11B2 in breast cancer. Our ultimate goal was to establish HSD11B2 as an indicator usable for pan-cancer diagnosis and prognosis, and to explore its potential as a candidate therapeutic target in breast oncology. Publicly available transcriptomic and clinical datasets, chiefly from TCGA and GTEx, were collected and merged. Using the R computing environment together with multiple multi-omics bioinformatics platforms, we characterized the HSD11B2 expression landscape, its prognostic and diagnostic significance, genetic alterations, epigenetic control, immune infiltration patterns and associated functional pathways across pan-cancer cohorts. How HSD11B2 regulates the proliferative, migratory and invasive behaviors of breast cancer cells was then examined experimentally, using qRT-PCR, Western blotting and immunohistochemistry together with CCK-8, colony formation, Transwell and wound healing assays and a nude mouse subcutaneous xenograft model. HSD11B2 showed broad expression disturbance across the pan-cancer spectrum, being markedly elevated in tumors such as BRCA, CHOL and LIHC but evidently reduced in COAD, KIRC, THCA and additional malignancies. Its transcript level showed significant prognostic associations in eight cancer types and acted as an independent outcome predictor in five of them, and the nomogram built on these variables achieved satisfactory predictive accuracy. Moreover, HSD11B2 transcripts distinguished malignant from normal tissues with excellent accuracy (AUC > 0.9) for CHOL, COAD, KIRC, KIRP and READ. At the regulatory level, HSD11B2 abundance was associated with copy number gain, promoter hypomethylation and m6A regulatory signatures. Tumors with abundant HSD11B2 displayed an immune-desert “cold tumor” phenotype, tightly linked to an immunosuppressive microenvironment. Enrichment analyses connected HSD11B2 predominantly to steroid hormone metabolism, cell-proliferation and immune-regulation pathways. Cellular and animal experiments consistently demonstrated that silencing HSD11B2 markedly weakened the proliferative, migratory and invasive capacities of breast cancer cells in vitro, and xenograft tumors in nude mice grew more slowly upon HSD11B2 knockdown. HSD11B2 holds important clinical significance for prognosis assessment and diagnosis across pan-cancer settings. Through multi-dimensional regulatory control it participates in tumor progression and displays oncogenic activity in breast cancer. Collectively, HSD11B2 represents a promising indicator for pan-cancer diagnosis and prognosis, as well as a potential therapeutic target against this malignancy.

https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-0.title: Integrated computational biology approaches provide insights into the potential mechanisms underlying arrhythmias induced by anthraquinone-related antitumor drugs
https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-0.abstract: Despite the significant cardiac toxicity and arrhythmia-inducing potential of anthraquinone-related antitumor drugs (including anthracyclines and anthracenediones) in clinical practice, the underlying common systemic molecular mechanisms remain unknown. Therefore, this study aims to systematically elucidate the multi-target and multi-pathway arrhythmogenic mechanisms of seven representative drugs, with the expectation of providing theoretical support for safe clinical use and the development of related toxicity intervention strategies. This study first employed network toxicology techniques to screen out potential arrhythmogenic targets of seven representative drugs from databases such as PubChem, Novo Pro, and SwissTargetPrediction. Subsequently, based on the STRING database and with the aid of Cytoscape 3.10.1, protein-protein interaction networks and a multi-dimensional “arrhythmia-drug-target” network were constructed. Further, GO and KEGG enrichment analyses were conducted to explain the toxicity-related biological processes and key signaling pathways, and their roles in immune infiltration were explored. Finally, molecular docking was used to assess the potential binding interactions between drugs and core targets. Two drug–SRC complexes were selected for further molecular dynamics simulations to evaluate the stability. Combined with ADMET assessment, these computational analyses provide a comprehensive and hypothesis-generating assessment of the potential toxicological profiles and underlying mechanisms of anthraquinone-related antitumor drugs. Through network pharmacology, 195 potential toxicity targets (such as AKT1, SRC, TNF, TP53) were identified, and they were significantly enriched in key signaling pathways such as PI3K-Akt and MicroRNAs in cancer. Immune infiltration analysis further suggested that this process might be related to the regulation of immune cells such as Mast cells activated, T cells CD8 and B cells memory. Molecular docking suggested potential interactions between the drugs and the core target, while dynamic simulations further evaluated the stability of the SRC complex of the two selected drugs. Finally, ADMET predictions indicated that Mitoxantrone and Losoxantrone might block the cardiac hERG potassium channel, prolong the QT interval, and thereby may contribute to arrhythmia. This study provides insights into the potential mechanisms by which anthraquinone-related antitumor drugs induce arrhythmias.

https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-0.title: Computational analysis links methylparaben responses in colonic cell models to MAOB and Hippo/Wnt signaling
https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-0.abstract: Methylparaben (MP) is a widely used preservative in personal care products, foods, and pharmaceuticals, resulting in widespread human exposure through dermal contact, dietary intake, and pharmaceutical use. Although the gastrointestinal tract represents a major site of MP absorption following oral exposure, its effects on colonic epithelial homeostasis and the underlying molecular mechanisms remain poorly understood. We employed an integrative approach combining network toxicology, bulk transcriptomic analysis (N = 685 from four GEO datasets), weighted gene co-expression network analysis (WGCNA), systematic evaluation of 101 machine-learning strategies, molecular docking, 100 ns molecular dynamics (MD) simulations, and single-cell transcriptomic analysis (GSE132465, 33 samples) to investigate MP-associated molecular alterations in colorectal cancer (CRC). The biological effects of MP were further evaluated in normal human colonic epithelial NCM460 cells and colorectal cancer RKO cells using colony formation, wound-healing, and Transwell assays. MP exposure reduced colony formation, wound closure, and invasion in NCM460 cells, whereas the opposite responses were observed in RKO colorectal cancer cells under the tested in vitro conditions. Integration of computationally predicted MP targets with CRC-associated transcriptomic alterations identified 52 overlapping candidate genes. Among 101 machine-learning strategies, the LASSO–Random Forest (LASSO–RF) model showed the best predictive performance for CRC classification and identified six feature genes, including monoamine oxidase B (MAOB), which emerged as a candidate molecular feature. Molecular docking and 100 ns molecular dynamics simulations suggested a potentially stable binding conformation of MP within the MAOB catalytic pocket. Single-cell analysis revealed relatively higher MAOB expression in normal colonic epithelial cells than in inferred aneuploid malignant cells. In silico MAOB perturbation further suggested associations between MAOB-related transcriptional changes and Hippo/Wnt-associated signaling pathways. MP exposure was associated with distinct phenotypic responses in non-transformed colonic epithelial cells and colorectal cancer cells under the tested in vitro conditions. Integrative computational analyses identified MAOB and Hippo/Wnt-associated signaling as candidate molecular features for further investigation. However, the proposed molecular relationships remain hypothetical, and their causal roles in MP-associated cellular responses require direct experimental validation.

https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.64898.title: EWSR1::ATF1 hyperactivation via TRIM11 depletion triggers lethal metabolic rewiring in clear cell sarcoma
https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.64898.abstract: Clear cell sarcoma (CCS) is an ultra-rare and aggressive soft tissue sarcoma driven by the EWSR1::ATF1 fusion oncoprotein. Currently, no effective and well-tolerated treatment options are available to CCS patients. Direct inhibition of fusion transcription factors is precluded by the absence of defined ligand-binding pockets, whereas their abundance is under the control of the ubiquitin-proteasome system (UPS), offering an alternative avenue for biology-guided treatment. Here we show the abundance of EWSR1::ATF1 is tightly regulated by the UPS, and that release of this constraint is lethal to CCS cells. A reporter-based CRISPR/Cas9 knockout screen of UPS components identified TRIM11 as an E3 ligase that regulates turnover of EWSR1::ATF1, which it recognises as a neosubstrate without altering wild-type EWSR1 or ATF1. Depletion of TRIM11 increased nuclear fusion protein abundance, amplified the fusion-driven transcriptional programs and reduced viability. Proteomic analysis identified the cataplerotic enzyme phosphoenolpyruvate carboxykinase 1 (PCK1), a direct EWSR1::ATF1 target, as the key mediator of lethal effects of fusion hyperactivation. Extracellular flux analysis, isotope tracing and quantitative metabolomics revealed excessive cataplerotic carbon withdrawal and impaired oxidative phosphorylation as the underlying mechanism. In patient tumors, high PCK1 expression associated with metastatic transcriptome programs and disease presentation, as well as shorter survival. Taken together, we report that hyperactivation of EWSR1::ATF1 opens a metabolic vulnerability, establishing TRIM11 as an actionable dependency and PCK1 as a candidate prognostic biomarker in CCS.

https://www.nature.com/articles/s41392-0.title: Glycolipid-lectin driven endocytosis as a therapeutic vulnerability in breast cancer
https://www.nature.com/articles/s41392-0.abstract: Aberrant endocytosis has long been associated with epithelial plasticity and tumorigenesis, but direct in vivo evidence of its causal role in tumor progression and metastasis has been lacking. Here, we identify and molecularly characterize a previously unrecognized form of E-cadherin (ECAD) internalization in mammary epithelial cells. This process is n mediated by the endocytic adapter Epsin 3 (EPN3) through glycolipid-lectin (GL-Lect)-driven endocytosis requiring galectin-3 and Eps15-family adapters. We further define the molecular basis of this pathway, identifying EPN3-specific interaction surfaces that promote ECAD clustering and galectin-3 recruitment, thereby driving clathrin-independent ECAD internalization. Leveraging an EPN3 knock-in mouse model, we show that dysregulation of GL-Lect-driven endocytosis disrupts mammary gland morphogenesis, induces epithelial-to-mesenchymal plasticity (EMP), and activates transcriptional programs associated with tissue remodeling and alveologenesis. These alterations synergize with the ERBB2/Neu breast oncogene to accelerate tumor onset and promote lung metastasis. Importantly, enhanced ECAD endocytosis was directly demonstrated in the intact mammary epithelium and shown to underlie the morphogenetic and invasive phenotypes. Pharmacologic inhibition of the GL-Lect mechanism suppressed ECAD internalization and reversed morphogenetic, polarity, and invasive phenotypes ex vivo, providing proof-of-concept for therapeutic targeting. These findings establish GL-Lect-driven endocytosis as a physiological regulator of mammary epithelial plasticity. When dysregulated, it drives metastatic progression and uncovers a tractable therapeutic vulnerability in breast cancer.

https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.64898.title: Ultra-low-dose same-target combinations control drug resistance across stages
https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.64898.abstract: The emergence of drug resistance continues to limit the long term effectiveness of cancer therapies [1], as tumour cells adapt to therapeutic selective pressure through diverse genetic and non-genetic routes [2,3]. Despite advances in more potent and next generation inhibitors and mechanism based combination therapies [4,5], durable disease control remains difficult to achieve. Here we tested an alternative strategy: combining multiple inhibitors directed against the same oncogenic driver, each at ultra low doses with minimal individual activity, to delay resistance emergence. In epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) driven cancer models, such ultra low dose same target combinations (ULDCs) distributed individually weak perturbations across multiple inhibitors directed against the same target and achieved substantial growth inhibition in vitro and antitumour activity in vivo despite weak effects of the corresponding single agents. Under similar levels of growth inhibition (~50%), single-agent EGFR inhibitors generated resistant outgrowth, whereas a five drug ULDC delayed resistance emergence. Increasing the number of inhibitors further delayed resistance emergence, with no detectable resistant outgrowth observed for combinations containing 8 to 14 inhibitors within the experimental timeframe. The five drug ULDC also retained measurable growth inhibitory activity against gefitinib resistant PC-9/GR cells, and resistant cells arising under five drug ULDC treatment exhibited markedly greater reversibility following drug withdrawal than those arising under single agent treatment. Although pharmacological additivity or synergy may contribute to the collective growth inhibitory effects of ULDCs, the divergent long term resistance outcomes observed under similar levels of growth inhibition indicate that resistance behaviour is not determined by inhibitory strength alone. Instead, our findings support a model in which increasing same target inhibitor diversity progressively constrains the adaptive trajectories available during resistance evolution, while therapeutic perturbation architecture may also influence the stability of resistant states that emerge. More broadly, these findings support the concept of same target collective suppression, in which multiple individually weak perturbations directed against the same target can collectively produce substantial antitumour activity and constrain resistance evolution across multiple stages. We propose that increasing same target inhibitor diversity may restrict accessible adaptive trajectories, while therapeutic perturbation architecture may also influence the stability of resistant states.

https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.64898.title: Developing a Multimodal miR-15a Mimic to Overcome Gemcitabine and RAS(ON) Inhibitor Daraxonrasib Resistance in Pancreatic Ductal Adenocarcinoma
https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.64898.abstract: Gemcitabine remains a mainstay of pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) treatment, while the RAS(ON) inhibitor daraxonrasib has recently demonstrated improved survival in previously treated metastatic disease. However, acquired resistance to both therapies remains a major clinical challenge. Here, we developed MTX-5-FU-Gem-miR-15a, a multimodal microRNA (miRNA)-based therapeutic, by chemically modifying tumor-suppressive miR-15a with methotrexate (MTX), 5-fluorouracil (5-FU), and gemcitabine (Gem) to combine sequence-specific gene regulation with disruption of nucleotide metabolism. MTX-5-FU-Gem-miR-15a exhibited low-nanomolar potency across five PDAC cell lines and retained activity in gemcitabine- and daraxonrasib-resistant models under vehicle-free conditions, substantially exceeding that of stoichiometrically matched free antimetabolites. Treatment induced S-phase accumulation, increased DNA damage and apoptosis, and suppressed checkpoint and survival-associated proteins, including WEE1, CHK1, YAP1, and BCL-2. Transcriptomic and proteomic analyses revealed increased DNA replication, replication-stress, and repair-associated programs, together with reduced oncogenic signaling. In gemcitabine-resistant cells, treatment restored the gemcitabine-activating enzyme dCK, reduced ABCC1 and ABCC3 expression, and suppressed resistance-associated signaling programs, indicating partial remodeling of resistance-associated pathways. MTX-5-FU-Gem-miR-15a also synergized with daraxonrasib (mean Bliss synergy score, 22.52) and activated tumor-cell-intrinsic STING-TBK1 signaling, accompanied by increased interferon stimulated gene expression and IFN-{beta} and CXCL10 secretion. Finally, MTX-5-FU-Gem-miR-15a retained low-nanomolar potency in three patient-derived PDAC organoids and significantly suppressed metastatic tumor growth in vivo at 4 mg/kg. Together, these findings support a multimodal miRNA therapeutic strategy that combines replication-associated DNA damage, checkpoint protein suppression, and innate immune activation-associated responses to target therapeutic resistance in PDAC.

https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.64898.title: Miniaturized Traceless Staudinger Ligation Enables Direct-to-Biology Screening of Potent BRD4 PROTACs
https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.64898.abstract: Direct-to-biology (D2B) approaches accelerate PROTAC discovery by enabling biological screening of crude reaction mixtures without intermediate purification. However, the range of chemical transformations compatible with these workflows remains limited. Herein, we establish a miniaturized, base-free traceless Staudinger ligation platform diversifying linker chemistry for a preexisting library of E3-ligand-linker adducts bearing azide moieties. As a proof-of-concept target, BRD4 was chosen, yielding amide-linked BRD4-targeting PROTACs. By combining phosphine-functionalized JQ1 derivatives with 72 selected azide building blocks, reactions were performed on a 5 L scale in 384-well plates, achieving a mean LC-MS conversion of approximately 65%. Spiking experiments confirmed that the phosphine starting materials had no significant impact on BRD4 degradation, supporting the direct biological evaluation of crude reaction mixtures in the presence of residual starting material. Cellular screening identified 23 hits at 250 nM screening concentration, reducing BRD4 levels below 40%. Two resynthesized and purified PROTACs were subsequently validated, displaying pDC50 values of 8.2 and 7.0 and a Dmax of 90% and 96%, respectively. This work establishes traceless Staudinger ligation as a complementary D2B strategy for the rapid discovery of amide-linked PROTACs.

https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.64898.title: Development of a Thyroid Cancer to Lung Metastasis-on-a-Chip Model
https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.64898.abstract: Background: Study of the metastatic cascade in differentiated non-medullary thyroid cancer (NMTC) is hampered by the relative lack of preclinical models that metastasize from primary tumors to other organs. We previously identified regulator of calcineurin 1 isoform 4 (RCAN1.4) as a suppressor of NMTC cell growth, invasion, and metastasis using in vitro systems and tail vein injections in immunocompromised mice. We then reported a microfluidic device mimicking the mouse tail vein injection where cancer cells were allowed to flow directly to lung organoid constructs. We now report the development of a full primary tumor to lung metastasis-on-a-chip (MOC) model for TC. Methods: Resin molds for primary and secondary sites connected by a channel were 3D printed and filled with polydimethylsiloxane to create a molded silicone elastomer. The primary site was seeded with an organoid composed of a hyaluronic acid and collagen-based hydrogel into which FTC236 and HTh74 NMTC cells with and without knockdown of RCAN1.4 were engrafted. The secondary site consisted of a hydrogel organoid into which bronchial epithelial cells and lung fibroblasts were seeded. Culture media was circulated and movement of NMTC cells to the secondary site was assessed. Results: Both cell lines that expressed RCAN 1.4 metastasized to the secondary lung site. RCAN1.4-reduced FTC236 cells had increased metastatic behavior vs controls while HTh74 was less affected by RCAN1.4 loss, similar to prior studies. To determine if the MOC could be used for incorporation of immune components and therapeutic modeling, NK-92 cells were added and were shown to be reduce metastases for both cell lines in the presence or absence of RCAN1.4. Analysis of MOC circulating fluid revealed elevated levels of granzyme B, consistent with NK-92 cell activation. Cytokine profiling identified elevated probable NMTC and NK-92-derived factors. Conclusions: These results indicate that NMTC metastatic behavior can be modeled using a novel MOC system for mechanistic and preclinical therapeutic studies.

https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-0.title: Podophyllotoxin disrupts the XIAP–caspase-9 interaction to promote apoptosis: insights from a quantitative split-luciferase complementation assay
https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-0.abstract: Podophyllotoxin (PTOX), a plant-derived lignan with potent anticancer properties, is hypothesized to mimic Smac activity by interacting with Inhibitor of Apoptosis Protein (IAP) BIR domains. However, the precise molecular mechanisms governing these interactions remain poorly understood. In this study, we developed and validated a highly sensitive, cell-free split-luciferase complementation assay designed to quantify the real-time interaction dynamics between the BIR2–BIR3 domains of XIAP and its key targets, caspase-3 and caspase-9. Our results demonstrate that the BIR2–BIR3–NLuc/caspase-9-CLuc interaction is significantly more robust and stable than the BIR2–BIR3–NLuc/caspase-3-CLuc interaction, highlighting a preferential binding mechanism at the initiator caspase level. Utilizing this platform, we investigated the effects of PTOX in modulating this interaction. Consistent with in silico docking predictions, PTOX disrupted the XIAP–caspase-9 complex in a concentration-dependent manner, leading to a marked reduction in luminescence and a subsequent restoration of caspase-9 enzymatic activity. While PTOX showed a minor inhibitory effect on the XIAP–caspase-3 interaction, its impact on the caspase-9 axis was markedly more pronounced. Furthermore, Carboplatin, a DNA-crosslinking agent, exhibited no significant impact on these protein-protein interactions, confirming the specificity of the observed PTOX-mediated effects. These findings establish a sensitive, real-time platform for monitoring the XIAP–caspase axis and provide compelling evidence that PTOX acts as a targeted modulator of the apoptotic pathway, warranting its further development as a pharmacological agent.

https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-0.title: Quantifying high-LET heavy-ion-induced non-DSB clustered DNA lesions using Geant4-DNA
https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-0.abstract: Ionizing radiation induces complex DNA damage that can challenge repair processes and contribute to genomic instability. In this study, we extend Geant4-DNA to quantify oxidative non-DSB damage containing 8-oxo-7,8-dihydro-2′-deoxyguanosine (8-oxo-dG) and thymidine glycol (dTg) from direct and hydroxyl-radical pathways. Simulations were performed in a reduced-scale human fibroblast chromatin geometry for 12C, 28Si, 40Ar, and 56Fe ions (LET 13–148 keV/μm). For 12C irradiation at 94.55 MeV/u, including direct and quasi-direct oxidation raised the simulated 8-oxo-dG yield from 0.0059 ± 0.0002 to 0.0239 ± 0.0005 lesions/Mbp/Gy, approaching published experimental values. Simulated lesion frequencies matched experimental orders of magnitude, although discrepancies remained and the experimental assays and biological conditions were not fully equivalent to the simulated observables. The resulting damage profiles resolved lesion identity and local multiplicity. Clusters containing one single-strand break and one oxidative base lesion were the predominant non-DSB clustered configurations, particularly SSB + 8-oxo-dG (9.4%–13.2%) and SSB + dTg (8.5%–12.8%). This framework extends Geant4-DNA beyond conventional strand-break analysis, offering lesion-resolved inputs for mechanistic base excision repair models under heavy-ion irradiation.

https://www.nature.com/articles/s41375-0.title: Mediator kinase inhibition exposes a transcriptional vulnerability and synergizes with venetoclax in AML
https://www.nature.com/articles/s41375-0.abstract: Acute myeloid leukemia (AML) is a heterogeneous and aggressive hematologic malignancy associated with poor survival despite recent therapeutic advances. To identify novel anti-leukemic agents, we performed a high-throughput viability screen of 10,000 small molecules across 56 genetically diverse primary AML samples. Compounds with similar activity profiles were grouped into Compound Correlation Clusters (CCCs), leading to the identification of CCC163, which includes AML874, as a potent and selective hit. Integrated pharmacological and CRISPR-Cas9 approaches identified the Mediator complex as the molecular target of AML874. We demonstrated that AML874 acts as a selective CDK8/CDK19 inhibitor, disrupting Mediator-dependent transcription. FLT3-mutated AML showed increased sensitivity to AML874, suggesting a subtype-specific vulnerability. Notably, CDK8 inhibition synergized with venetoclax in AML cell lines and patient-derived xenograft models, resulting in enhanced anti-leukemic activity in vivo. Collectively, these findings establish CDK8/CDK19 inhibition as a therapeutically relevant strategy in AML.

https://www.nature.com/articles/s44484-0.title: Ligs-Mamba: a synergistic Mamba network for video breast Cooper’s ligament segmentation
https://www.nature.com/articles/s44484-0.abstract: Accurate segmentation of breast Cooper’s (BC) ligaments in endoscopic mastectomy videos is difficult because of their low contrast, indistinct boundaries, and interference from surrounding tissues. Reliable delineation supports anatomical identification during surgery. Mamba has shown promise in medical image analysis.
