Compared with Transformer self-attention, its selective scanning mechanism adaptively emphasizes informative features in long sequences. We propose Ligs-Mamba, a Mamba-based framework for video BC ligament segmentation. It comprises an anatomy-aware global Mamba (AGM) module and an uncertainty-focused local Mamba (ULM) module. AGM uses coarse ligament predictions to direct global feature scanning toward anatomically relevant regions, whereas ULM uses uncertainty priors to focus local scanning on ambiguous boundaries. Together, these modules strengthen the representation of low-contrast ligaments while reducing background interference. We also collect and annotate the video-based BC ligament segmentation (VLS) dataset, which contains 90 videos and 6403 frames. To our knowledge, VLS is the first annotated dataset for video BC ligament segmentation, and Ligs-Mamba is the first framework designed for this task. Experiments on VLS show that Ligs-Mamba outperforms state-of-the-art methods in quantitative and qualitative evaluations, producing more accurate ligament masks under challenging conditions.

https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-0.title: Unveiling the antitumor and chemo-sensitizing effects of ondansetron in the treatment of MCF-7 breast cancer cells
https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-0.abstract: Breast cancer (BC) remains one of the global leading causes of cancer-related deaths among women. Resistance to chemotherapy and metastatic progression are key challenges. Serotonin (5-HT) and its receptor subtypes are implicated in tumor proliferation, but the oncogenic role of 5-HT3-Rs in BC is not well defined. The widely-used antiemetic, Ondansetron, is a selective 5-HT3 receptor antagonist, that is investigated in this study to explore the potential previously-unrecognized anticancer properties in MCF-7 human BC cells. To investigate the potential effect of Ondansetron, alone or in combination with Doxorubicin, in inhibiting proliferation, survival and migration of MCF-7 BC cells, and to explore some of the underlying molecular mechanisms. MCF-7 cells were treated with Ondansetron and/or Doxorubicin. Cell viability- (MTT), migration- (wound healing), and survival- (clonogenic) assays were conducted. The regulation of some downstream signaling pathways were analyzed by ELISA, Western blotting, or immunofluorescence to assess the modulations of migratory/metastatic (RAS/mTOR/SRC/FAK/MMP-2), survival/angiogenic (Cyclin D1/VEGF-A), and apoptotic (Bcl-2/Cytochrome c/cleaved-caspase-7) biomarkers. Ondansetron significantly reduced cell viability and migration capability and markedly potentiated the cytotoxic effects of Doxorubicin. The combination regimen, downregulated key oncogenic signaling molecules (RAS/mTOR/SRC/FAK/MMP-2/VEGF-A/Cyclin D1) with enhanced Cytochrome c/cleaved-caspase-7 activation, and suppressed the anti-apoptotic protein, Bcl-2. Pharmacological targeting of 5-HT/HTR3 with Ondansetron induces antitumor effects in MCF-7 BC cells by suppressing 5-HT3-mediated survival signaling and metastatic pathways, and increases MCF-7 cells sensitivity to chemotherapy. This study proposes using Ondansetron as a potential adjuvant to Doxorubicin-based treatment of BC, to improve efficacy and reduce toxicity of the chemotherapy.

https://www.nature.com/articles/s41416-0.title: Toxicity, health-related quality of life and sexuality after molecular profile-based adjuvant treatment in high-intermediate risk endometrial cancer, PORTEC-4a
https://www.nature.com/articles/s41416-0.abstract: PORTEC-4a was the first to incorporate molecular-integrated profile-guided adjuvant treatment in early-stage high-intermediate-risk endometrial cancer (EC), demonstrating non-inferiority. Here, adverse events (AE), health-related quality of life (HRQoL) and sexual health are reported. 564 patients were randomised to molecular-based adjuvant treatment (n = 367) or standard vaginal brachytherapy (VBT, n = 197). In the molecular-profile arm, patients underwent observation, VBT or pelvic radiotherapy according to molecular-integrated profile. HRQoL and sexual functioning were assessed with EORTC QLQ-C30 and EN24 modules and compared with age-matched normative data. Median follow-up was 58.1 months; 523 (92.7%) patients were evaluable. Grade 1–2 AEs were less frequent in the molecular-profile arm at treatment completion compared with the standard arm (28.3% vs. 45.2%, p < 0.01), without differences in grade 3–4 AEs (p = 0.46). Throughout follow-up, treatment-related grade 3–4 AEs were rare (1% vs. 2%). HRQoL remained comparable to normative data over time. Sexual interest/activity was similar between arms, but lower than normative values. 75.5% of patients reported ≥1 reason for sexual inactivity; disease-related sexual inactivity decreased from 24.2% to 9.2% at 3 years. Molecular-guided adjuvant treatment for patients with high-intermediate riskEC is associated with low toxicity, preserved HRQoL and slightly reduced sexual activity due to personal factors (no partner, sex not important in their relationship or partner-related medical issues) rather than their own illness.

https://www.nature.com/articles/s41419-0.title: A non-canonical mitochondrial function of MAFG drives HCC progression by stabilizing PGAM5 to promote fission
https://www.nature.com/articles/s41419-0.abstract: Excessive mitochondrial fission is a hallmark of hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), yet the upstream regulatory mechanisms driving this pathological process remain poorly understood. While the transcription factor V-Maf avian musculoaponeurotic fibrosarcoma oncogene homolog G (MAFG) is known to be overexpressed in HCC, its potential role in mitochondrial dynamics has not been explored. In this study, we identify a novel, non-canonical, extra-nuclear function of MAFG in promoting mitochondrial fission and HCC malignancy. Mechanistically, we demonstrate that a subpopulation of MAFG is detected in the mitochondrial fraction where it directly interacts with the protein phosphatase PGAM5. By binding to the Arg251 residue of PGAM5 via its Lys81 residuum binding suppresses PGAM5 ubiquitination. The resulting stabilization of PGAM5 enhances the dephosphorylation of dynamin-related protein 1 (DRP1) at Ser637, thereby driving excessive mitochondrial fission and fueling HCC progression. Functionally, ectopic expression of PGAM5 rescues the impaired malignant phenotypes caused by MAFG knockdown, whereas PGAM5 inhibition attenuates MAFG-driven oncogenesis. Clinical analyses further confirm that the MAFG-PGAM5-DRP1 axis is significantly activated in HCC tissues and strongly correlates with poor patient prognosis. Our findings reveal a previously unrecognized, transcription-independent oncogenic pathway in which mitochondrial MAFG stabilizes PGAM5 to orchestrate pathological fission. These results suggest that targeting the specific MAFG-PGAM5 interaction may represents a promising therapeutic strategy for the treatment of HCC.

https://www.nature.com/articles/s41420-0.title: Transcriptional upregulation of NDUFA10 by ATF3 sustains mitochondrial bioenergetics and malignant phenotypes in NSCLC
https://www.nature.com/articles/s41420-0.abstract: Non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) remains a leading cause of global cancer mortality, necessitating the identification of novel therapeutic vulnerabilities. This study identifies NDUFA10, a key mitochondrial Complex I subunit, as a critical driver of NSCLC pathogenesis. Multi-cohort analysis of TCGA and clinical datasets revealed significant NDUFA10 upregulation in neoplastic tissues, which correlated with advanced pathological stage, metastasis, smoking history, and poor overall survival. Single-cell RNA sequencing further localized NDUFA10 enrichment to proliferating malignant epithelial subpopulations, where its expression positively associated with oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS) and ATP synthesis across primary and metastatic sites. Functionally, NDUFA10 ablation (shRNA or CRISPR/Cas9) in primary NSCLC and A549 cells disrupted mitochondrial homeostasis—evidenced by impaired respiration, attenuated Complex I activity, and augmented ROS production—while inhibiting cell viability, migration, and invasion. Mechanistically, NDUFA10 modulates the Akt-mTOR signaling axis; constitutively active Akt1 partially rescued the proliferative and survival deficits induced by NDUFA10 silencing. Furthermore, intersectional bioinformatics and ChIP-qPCR identified ATF3 as the direct transcriptional activator driving NDUFA10 overexpression. In vivo, NDUFA10-silenced xenografts exhibited significantly attenuated growth, characterized by compromised mitochondrial function and inhibited Akt-mTOR activation. In summary, our findings characterize NDUFA10 as a critical metabolic checkpoint in NSCLC, where its ATF3-driven its overexpression coordinates mitochondrial bioenergetics and Akt-mTOR signaling to sustain malignant progression.

https://www.nature.com/articles/s41419-0.title: Glycolytic metabolism as a central regulator of T cell fate and function in the tumor microenvironment
https://www.nature.com/articles/s41419-0.abstract: T cells are the central effectors of antitumor immunity, yet their function is profoundly constrained by the metabolically hostile tumor microenvironment (TME). In order to meet the bioenergetic and biosynthetic demands of activation and differentiation, T cells undergo metabolic reprogramming, particularly enhanced glycolysis, upon antigen recognition. However, intratumoral glucose deprivation and lactate accumulation driven by the Warburg effect of cancer cells create a metabolic tug-of-war that differentially impacts T cell subsets. The present review systematically elucidates how glycolytic metabolism governs the fate and function of CD4⁺ T cells, CD8⁺ T cells, regulatory T cells (Tregs), and CAR-T cells within the TME. It highlights the striking metabolic dichotomy between effector T cells that depend on aerobic glycolysis and Tregs, which exhibit metabolic plasticity enabling them to thrive under nutrient-limited conditions. Key signaling nodes, including calcium-NFAT, CD38/NAD⁺/SIRT1, MAPK/AP1, and PI3K/Akt/mTOR, converge to integrate microenvironmental cues with transcriptional and epigenetic programs that shape T cell immunity. The report also discusses how shared metabolic mechanisms intersect with synthetic receptor architecture to influence persistence and exhaustion in CAR-T cells. By exploring recent advances, this review aims to provide a framework for targeting glucose metabolism to enhance antitumor immune responses and optimize next-generation immunotherapies.

https://www.nature.com/articles/s41419-0.title: Macrophage-specific Smad7 restrains colorectal cancer progression by suppressing STAT6-mediated M2 polarization
https://www.nature.com/articles/s41419-0.abstract: Macrophages play a crucial role in the tumor microenvironment, and their polarization states significantly impact the progression of colorectal cancer (CRC). In this study, we explored the macrophage-intrinsic function of Smad7 using patient datasets, tissue-based analyses, conditional knockout mouse models, and macrophage cell systems. Smad7 expression was reduced in clinically aggressive CRC and was preferentially decreased within CD206-positive macrophage-associated regions, where it inversely correlated with CD206 expression, whereas no comparable reduction was observed in E-cadherin-positive epithelial regions. The macrophage-specific deletion of Smad7 led to a marked increase in CRC incidence, accompanied by a shift toward an M2-like phenotype. Smad7-deficient macrophages exhibited heightened expression of M2 markers and decreased levels of M1-associated genes, which correlated with increased phosphorylation of STAT6 following IL-4/IL-13 stimulation. In contrast, overexpression of Smad7 inhibited M2 polarization and enhanced the expression of M1 markers. Mechanistically, Smad7 positively influenced the transcription of protein tyrosine phosphatase non-receptor type 2 (PTPN2), a negative regulator of STAT signaling, by functioning as a coactivator of IRF1 at the PTPN2 promoter. The loss of Smad7 resulted in reduced PTPN2 expression, leading to sustained STAT6 activation and promoting M2 polarization. Notably, knocking down PTPN2 mirrored the expression patterns of M2 markers observed with Smad7 deficiency, and the absence of PTPN2 in Smad7-overexpressing cells negated the suppression of STAT6 signaling and M2 marker expression. Overall, these findings reveal a previously unrecognized role for Smad7 in macrophages as a transcriptional regulator of PTPN2, which restricts STAT6-mediated M2 polarization and limits colorectal tumorigenesis. Targeting the Smad7–PTPN2–STAT6 axis may offer new therapeutic avenues for reprogramming macrophage function in CRC.

https://www.nature.com/articles/s41420-0.title: HSPB8 regulates CTP synthase filaments to couple nucleotide metabolism and autophagy in tumors
https://www.nature.com/articles/s41420-0.abstract: Metabolic adaptation and proteostasis are essential for tumor survival under nutrient stress, yet how these processes are mechanistically integrated remains unclear. Here, we identify CTP synthase (CTPS) filament dynamics as a regulatory nexus linking nucleotide metabolism to autophagic flux. Under glutamine deprivation—a hallmark of poorly vascularized solid tumors—CTPS undergoes polymerization into filamentous assemblies that exhibit reduced enzymatic activity. We demonstrate that filament formation is driven by intracellular asparagine availability and regulated by the accumulation of misfolded proteins. Using APEX2-based proximity labeling and proteomics, we identify the small heat shock protein HSPB8 as a filament-associated regulator. HSPB8, acting within the chaperone-assisted selective autophagy (CASA) pathway, antagonizes CTPS polymerization by promoting clearance of misfolded proteins, thereby restoring soluble, catalytically active CTPS. Filament disassembly increases CTP production and enhances synthesis of autophagy-related phospholipids, including phosphatidylinositol and phosphatidylethanolamine, resulting in accelerated autophagic flux. Cells expressing filament-deficient CTPS mutants display elevated autophagosome formation and increased LC3-II accumulation upon lysosomal blockade, confirming enhanced flux. In vivo, disruption of CTPS filament assembly impairs xenograft tumor growth and is associated with excessive autophagy. Analysis of TCGA datasets further reveals that high CTPS and low HSPB8 expression correlate with poor patient survival across multiple cancers. Collectively, our findings establish CTPS filament dynamics as a proteostasis-sensitive metabolic switch that coordinates nucleotide biosynthesis with autophagy, revealing a previously unrecognized vulnerability in tumors adapting to nutrient limitation.

https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-0.title: Synthesis, characterization, and anticancer effect of nanoformulated Zataria multiflora Boiss. extract against prostate and breast cancer cells in vitro
https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-0.abstract: This study aimed to investigate the effect of nanoformulated Zataria multiflora Boiss. (Shirazi thyme) extract on inhibiting the growth of PC3 prostate and MDA-MB-231 breast cancer cell lines by regulating autophagy. The hydroalcoholic extract of Zataria multiflora Boiss. (ZM) was prepared by ultrasonic-assisted maceration in 70% ethanol. Blank (Gel NP) and extract-loaded gelatin nanoparticles (ZM.Gel NPs) were synthesized via a two-step desolvation method and characterized in terms of size, surface charge, morphology, chemical structure, loading parameters, and in vitro release kinetics. PC3 and MDA-MB-231 cell lines were treated with various concentrations of the free extract, Gel NPs, and ZM.Gel NPs (with equivalent encapsulated ZM extract) for 48 and 72 h. Cell proliferation was evaluated using the MTT assay, and IC50 values were calculated. The expression of apoptosis- and autophagy-related genes was determined using Real-Time PCR. Gel NPs and ZM.Gel NPs exhibited spherical morphology, with smooth surfaces and suitable physicochemical properties, while providing sustained release of ZM extract over time. ZM.Gel NPs significantly enhanced the antiproliferative potential of the free extract, thereby reducing the IC50 value. ZM.Gel NPs significantly upregulated TP53 and BAX and downregulated BCL2, while decreasing Beclin-1, ATG5, ATG7, and LC3A expression compared with the free extract. Gel NPs enhanced the antiproliferative and cytotoxic effects of ZM extract, upregulating pro-apoptotic genes and downregulating autophagy-driven genes in prostate and breast cancer cell lines.

https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-0.title: Evaluation of extracellular vesicle-enriched fraction-derived miR-105, miR-1908, and miR-122 expression profiles in prostate cancer and benign prostatic hyperplasia
https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-0.abstract: Prostate cancer (PCa) remains a critical challenge in oncology. There is a need to explore novel, minimally invasive indicators to help evaluate differences between PCa and benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH), which often mimics PCa symptoms and whose clinical evaluation is complicated by overlapping PSA levels. This study exploratively investigated the expression profiles of extracellular vesicle (EV)-enriched fraction-derived miR-105, miR-1908, and miR-122 miRNAs previously associated with epithelial-mesenchymal transition, metastatic signaling, and metabolic reprogramming to evaluate their potential associations with urological malignancies. EV-like particles were isolated from the plasma of 25 patients with BPH, 50 with PCa (25 localized, 25 metastatic), and 21 healthy controls. Transmission electron microscopy characterized the morphology of EV-like particles and revealed a significant increase in particle size within the PCa cohorts compared to the BPH and control groups (p < 0.05). Following cDNA synthesis and miRNA profiling, miR-1908 expression was significantly downregulated in the PCa groups (LPCa and especially MPCa) relative to the BPH group (p < 0.05). No significant differences were observed in the expression levels of miR-105 and miR-122. These results suggest that miR-1908 levels may be associated with prostate pathological status. While miR-1908 warrants further investigation as an exploratory candidate, large-scale studies are necessary to validate these preliminary associations and determine their potential clinical relevance.

https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-0.title: Epigenetic heterogeneity in breast tumours informs diagnosis and prognosis
https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-0.abstract: Breast cancer, the most diagnosed cancer among women, is stratified by gene expression patterns into luminal and basal-like subtypes, and the latter is associated with worse prognosis1–3. Recent advances in single-cell technologies have underscored the presence of intratumour heterogeneity, which poses substantial challenges in cancer treatment and achieving long-term disease-free survival4–7. Here we extensively profile epigenetic heterogeneity in a cohort of treatment-naive human luminal tumours, which were obtained directly after surgical resection. By applying a single-cell epigenetic approach based on cytometry by time-of-flight, we identify a recurrent subpopulation of basal-like cells in luminal tumours with a conserved epigenetic signature across patients. These basal-like cells, also identified by deconvolution of whole-genome DNA methylation patterns, are characterized by high expression of aggressive oncogenic traits and downregulation of hormone receptor signalling. Direct comparison of single-cell proteomic and genomic profiling of monomethylation and trimethylation of histone 3 on lysine 4 revealed that these marks are key features associated with loss of luminal identity. Finally, we highlight the potential of concomitant single-molecule profiling of histone modifications on cell-free nucleosomes in blood as an epigenetic liquid biopsy approach for early diagnosis of breast cancer. Moreover, the epigenetic basal signature measured in blood is linked to prognosis, which enables the identification of patients at increased risk for disease relapse. Single-cell epigenetic analyses reveal a conserved epigenetic signature across patients that may help identify those at increased risk for disease relapse in breast cancer.

https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-0.title: Evolutionary dynamics in the years preceding acute myeloid leukaemia
https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-0.abstract: Somatic evolution in ageing tissues underlies many cancers1,2. However, our quantitative understanding of the rules governing this pre-cancerous evolution remains incomplete. Here we exploit a unique collection of serial blood samples3, collected annually for up to a decade and beginning as early as 15 years before diagnosis of acute myeloid leukaemia, to provide a quantitative description of pre-cancerous evolutionary dynamics. Using deep duplex sequencing and evolutionary theory, we quantify the acquisition ages and fitness effects of the key driver events in acute myeloid leukaemia development. The first driver mutations are typically acquired in the first few decades of life, when the blood remains highly polyclonal. These early slow-growing clones subsequently acquire multiple further driver mutations that confer selective advantages up to 100-fold larger than the early drivers. These faster-growing clones harbouring multiple driver mutations can cause complete somatic sweeps of the blood decades before diagnosis, a feature strongly associated with future acute myeloid leukaemia. Our data show that the clonal dynamics of blood are consistent with a set of remarkably simple evolutionary rules that strike a balance between chance and determinism. The somatic evolutionary histories of haematopoietic cells in the years preceding acute myeloid leukaemia diagnosis show that the clonal dynamics of blood comply with a set of simple evolutionary rules.

https://www.nature.com/articles/s41585-0.title: International multidisciplinary Delphi consensus on advanced practice in non-metastatic upper tract urothelial carcinoma (IMPACT UTUC)
https://www.nature.com/articles/s41585-0.abstract: Non-metastatic upper tract urothelial carcinoma (UTUC) is characterized by limited high-level evidence and substantial heterogeneity in clinical practice across diagnosis, staging and treatment, highlighting the need for expert-driven guidance to reduce variability and improve patient outcomes. To address this gap, we conducted the international multidisciplinary Delphi consensus on advanced practice in non-metastatic upper tract urothelial carcinoma (IMPACT UTUC). This two-round, web-based Delphi survey involved 73 international UTUC experts (urologists and medical oncologists) from Europe, the Americas and Asia. A total of 40 statements covering two domains (diagnosis and staging, and treatment) were rated on a 9-point Likert scale, with predefined thresholds for consensus agreement and disagreement. Overall, consensus was achieved for 32 of 40 statements (80%) across both rounds. IMPACT UTUC provides the first structured international Delphi consensus spanning the entire non-metastatic UTUC care pathway, offering pragmatic expert-informed recommendations that could guide current clinical practice and inform the design of future prospective studies. In this Consensus Statement, an international, multidisciplinary panel of experts within the international multidisciplinary Delphi consensus on advanced practice in upper tract urothelial carcinoma (IMPACT UTUC) initiative provide recommendations on clinically relevant topics in the management of non-metastatic upper tract urothelial carcinoma, spanning diagnosis, imaging, molecular assessment, and surgical and systemic therapies.

https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-0.title: Domain-alteration chimeras rewire oncogenic complexes in prostate cancer
https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-0.abstract: Transcriptional addiction to the androgen receptor (AR) underlies metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer1, in which AR maintains oncogenic programs through domain-specific interactions with the acetyltransferases p300 and CBP (collectively p300/CBP)2. Here we describe a novel therapeutic modality, domain-alteration chimeras (DALTACs), that rewire endogenous protein complexes by enforcing non-native domain–domain interactions. Our first-in-class AR–p300/CBP DALTAC-1 induces synthetic proximity between the ligand-binding domain of AR and the bromodomain of p300/CBP, misconfiguring their native interface and locking the complex in a non-productive state. DALTAC-1 triggers a ‘super-inhibitory’ effect, suppressing AR-driven transcription and proliferation more potently than combined AR and p300/CBP inhibition. Mechanistically, DALTAC-1 reprograms p300/CBP substrate engagement, abolishing the histone mark H2B N-terminal acetylation and inducing neomorphic acetylation of AR and coactivators, ultimately collapsing the AR neo-enhanceosome. Chromatin profiling revealed redistribution of AR and p300/CBP towards palindromic androgen response elements, accompanied by disruption of cofactor and transcriptional machinery recruitment at oncogenic AR and ERG neo-enhancers. DALTAC-1 exhibits exquisite lineage selectivity, displaying potent activity in AR–p300/CBP dual-dependent cells and sparing AR-negative cells. In multiple in vivo models, DALTAC-1 induces deep and durable tumour regressions. Together, these findings establish DALTACs as a broadly applicable strategy to rewire disease-defining complexes through domain-topology alteration, expanding induced-proximity therapies, and the precise lineage selectivity of DALTAC-1 supports its translational potential in AR-driven prostate cancer. A novel therapeutic modality enforces non-native androgen receptor (AR)–p300/CBP interactions to collapse AR transcriptional programs, producing super-inhibitory, lineage-selective suppression of metastatic prostate cancer and establishing domain-alteration chimeras as a broadly applicable therapeutic strategy leveraging induced proximity.

https://www.nature.com/articles/s41591-0.title: Normalized membrane ratio of TROP2 as a predictor of clinical outcomes with datopotamab deruxtecan in non-small-cell lung cancer
https://www.nature.com/articles/s41591-0.abstract: Datopotamab deruxtecan (Dato-DXd)—a trophoblast cell surface antigen 2 (TROP2)-directed antibody–drug conjugate—has demonstrated efficacy in patients with advanced nonsquamous non-small-cell lung cancer (NSCLC) ± actionable genomic alterations. However, TROP2 expression by pathologist assessment using conventional immunohistochemistry with visual scoring does not predict response to TROP2-directed antibody–drug conjugates in NSCLC. We developed TROP2 quantitative continuous scoring (QCS)—a fully supervised computational pathology approach that quantifies TROP2 expression in individual NSCLC cells and subcellular components from immunohistochemistry-stained slides. Using QCS to determine TROP2 expression at the tumor cell membrane and cytoplasm, normalized membrane ratio (NMR) was developed (ratio of membrane relative to membrane + cytoplasmic TROP2) in the biomarker-evaluable population of patients with advanced NSCLC in the TROPION-PanTumor01 study (n = 115). The TROP2 NMR cut-point was optimized and validated in patients with nonsquamous NSCLC without actionable genomic alterations (primary intended-use population, n = 221) in the biomarker-evaluable population (n = 352) of the TROPION-Lung01 trial. Association with clinical outcomes was assessed. Progression-free survival was longer in Dato-DXd-treated (median 7.2 versus 4.0 months; hazard ratio 0.40, 95% confidence interval 0.25–0.64) but not docetaxel-treated (median 4.1 versus 4.4 months; hazard ratio 0.94, 95% confidence interval 0.59–1.49) patients with TROP2 NMR-positive versus TROP2 NMR-negative samples (treatment by biomarker status interaction P = 0.0098), indicating that TROP2 NMR may be a predictive biomarker for Dato-DXd. This work developed and validated a computational pathology biomarker—the TROP2 normalized membrane ratio—that quantifies subcellular TROP2 localization and predicts improved progression-free and overall survival with datopotamab deruxtecan in patients with nonsquamous non-small-cell lung cancer lacking actionable genomic alterations.

https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-0.title: Radical prostatectomy outcomes in men aged 75 or older with high-risk localized or locally advanced prostate cancer
https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-0.abstract: We evaluated whether radical prostatectomy is safe and effective in elderly patients with high-risk localized or locally advanced prostate cancer. We retrospectively analyzed 757 patients at four Chinese tertiary centers (2012–2022): 201 aged 75 or older, 556 younger. Elderly patients had longer operative time (165 vs. 155 min, p = 0.002), greater blood loss (350 vs. 280 mL, p < 0.001), and more Clavien-Dindo grade III or higher complications (8.0% vs. 3.8%, p = 0.018), but 30-day mortality was 0.5%. Pathological characteristics, including stage distribution, were broadly similar. At five years, biochemical recurrence-free survival was 72% vs. 79% (hazard ratio 1.32, p = 0.021), cancer-specific survival 94% vs. 95% (hazard ratio 1.45, p = 0.203), overall survival 88% vs. 96% (hazard ratio 2.18, p < 0.001), and metastasis-free survival 91% vs. 93% (hazard ratio 1.56, p = 0.028). Most deaths in elderly patients were non-cancer related (13 of 25). Propensity matching and weighting preserved effect directions, although evidence weakened in some adjusted analyses (weighted recurrence p = 0.053; competing-risk p = 0.062). A recurrence nomogram showed modest discrimination (C-index 0.63). Radical prostatectomy is feasible in carefully selected fit older patients, but age alone should not guide decisions; comorbidity and life expectancy must be considered.

https://www.nature.com/articles/s42003-0.title: Lysine 69 deacetylation of NFIC drives autophagy-induced epithelial–mesenchymal transition and chemoresistance in glioblastoma
https://www.nature.com/articles/s42003-0.abstract: Acquired temozolomide (TMZ) resistance is a major obstacle in improving glioblastoma multiforme (GBM) treatment. Accumulating evidence has indicated that autophagy has dual effects on the regulation of chemoresistance. In our previous study, we reported that autophagic inducers can upregulate the E3 ligase HERC3 and then mediate TMZ resistance by activating the HERC3/SMAD7/TGF-β pathway. However, the underlying mechanism within the increasing expression of HERC3 induced by autophagy is still unknown. Herein, we show that autophagy promotes the deacetylation of nuclear factor I C (NFIC) at lysine 69, which induces the transcriptional activation of forkhead box protein K1 (FOXK1) and thus promotes HERC3 dependent epithelial‒mesenchymal transition (EMT). The dynamic equilibrium of NFIC K69Ac is controlled by the acetyltransferase P300 and the deacetylase HDAC6. Pe-k69, a cell-penetrating peptide, can specifically block NFIC K69 deacetylation and sensitise GBM cells to TMZ. Our study reveals an acetylation-dependent regulatory mechanism, which may provide mechanistic clues for targeting NFIC to overcome GBM chemoresistance. Autophagy-induced the deacetylation of NFIC at Lysine 69 site accelerates tumorigenesis by activating FOXK1/HERC3 axis, revealing an acetylation-dependent mechanism that can be targeted by peptide Pe-k69 to overcome TMZ resistance in glioblastoma.

https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-0.title: Synergistic effect of XYL-1 and Olaparib in BRCA-proficient TNBC cells is associated with RAD51 and BRCA1 downregulation
https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-0.abstract: Poly-ADP-ribose polymerase1/2 (PARP1/2) inhibitors are approved for HER2-negative breast cancer harboring germline BRCA1/2 mutations, including TNBC. However, the majority of patients with BRCA-proficient derive limited benefit from these agents. In this study, we demonstrate that the efficacy of the PARP1/2 inhibitor Olaparib in BRCA-proficient TNBC cell lines can be markedly enhanced by co-treatment with the PARP7 inhibitor XYL-1. Our results demonstrated that the combination of Olaparib and XYL-1 significantly inhibited the proliferation of BRCA-proficient MDA-MB-231 and MDA-MB-468 cells compared with either monotherapy, with the strongest synergistic effect observed at a 1:1 molar ratio in MDA-MB-231 cells. Furthermore, the combination of Olaparib and XYL-1 significantly increased cellular ROS levels, induced DNA double-strand breaks (DSBs), and ultimately promoted apoptosis. In vivo, the combined treatment significantly suppressed MDA-MB-231 tumor growth compared with either monotherapy, while exhibiting a favorable safety profile. Mechanistically, co-treatment with XYL-1 and Olaparib significantly downregulated RAD51 and BRCA1 expression, which may be associated with impaired homologous recombination (HR)-mediated DNA repair. Collectively, these findings suggest that dual targeting of PARP7 and PARP1/2 represents a promising combination strategy for the treatment of BRCA-proficient TNBC.

https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-0.title: Functionally divergent RHOA mutations drive peripheral T cell lymphoma development by engaging a common neomorphic pathway
https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-0.abstract: RHOA, a RAS superfamily member, is frequently mutated in peripheral T-cell lymphoma (PTCL). These mutations are puzzling because variants have opposite effects on conventional RHOA signaling: some (e.g., RHOAG17V) inhibit normal RHOA function, whereas others (e.g., RHOAC16R) are constitutively active. Here we show that all PTCL-associated RHOA mutants acquire a non-canonical VAV1-like activity that activates the transcription factor NFAT. This activity is mediated by complexes between mutant RHOA and the RAP1GDS1607 isoform, is enhanced by T-cell receptor stimulation, and requires components of the T-cell receptor–VAV1 pathway, including PLCγ1 and calcineurin. Unlike canonical RAS superfamily signaling, this neomorphic activity does not require prenylation, the lipid modification anchoring RHOA to membranes. Genetic or pharmacological disruption of this pathway impairs RHOA-mutant PTCL in mouse models and patient-derived cells. These findings explain how mutations with opposing canonical effects converge on a shared oncogenic mechanism and reveal a potential therapeutic vulnerability in RHOA-mutant PTCL. RHOA mutation variants, exerting opposite effects on canonical RHOA signaling, are associated with peripheral T-cell lymphomas (PTCL). Here, the authors show that different RHOA mutants share a neomorphic activity that activates the transcription factor NFAT to drive PTCL.

https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-0.title: Deep learning model based on dynamic contrast-enhanced ultrasound to predict thyroid malignancy and BRAFV600E mutation
https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-0.abstract: To develop a video vision transformer (ViViT) model based on thyroid contrast-enhanced ultrasound (CEUS) video, applying it to distinguish malignant thyroid nodules and predict BRAFV600E mutation in papillary thyroid carcinoma (PTC). We retrospectively collected thyroid nodules with CEUS videos and divided them into training, validation, and testing sets in a ratio of 4:3:3. The ViViT-CEUS diagnostic model was developed and validated. Its performance was compared with two-dimensional convolutional neural networks (2D-CNN), three-dimensional convolutional neural networks (3D-CNN) and traditional radiomics models. Radiologists with different levels of clinical experience were served as the comparator group. 428 thyroid nodules were included (69 benign, 359 malignant). All malignant nodules were PTC, comprising 267 BRAFV600E mutated and 92 non-mutated cases. The AUC of ViViT-CEUS for diagnosing malignancy was 0.938, which was significantly higher than that of 2D-CNN (AUC = 0.767), 3D-CNN (AUC = 0.790), and radiologists (AUC range : 0.617–0.815). The AUC of ViViT-CEUS for predicting BRAFV600E was 0.865, outperforming 2D-CNN (AUC = 0.704), 3D-CNN (AUC = 0.597), and traditional radiomics models (AUC = 0.682). The ViViT-CEUS model demonstrated high accuracy in identifying malignant thyroid nodules and improved prediction of PTC BRAFV600E mutations compared to alternative methods, providing a basis for identifying molecular features based on dynamic CEUS videos.

https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-0.title: Prognostic significance of immunohistochemical expression of chemerin and CD34-assessed microvessel density in patients with oral squamous cell carcinoma
https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-0.abstract: Oral squamous cell carcinoma (OSCC), the most commonly diagnosed oral cancer, has a poor prognosis, especially in the advanced stages. Chemerin, an adipokine that plays a significant role in inflammation and adipogenesis, has emerged as a prognostic biomarker in OSCC. The study evaluates immunohistochemical expression of chemerin and CD34-assessed microvessel density, and investigates their association with clinicopathological parameters and disease-free survival (DFS) in OSCC patients. The study consisted of tissue sections from 184 histopathologically diagnosed cases of OSCC stained by immunohistochemistry for chemerin. Microvessel density (MVD) was assessed using the hotspot method based on CD34 immunostaining. For survival analysis, three separate Cox regression models were constructed for chemerin expression, CD34-assessed microvessel density, and a composite score combining both to assess their effect on DFS. Composite scoring was based on chemerin expression and MVD. Group 1 includes low chemerin + low MVD; Group 2: low chemerin + high MVD; Group 3: High chemerin + low MVD; Group 4: high chemerin + high MVD. Kaplan–Meier survival curves were used for survival analysis, and the Cox regression model for risk assessment. p < 0.05 was considered statistically significant. High chemerin expression was associated with advanced histopathological grade (p < 0.001) and TNM stage (III-IV) (p = 0.013), the presence of perineural invasion (p = 0.022), increased depth of invasion (> 5 mm) (p = 0.002), and tumor size (pT) (> 4 cm) (p = 0.016). A statistically significant positive correlation was observed between high chemerin expression and increased microvessel density (MVD), highlighting its role in tumor angiogenesis (p < 0.001). Advanced TNM stage (III-IV) was an independent predictor of reduced DFS in all three models. Model 1 involving chemerin showed significance only in the univariate analysis (p = 0.001). Whereas model 2, involving CD34-assessed MVD, showed statistical significance only in the univariate analysis (p = 0.007). In the multivariate analysis involving model 3, the composite groups (2–4) showed higher hazard ratios for reduced DFS than the reference group 1. Chemerin overexpression is associated with tumor angiogenesis, and its combined evaluation helped in improving the prognostic value compared to individual marker analysis. These findings suggest that chemerin, when combined with other prognostic biomarkers, can help with risk stratification in OSCC, which further require external validation.

https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-0.title: MAMDC2 suppresses gastric cancer cells but promotes progression through cancer associated fibroblasts
https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-0.abstract: Gastric cancer (GC) remains a leading cause of cancer-related mortality worldwide, and novel biomarkers and therapeutic targets are urgently needed. MAMDC2 has been implicated in several malignancies, but its biological function and cellular origin in GC remain largely unknown. We integrated bulk RNA-seq data from GEO and TCGA databases to evaluate the diagnostic and prognostic value of MAMDC2 in GC. Single-cell RNA sequencing and spatial transcriptomics were used to delineate its cellular origin within the tumor microenvironment. In vitro functional assays, including CCK-8, colony formation, flow cytometry, wound healing, and Transwell assays, were performed to assess the effects of MAMDC2 overexpression in GC cell lines. Conditioned medium (CM) experiments using MAMDC2-overexpressing fibroblasts were conducted to evaluate the paracrine effects of fibroblast-derived MAMDC2 on GC cell migration, invasion, and EMT-like changes. Western blotting was used to explore the underlying signaling pathways. MAMDC2 was downregulated in GC tissues and cell lines and showed diagnostic value. Clinically, high MAMDC2 expression was associated with poor overall survival and independently predicted adverse prognosis. Single-cell and spatial transcriptomic analyses consistently revealed that MAMDC2 is predominantly expressed in cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs) rather than in malignant epithelial cells. Functional experiments showed that forced MAMDC2 overexpression in GC cells suppressed proliferation, migration, and invasion while promoting apoptosis. Notably, conditioned medium from MAMDC2-overexpressing CAFs enhanced MGC-803 cell migration and invasion, accompanied by EMT-like marker changes (E-cadherin downregulation, Vimentin and N-cadherin upregulation), suggesting that CAF-derived MAMDC2 may promote GC progression in a paracrine manner. These paracrine findings are proof-of-concept, as they were obtained using one commercial CAF line and one recipient GC cell line. Western blotting further showed that MAMDC2 overexpression was associated with altered MAPK pathway activation, including decreased p-JNK and p-p38 and increased p-ERK, although these changes are correlative and require functional validation. MAMDC2 plays context-dependent roles in GC. At the cancer cell-autonomous level, MAMDC2 overexpression suppresses proliferation, migration, and invasion. However, MAMDC2 is predominantly expressed in CAFs, and CAF-derived MAMDC2 may promote GC cell migration, invasion, and EMT-like changes through paracrine signaling, offering a plausible explanation for the association between high MAMDC2 expression and poor prognosis. These findings suggest that MAMDC2 may act as a context-dependent regulator and a potential stromal-derived modulator of the GC microenvironment, rather than a classical cell-intrinsic tumor suppressor. Further validation using additional GC cell lines, primary CAFs, and in vivo models is warranted.

https://www.nature.com/articles/s41523-0.title: Hypermethylation in CpG-rich cfDNA fragments enables accurate detection of circulating tumor DNA in BRCA1- and BRCA2-associated breast and ovarian cancer
https://www.nature.com/articles/s41523-0.abstract: Pathogenic BRCA1 and BRCA2 germline variants confer an increased risk of hereditary breast and ovarian cancer (HBOC). In this high-risk cohort, novel biomarkers are needed to support patient management. While circulating cell-free DNA-based conventional CpG-level averaging is promising, it dilutes tumor-specific signals in samples with low circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) fractions. Here, we developed a targeted ultra-deep NGS assay for detecting tumor-derived ctDNA based on fragment-level hypermethylation of CpG-rich cfDNA. A panel of 360 cancer-specific CpG-rich regions derived from 450k methylation array datasets from TCGA breast cancer and GEO ovarian cancer, was applied to plasma from 31 breast cancer, 16 ovarian cancer patients, and 26 healthy controls using enzymatic methylation sequencing. Hypermethylated ctDNA (hm-ctDNA) fragments, were significantly enriched in cancer cases, identifying 62.5% of ovarian and 38.7% of breast cancers at 100% specificity. Elevated hm-ctDNA was observed across different tumor stages, with higher burden in BRCA1-associated cases. This approach enables highly specific, non-invasive hypermethylated ctDNA detection in HBOC populations.

https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-0.title: Suppression of epithelial proliferation and tumorigenesis by IgA
https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-0.abstract: Immunoglobulin A (IgA) is the most abundant antibody isotype produced by mammals, and has a specialized role in mucosal homeostasis1. IgA is constantly secreted into the intestinal lumen and binds to commensal microorganisms to regulate their colonization and function2,3, with unclear implications for health. IgA deficiency is common in humans, but difficult to study, because of its complex aetiology and comorbidities4–8. Here we use genetically and environmentally controlled mice to show that various models of IgA deficiency result in increased susceptibility to several models of endogenous colorectal cancer. Cellular and molecular analyses revealed that, in the absence of IgA, colonic epithelial cells induce antibacterial factors and accelerate cell cycling in response to the microbiota. Oral treatment with IgA was sufficient to reduce steady-state proliferation and protect mice from tumours; however, this function was due to the structure of the antibody rather than to binding specificity. In a reductionist culture system, IgA directly suppressed epithelial growth. Co-immunoprecipitation mass spectrometry and targeted CRISPR screening identified DMBT1 as an IgA-binding epithelial surface protein that is required for IgA-mediated suppression of proliferation. Together, IgA and DMBT1 tune the normal cycling of absorptive colonocyte progenitors. In IgA-knockout mice, deleting the transmembrane and cytoplasmic signalling portions of DMBT1 was sufficient to reverse both the increased epithelial cell proliferation and the increased tumour susceptibility seen in these mice. These experiments establish a homeostatic function for IgA in tempering physiological epithelial responses to the microbiota to maintain mucosal health. Experiments in mouse models show that immunoglobulin A in the gut lumen has a role in regulating the turnover of colon epithelial cells and reduces the susceptibility of mice to colorectal cancer.

https://www.nature.com/articles/s41588-0.title: Saturation genome editing of BRCA1 across cell types improves interpretation of variant pathogenicity
https://www.nature.com/articles/s41588-0.abstract: Germline pathogenic BRCA1 variants predispose women to breast and ovarian cancer. Despite accumulation of functional evidence, over half of reported single-nucleotide variants in BRCA1 lack a definitive clinical interpretation. Furthermore, the consistency of variant effects across cell types remains largely unexplored. Here we performed saturation genome editing (SGE) of BRCA1 in HAP1 cells to score 4,113 previously unassayed variants. Additionally, we developed an SGE assay in human mammary epithelial cells (HMECs), allowing comparison of effects across cell lines, drug treatments and genetic backgrounds. We identified 538 variants impacting gene function through distinct mechanisms. HAP1 function scores discriminate between known pathogenic and benign variants with near-perfect accuracy. Intriguingly, however, nearly half of HAP1 loss-of-function variants scored neutrally in HMECs. We show that discordantly scored variants are hypomorphic and confer intermediate cancer risk. Overall, this work demonstrates how performing SGE across cell models improves the functional interpretation of rare variants. Saturation genome editing maps the functional effects of thousands of BRCA1 variants across two complementary cell models. Discordantly scored variants reflect the importance of context and provide insights for improving BRCA1 variant interpretation.

https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-0.title: Mitochondrial protein import defects enhance tumour immunogenicity
https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-0.abstract: Tumour cells evade detection and elimination by the immune system through a suite of adaptations1, including the repression of antigen presentation, which is required for the recognition of tumour cells by CD8+ T cells. Mitochondria have emerged as targets for enhancing antitumour immunity; however, the extensive mitochondrial proteome has remained largely unstudied for its ability to modulate immune responses. Here we show that defects in the mitochondrial protein import machinery promote tumour immunogenicity and synergize with immune checkpoint blockade treatment in melanoma models. Mitochondrial protein import perturbation, specifically through depletion of the TIM23 import complex subunit TIMM50, enhances tumour immunogenicity through a pathway involving mitochondrial DNA escape, cGAS–STING pathway activation and interferon-β (IFNβ) secretion. Secreted IFNβ signals through the type I IFN receptor to activate the JAK–STAT pathway, resulting in increased antigen presentation on MHC class I complexes. Mitochondrial DNA escape in Timm50-depleted cells is linked to the formation of mitochondrial-derived vesicles. Depletion of SNX9 and RAB9, involved in mitochondrial-derived vesicle formation2, suppresses mitochondrial DNA-dependent type I IFN production and signalling. By disrupting mitochondrial proteostasis and membrane architecture, defective protein import in Timm50-depleted cells drives the immune phenotype. This study shows that mitochondrial protein import inhibition causes tumour immunogenicity, including sensitization to immune checkpoint blockade, by promoting mitochondrial DNA escape and IFNβ-driven MHC class I antigen presentation. Inhibition of mitochondrial protein import can enhance tumour immunogenicity by promoting mitochondrial DNA release.

https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.64898.title: Serum extracellular vesicle proteomics reveals treatment-associated biomarkers in pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma
https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.64898.abstract: Background Longitudinal biomarkers of treatment response in pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) are needed. Extracellular vesicle (EV)-enriched serum proteomics may provide a minimally invasive approach for monitoring systemic and tumor-associated responses to therapy. Methods Paired pre-treatment and post-treatment serum samples were analyzed from 51 patients with pancreatic cancer, including 25 treated with FOLFIRINOX and 20 treated with gemcitabine-based therapy. EVs were enriched using the Mag-Net method and profiled by data independent acquisition mass spectrometry. After batch correction and filtering, 941 proteins were retained for differential and pathway analyses. Paired linear models and gene set enrichment analyses were used to assess treatment-associated changes. Baseline protein abundance and longitudinal changes were evaluated in relation to overall survival (OS) using Cox models. Results A total of 2,089 EV-associated proteins were identified, with an average of 1,186 proteins quantified per sample. Across the cohort, 26 proteins differed between post- and pretreatment samples. Proteins that increased after treatment were primarily related to extracellular matrix organization and cell adhesion, whereas proteins that decreased after treatment were associated with actin cytoskeletal organization, coagulation, and hemostasis. Treatment-associated changes were more pronounced in the FOLFIRINOX group, in which 32 proteins were differentially expressed. FOLFIRINOX was characterized by coordinated reductions in platelet- and coagulation-associated proteins, including PF4, PF4V1, PPBP, GP5, ITGA2B, and ITGB3, accompanied by enrichment of platelet activation, coagulation, and hemostasis pathways among down-regulated processes. No individual proteins met the same significance threshold in the gemcitabine group. A composite seven-protein platelet score decreased significantly after FOLFIRINOX but not for gemcitabine, and the between-regimen difference in score change was significant. Higher pretreatment ITGB1 abundance was associated with longer OS after multiple-testing correction (HR, 0.112; BH-FDR = 0.0063). In multivariable analysis, greater treatment-associated platelet-score depletion was independently associated with shorter OS (HR per unit increase in {Delta}score, 0.56; P = 0.030). Conclusions Longitudinal serum EV-enriched proteomics identified treatment-associated biological changes in PDAC, including a coordinated platelet-related response predominantly observed after FOLFIRINOX. Baseline ITGB1 abundance and longitudinal platelet-score changes represent potentially complementary prognostic and pharmacodynamic markers. These findings are exploratory and require validation in larger, independent cohorts incorporating platelet counts, coagulation measurements, and targeted proteomic assays.

https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.64898.title: Genotype-Informed Drosophila Kinome Screening Prioritizes PRKX as a Candidate Vulnerability in Bladder Cancer
https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.64898.abstract: Muscle-invasive bladder cancer is molecularly heterogeneous, and the basal/squamous subtype frequently exhibits elevated EGFR expression and TP53 and RB1 alterations. Functional vulnerabilities associated with these alterations remain incompletely defined, while large-scale in vivo screening in mammalian models is experimentally demanding. Therefore, we developed a genotype-defined Drosophila melanogaster model combining Egfr overexpression, mutant p53, and Rbf suppression in Malpighian tubules. The resulting 3-hit model showed increased Malpighian tubule volume and reduced adult eclosion rate. A dominant modifier screen targeting 216 kinase genes identified 72 genes whose perturbation significantly increased the eclosion rate, and a complementary RNA interference screen identified eight kinases whose knockdown increased the eclosion rate. Among these hits, Pka-C3, which is a Drosophila ortholog of human PRKX, emerged as one of the strongest suppressors of the 3-hit phenotype. PRKX was prioritized for further study because public transcriptomic datasets showed higher PRKX expression in bladder tumors than in normal bladder tissue. PRKX knockdown reduced spheroid volume in four human bladder cancer cell lines with distinct EGFR, TP53, and RB1 profiles. Both small interfering RNAs produced significant reductions in two cell lines, whereas only one siRNA reached significance in the other two. These findings nominate PRKX as a candidate vulnerability in bladder cancer and highlight a cross-species approach that combines genotype-informed Drosophila screening with functional testing in human cancer cells to prioritize targets for further investigation.

https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.64898.title: The Phospholipase A2 Activity of Peroxiredoxin 6 Protects Hepatocarcinoma Cells Against Ferroptosis and Mitophagy Impairment
https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.64898.abstract: Peroxiredoxin 6 (PRDX6) is a moonlighting protein that plays a key role in regulating redox homeostasis and lipid metabolism through its unique dual peroxidase and calcium-independent phospholipase A2 (iPLA2) activities. Here, we generated a stable HepG2 cell line harboring a D140A mutation to selectively ablate iPLA2 activity, and we compared its phenotype with that of wild-type (WT) and PRDX6-knockout (KO) cells. D140A exhibited low ROS leves, similar to WT cells, confirming that oxidative stress is due to peroxidase deficiency. In contrast, D140A cells displayed higher lipid peroxidation than WT cells, though significantly lower than that of KO cells. Furthermore, the D140A mutant mirrored the KO phenotype regarding intracellular ferrous iron accumulation, impaired lipid droplet biogenesis, and the downregulation of the key ferroptosis regulator GPX4. Mechanistically, integrated proteomic, lipidomic, and enzymatic analyses revealed that a deficiency in iPLA2 activity of PRDX6 disrupted the release of key lipid species necessary for cell structure and signaling. Consequently, organelles involved in lipid synthesis and trafficking, such as peroxisomes, endoplasmic reticulum, mitochondria and lipid droplet, were affected. Specifically, we found that mitochondria exhibited a reduction in cristae and a diminished capacity for mitophagy and autophagy, which ultimately makes cells much more susceptible to erastin-induced ferroptotic cell death. Taken together, our findings demonstrate that PRDX6 iPLA2 activity uniquely coordinates organelle lipid homeostasis and mitophagy to protect cancer cells from ferroptotic cell death. Consequently, the use of iPLA2 inhibitors such as MJ33, which decreased PRDX6 iPLA2 activity to a level comparable to the mutant D140A, could represent a promising therapeutic strategy for inducing ferroptotic cell death in hepatocellular carcinoma.

https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.64898.title: BAF complexes cooperate with lineage-restricted transcription factors to establish cell-state-specific regulatory programs
https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.64898.abstract: BRG1/BRM-associated factor (BAF) complexes are essential regulators of chromatin organization and cell identity. Genes encoding BAF subunits are among the most frequently mutated in human cancer. Yet, how disruption of a single subunit gives rise to distinct tumor states remains poorly understood. Atypical teratoid rhabdoid tumors (ATRTs) provide a compelling model, as they are uniformly driven by bi-allelic loss of the BAF subunit SMARCB1, yet segregate into distinct molecular subtypes. Using integrated multi-omics profiling of patient-derived ATRT organoids and primary tumor tissues, we show that transcriptional and chromatin accessibility changes upon SMARCB1 reconstitution are directed by subtype- and lineage-specific transcription factor (TF) repertoires. Genome-wide binding and transcriptomic analyses reveal that SMARCB1 reconstitution enables the lineage-specific TF RFX4 to engage regulatory elements and activate neuronal differentiation programs, partially reprogramming ATRT-MYC toward an ATRT-SHH-like identity. Together, these findings demonstrate that SMARCB1 loss disrupts TF-dependent chromatin priming, revealing that the lineage-specific regulatory output of BAF complexes is constrained by the underlying TF repertoire.

https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.64898.title: Curvature-based schedule ordering is preserved in homogeneous and heterogeneous tumors
https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.64898.abstract: During treatment, dosing protocols with identical total dose may favor one schedule over another depending on how exposure is distributed over time. In homogeneous cell populations, Jensen's inequality has been shown to predict whether continuous or intermittent high-dose followed by low-dose is favored, based on the curvature of the concentration-effect function. Scheduling ordering can be performed based on curvature only: concave functions favor continuous dosing while convex functions favor intermittent dosing schedules with a high time-variance. However, tumors exhibit heterogeneous drug sensitivities, and treatment preferentially eliminates drug-sensitive cells, progressively shifting the surviving population toward greater drug resistance. Whether this treatment-induced selection can reverse curvature-based schedule ordering remains unclear. We develop a mathematical framework in which phenotypes share a common concentration-effect function but differ by fixed, nonnegative sensitivity scales. We prove that the ordering of equal-mean schedules is administrated solely by the scalar cumulative treatment effect, that is, by the curvature of the effect function alone. Consequently, baseline heterogeneity and treatment-induced selection can alter the magnitude of treatment response and the composition of surviving cells, but cannot reverse the ordering of equal-mean schedules predicted by the curvature of the single-cell concentration-effect function. This preservation holds across different temporal dosing profiles and repeated treatment cycles. Our work uncovers a general principle that curvature-based schedule ordering is preserved in heterogeneous tumors despite treatment-induced selection toward resistance.

https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.64898.title: Enhanced antitumour activity of combined PD-1 blockade and HER2-targeted therapy is associated with reduced epithelial-mesenchymal transition and extracellular matrix-remodelling signatures in gastric cancer
https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.64898.abstract: Background The combination of PD-1 blockade, HER2-targeted therapy and chemotherapy improves outcomes in HER2-positive advanced gastric and gastro-oesophageal junction adenocarcinoma. However, chemotherapy can independently alter the tumour microenvironment, making the biological effects of PD-1 and HER2 targeting difficult to distinguish. We therefore investigated how PD-1 and HER2 blockade, alone and in combination, affect tumour growth and associated transcriptional programmes. Methods Immunodeficient NOG mice received human PBMCs by tail-vein injection. Three days later, NCI-N87 gastric cancer cells were implanted subcutaneously. Mice were randomised to vehicle, pembrolizumab, trastuzumab, or combination treatment. Tumour growth was assessed, and bulk RNA sequencing was used to identify treatment-associated changes in gene expression, pathway enrichment, and tumour, stromal, and immune cell-associated signatures. Results Combined treatment produced greater tumour growth control than either monotherapy. Trastuzumab-treated tumours showed enrichment of immune activation, epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT), and TGF{beta}-associated signatures, whereas pembrolizumab alone produced a limited transcriptional effect. Combination treatment was associated with reduced proliferation, EMT, and stromal-remodelling signatures, alongside increased cytotoxic immune-associated signatures. Expression of extracellular matrix-associated genes, including VCAN, SPARC, POSTN, collagen genes, and FAP, was lower in combination-treated tumours. Complement-related transcriptional pathways were also enriched. Conclusions In this chemotherapy-free model, combined PD-1 blockade and HER2-targeted therapy was associated with greater tumour growth control, enrichment of cytotoxic immune-associated transcriptional signatures, and reduced EMT and extracellular matrix remodelling signatures. These findings provide hypotheses for further mechanistic validation.
